items.name: Thermodynamic headroom at point sources is small: real amine plants already run at ~27-40% second-law efficiency
items.mechanism: Comparison of OptiLex verifier minimum work (separation at 90% capture + isothermal compression to 110 bar) with measured or derived real energy use. Floors: coal flue (12%) 0.155 GJ/t separation, NGCC flue (4%) 0.219, cement (25%) 0.110, plus 0.23-0.26 GJ/t compression, so 0.37-0.48 GJ/t in total. Real plants: a reboiler duty of 2.4-3.6 GJ heat/t at 120-135C carries 0.58-0.97 GJ/t of exergy. Adding about 0.45 GJ_e/t for compression and auxiliaries gives 1.0-1.4 GJ_e-equivalent/t. Boundary Dam 3 lost 50 MW of net output (160 to 110 MW) at a design rate of 3,240 t/d, which is 1.33 GJ_e/t (0.37 MWh/t). At the 2025 operating rate of 2,826 t/d it is 1.53 GJ_e/t.
items.energy: Second-law efficiency: about 31% for BD3 (derived from the 50 MW derate, which also covers SO2 capture, so the true CO2-only efficiency is somewhat higher) and 33-47% for modern solvents (modelled). DAC, by comparison, runs at about 5-10%.
items.cost: Energy cost at the thermodynamic floor (sep + compression, all bought as electricity at $60/MWh) is $6-8/t. Real energy cost at BD3's derate is $15/t at $40/MWh, $22/t at $60/MWh and $37/t at $100/MWh. A perfect solvent therefore saves at most about $10-15/t of a $60-120/t total.
items.trl_and_scale: Amine post-combustion capture: TRL 9 (several plants at 0.5-1.4 Mt/yr)
items.potential: Energy savings are worth about 3x at most. Most of the cost sits in capex, availability, capacity factor and transport and storage. An idea engine should not spend its effort on finding a better solvent molecule.
items.bottleneck: Not thermodynamics. Capex per tonne and integration are the binding constraints.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4/S5: energy penalty is the visible complaint, but the derate is mostly capex-driven lost sales. S2: consistent with literature that point-source capture is near its practical efficiency.

items.name: Boundary Dam 3 (SaskPower, coal, Shell Cansolv amine, since Oct 2014): measured long-run performance
items.mechanism: Post-combustion amine scrubbing on a rebuilt 160 MW (net) lignite unit. Combined SO2 and CO2 capture, with CO2 sold for EOR and sulphuric acid sold as a by-product.
items.energy: Net output fell from 160 to 110 MW with CCS running, a 31% derate; SaskPower cites a parasitic load of about 21%. Reported reboiler duty for Cansolv is 2.4-3.2 GJ/t (vendor figure).
items.cost: About C$1.5bn total for the retrofit, including the power-island rebuild. Capex alone is about $1,100 per t/yr of capacity, or about $103/t annualised at design throughput and about $143/t at the 2025 actual throughput (my calc, 8%/25 yr; confound: the total includes the turbine rebuild).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9. Design rate 1 Mt/yr (about 3,240 t/d). 2025 measured: 721,239 t (72% of design). Q4 2025: 232,826 t, 99.3% availability, 2,826 t/d while online. Cumulative since 2014: 7,327,868 t, an average of about 0.65 Mt/yr over 11 years.
items.potential: Proves that amine capture on coal flue gas works for a decade. The emissions intensity of 348 t/GWh (Aug 2023-Aug 2024) implies roughly 76-80% capture while running (my back-calculation assuming 1.0-1.2 t/MWh unabated), against a 90% design.
items.bottleneck: Early-years availability: IEEFA estimated about 50% underperformance against capacity over the lifetime to 2022. Also flue-gas contaminants, fly ash fouling the absorber, and the capex of retrofitting a small unit.
items.permanence_or_durability: CO2 goes mainly to EOR at Weyburn, with some to the Aquistore saline storage site
items.stakeholder_positions: S5: SaskPower reports records. S1/IEEFA: cites it as a failure (target cut to about 65%). S6: kept a coal unit and its jobs running. S3: EOR buyer (Cenovus/Whitecap).

items.name: Petra Nova (W.A. Parish, Texas; MHI KM-CDR amine; 2017-2020, restarted Sept 2023)
items.mechanism: Amine capture on a 240 MW-equivalent slipstream of a coal unit. Steam and power come from a dedicated gas-fired cogeneration unit whose own emissions are not captured. The CO2 is sold for EOR at West Ranch.
items.energy: KM-CDR reboiler duty is about 2.6 GJ/t on a 10% CO2 feed (vendor figure)
items.cost: About $1.0bn capex, including a $195M DOE grant. That is about $714 per t/yr of design capacity, or $67/t annualised at design and $82/t at actual throughput (my calc).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9. Design 1.4 Mt/yr. Captured 3.8M short tons (about 3.45 Mt) in the first 3 years against 4.6M expected (about 83%). Capture averaged 92.4% while running. There were 367 outage days in 3 years, 88 of them caused by the second-hand cogeneration unit.
items.potential: Shows that capture above 90% is routine while the plant is online. Losses came from equipment around the capture plant and from the revenue model.
items.bottleneck: Revenue tied to oil prices through EOR: NRG mothballed the plant in May 2020 when oil prices collapsed. Uptime of auxiliaries was also a problem. This failure mechanism still applies to any EOR-dependent project.
items.permanence_or_durability: EOR storage; how much CO2 stays down depends on monitoring
items.stakeholder_positions: S3/S5: JX Nippon restarted it in 2023. S1 (energyandpolicy.org, IEEFA): cites it as proof CCS is a fossil subsidy. CATF (an NGO): 'six ways Petra Nova shows capture works'.

items.name: Gas processing and LNG reservoir CO2 (Sleipner since 1996, Snohvit, Gorgon): the capture step is cheap and mature, and storage is the binding constraint
items.mechanism: CO2 must be stripped from raw natural gas to meet sales specifications anyway (the stream is concentrated, often above 90%). The separated CO2 is then compressed and injected into saline aquifers.
items.energy: Near zero extra separation energy, because separation happens anyway for sales specifications. The cost is compression (floor about 0.23-0.26 GJ/t).
items.cost: IEA (2019) gives about $15-25/t for capture in gas processing. Gorgon's realized cost is about $200/t against $70/t originally estimated (press figure, per IEEFA).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9. Sleipner has run at about 1 Mt/yr since 1996. Gorgon FY2024-25: 1.33 Mt injected against 5.22 Mt of reservoir CO2 removed (25%). The approval condition was 80%, or about 4 Mt/yr.
items.potential: The cheapest tonnes are available today. IEEFA (2022) found Sleipner and Snohvit to be the two best performers of 13 flagship projects, helped by the Norwegian offshore CO2 tax since 1991.
items.bottleneck: Subsurface pressure management. Gorgon has to produce reservoir brine to inject CO2, and the brine handling and wells (sand, contaminants) limit injection. Chevron says the problems lie in produced-water handling rather than in capture.
items.permanence_or_durability: Saline aquifer storage; Sleipner has decades of seismic monitoring with no leakage reported
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: Chevron bought offsets for the shortfall. S7 (Western Australia): approval was conditional on 80%. S1/IEEFA: cites Gorgon as a flagship failure. S10: Gorgon is a stranded-cost risk example.

items.name: Brevik CCS (Heidelberg Materials, Norway; SLB Capturi amine; first cement-scale CCS, opened 18 June 2025) plus Northern Lights storage
items.mechanism: Amine capture on cement-kiln flue gas (about 20-25% CO2), with regeneration heat drawn largely from recovered kiln and compressor waste heat. The CO2 is liquefied, shipped and injected 2,600 m below the North Sea seabed (Northern Lights, first injection 25 Aug 2025).
items.energy: Waste heat integration covers much of the reboiler duty. Waste heat limits capture to about 50% of the plant's CO2, the share that can be served without new fuel. No published measured GJ/t was found.
items.cost: Longship, including about 10 years of operation, costs about NOK 34bn, of which about NOK 22bn is state grants. Heidelberg took on the capture-plant overruns in exchange for a larger upside share. Rough average: about $400/t if spread over 8 Mt (my undiscounted calc). Confound: first-of-a-kind, and the storage is sized for Phase 2.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 for cement. 400 kt/yr design, which is 50% of plant emissions. About 50 kt was shipped by end-2025 in 10 shipments. 90% performance was reported after 8 months (company claim). Northern Lights Phase 1 is 1.5 Mt/yr; Phase 2 (5 Mt/yr) has reached FID.
items.potential: Cement process CO2 (about 60% of cement emissions, from limestone) has no fuel-switch alternative, so CCS is the main route for this sector. The ship-based shared storage model lets small coastal emitters connect without a pipeline.
items.bottleneck: Capex and subsidy dependence. Capture is limited to the share waste heat can serve (50%). Cement buyers' willingness to pay a 'green' premium is untested.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4: Heidelberg is selling 'evoZero' net-zero cement. S7: Norway framed it as a 'global breakthrough'. S6: keeps cement jobs in place. S1: some NGOs accept CCS for cement only. S10: first non-recourse CCS debt (NZT/NEP, UK) signals growing comfort.

items.name: Cost of capture scales with CO2 concentration and with capacity factor
items.mechanism: Dilute flue gas means large absorbers and fans (capex), and capex is spread over the tonnes actually captured. NETL Rev 4A (Oct 2022, modelled, 2018$, 85% capacity factor, $10/t transport and storage assumed): cost of capture for an F-class NGCC with 90% capture fell from $80/t (Rev 4) to $61/t (updated Cansolv quotes). Moving to 95% capture leaves cost almost unchanged. Adding capture raises NGCC overnight cost by 100-104% (H-class) and supercritical PC by 64-66%.
items.energy: Higher capture rates are nearly free thermodynamically. The marginal minimum work from 90% to 99% capture is 0.28 GJ/t for coal, 0.35 for NGCC and 0.43 for a 1% stream (my calc).
items.cost: IEA (2019, modelled): gas processing and ethanol about $15-35/t; cement and power about $50-120/t. NETL NGCC $61/t holds only at 85% capacity factor. With 50-70% of cost fixed, it rises to $95-109/t at 40% capacity factor and $134-163/t at 25% (my sensitivity calc).
items.trl_and_scale: n/a (cost model)
items.potential: Prioritize concentrated, baseload sources first. Gas plants that cycle to balance renewables become expensive capture hosts.
items.bottleneck: Capacity factor. As renewables grow, gas plants run less, so capture capex is spread over fewer tonnes.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5: utilities want capture to be flexible. S7 (US DOE/NETL): reference costs used for 45Q. S2: NETL's figures are broadly consistent with IEAGHG's.

items.name: Quest (Shell, Alberta; ADIP-X capture on SMR hydrogen, since 2015): partial capture of the concentrated stream
items.mechanism: Captures the concentrated process CO2 from steam-methane-reformer syngas. The dilute furnace flue gas is not captured.
items.energy: Low separation work, because the syngas stream carries about 15-20% CO2 at pressure (verifier floor about 0.13 GJ/t)
items.cost: No public per-tonne figure was verified
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9. Design about 1 Mt/yr; 5 Mt captured in under 5 years (by 2020).
items.potential: Shows the 'cheap fraction first' pattern: Shell said the facility was designed to capture about a third of site CO2. Global Witness (2022, NGO analysis) computed 48% of the plant's CO2 captured, or 39% including upstream methane.
items.bottleneck: Furnace and utility flue gas (dilute) is left uncaptured, and the headline 'capture rate' refers to the treated stream, not the facility.
items.permanence_or_durability: Saline aquifer storage with an extensive monitoring programme
items.stakeholder_positions: S1 (Global Witness): 'emits more than it captures'. S3 (Shell): analysis 'simply wrong', and the Polaris successor targets more than 90%. This shows the dispute is about accounting boundaries, not physics.

items.name: Ethanol fermentation CO2 (ADM Decatur, Illinois Basin): near-zero separation work, with risk moving to storage
items.mechanism: Fermentation off-gas is about 99% CO2, so it only needs drying and compression. It is injected into the Mt. Simon sandstone (EPA Class VI well).
items.energy: Compression only, about 0.23-0.26 GJ/t minimum (about 100 kWh/t real)
items.cost: IEA (2019): ethanol capture about $15-35/t, the cheapest industrial source
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9, about 1 Mt/yr scale
items.potential: High-purity biogenic CO2 gives negative emissions (BECCS) at the lowest cost per tonne.
items.bottleneck: Storage integrity and social licence. In 2024 EPA issued a notice of violation for fluid migration into an unauthorized zone (about 5,000 ft) caused by monitoring-well corrosion. ADM paused injection on 27 Sept 2024. Residents largely learned of it from the press.
items.permanence_or_durability: EPA found no drinking-water threat. Class VI rules require monitoring for 50 years after injection.
items.stakeholder_positions: S11: Mahomet Aquifer groups oppose injection. S4 (ADM): paused and remediating. S7 (EPA): enforcement. S1: uses the incident as evidence against CCS.

items.name: Waste-to-energy CCS (Hafslund Celsio Klemetsrud, Oslo): first-of-a-kind cost escalation
items.mechanism: Amine capture on incinerator flue gas (partly biogenic, so partly BECCS)
items.energy: Not reported
items.cost: Initial capex was NOK 5.5bn. It was paused in April 2023 at about NOK 10.5bn. After redesign it is capped at NOK 9.5bn (about $0.9bn) for about 0.35-0.4 Mt/yr. That is about $2,250 per t/yr, or about $211/t annualised capex alone (my calc, 8%/25 yr).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 8-9. Start of operation slipped from 2026 to Q3 2029.
items.potential: Waste incineration is an unavoidable, partly biogenic urban source, and the project could earn CDR credits.
items.bottleneck: Inflation, supplier pricing and currency drove a 70-90% capex escalation before construction
items.stakeholder_positions: S7 (Oslo municipality, Gassnova): co-funders. S10: cost escalation is the key risk. S1: generally supportive of BECCS from waste.

items.name: Oxy-combustion / Allam cycle (NET Power Project Permian, about 300 MW)
items.mechanism: Burns gas in oxygen with a supercritical CO2 working fluid, so CO2 leaves as a near-pure pressurized stream. There is no separation step; the energy cost moves to the air separation unit.
items.energy: Air separation unit oxygen production is the main parasitic load. A 50 MWth La Porte demo has operated; no utility-scale measured efficiency exists yet.
items.cost: Project Permian estimate rose from $750-950M to $1bn (Nov 2023) and then to $1.7-2.0bn (2025 FEED). Long-lead purchases are paused for value engineering.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 6-7. 50 MWth demo; the first utility plant's earliest start is now 2029.
items.potential: Inherently close to 100% capture with no flue-gas scrubbing.
items.bottleneck: Capex, and the first-of-a-kind turbo-machinery and combustor.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: backed by Occidental, Baker Hughes and Constellation. S10: share price fell on the cost update. S1: sceptical.

items.name: Direct separation / calcium looping for cement and lime process CO2 (Calix Leilac)
items.mechanism: Indirectly heated calciner. Limestone is heated through a steel wall, so process CO2 leaves pure and undiluted by combustion gas. No solvent is needed, and fuel CO2 is handled separately or electrified.
items.energy: Separation work is near zero for the process CO2. Calcium looping retrofits on power plants are modelled at an efficiency penalty of 6-8 percentage points (no recent measured GJ/t was found).
items.cost: Not published
items.trl_and_scale: Leilac-1 pilot at Lixhe (Belgium). Leilac-2 moved from Hannover to Ennigerloh (Germany) and will capture up to 100 kt/yr of process CO2. Construction began in 2025 and commissioning is expected mid-2026, followed by a 3-year test before ownership transfer.
items.potential: Process CO2 is about 60% of cement emissions. Combined with electric heating, it could remove the need for a dilute-gas scrubber.
items.bottleneck: Scale-up of high-temperature indirect heat transfer. Fuel CO2 still needs another solution.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4: Heidelberg JV partner. S2: reduces the solvent-energy problem.

items.name: Solid sorbents (Svante MOF/structured-sorbent filters)
items.mechanism: Rapid temperature-swing adsorption on thin structured sorbent sheets coated with MOFs or similar materials. This allows short cycles and small contactors, attacking capex directly.
items.energy: No independent measured GJ/t was found at commercial scale
items.cost: A $145M filter gigafactory in Burnaby opened May 2025, with capacity to make filters for up to 10 Mt/yr of capture (company claim)
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 6-7. CO2MENT at Lafarge Richmond started at about 1 t/d. Deployments are planned at Chevron Kern River and with GE Vernova for gas plants.
items.potential: Smaller contactors could cut the capex-dominated cost, the binding constraint identified above.
items.bottleneck: Sorbent lifetime under SOx, NOx and water, and the gap from a 1 t/d demo to Mt/yr scale
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 (Chevron): investor and host. S4 (Holcim/Lafarge): host. S10: venture-backed.

items.name: Membranes (MTR Polaris) and cryogenic (SES/Chart CCC): pilots in the tens to 150 t/d range
items.mechanism: Membranes: pressure-driven selective permeation, using electricity only. Cryogenic: cools flue gas until CO2 desublimates as a solid, also electricity only.
items.energy: Electrically driven, so no steam is needed. No independent measured GJ/t was found at pilot scale.
items.cost: Not published at scale
items.trl_and_scale: MTR's 150 t/d large pilot at the Wyoming ITC (Dry Fork coal station) completed long-duration testing in 2025. SES/Chart's 30 t/d engineering-scale plant at the Sugar Creek, Missouri cement plant has been extended to May 2026. A 30 t/d cryogenic pilot is planned at NEOM/SEC Duba.
items.potential: Electric-only capture suits plants with no spare steam. Membranes suit higher-concentration streams (cement, steel). Cryogenic capture can also remove SOx and NOx.
items.bottleneck: Membranes need compression or vacuum and are weak at 4% CO2. Cryogenic capture needs heat exchangers that tolerate frosting. Neither has reached 1 Mt/yr.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5 (Basin Electric) and S4 (Eagle Materials): hosts. S7 (US DOE): co-funding.

items.name: Electrochemical capture (e.g. Verdox) for very dilute industrial streams
items.mechanism: Redox-active electrodes bind CO2 when charged and release it when discharged. It is electricity-driven with no heat, and suits roughly 1% streams where amines are poor.
items.energy: Verifier floor at 1% CO2 and 90% capture: 0.30 GJ/t (my calc). No measured kWh/t was published.
items.cost: Not published
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 5-6. A 2-month trial on Hydro Sunndal aluminium smelter off-gas (about 1% CO2) reported no contaminant impact (2025-26, company claim).
items.potential: Aluminium smelters (about 1% CO2) are hard to decarbonize with any existing method.
items.bottleneck: Electrode durability, and cost per m2 of electrode at Mt scale
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (Hydro): host. S10: VC-funded ($80M raised in 2022).

items.name: Deployment and policy state (GCCSI 2025; US 45Q under OBBBA; UK NZT Power)
items.mechanism: Policy drives deployment. US 45Q pays $85/t for point-source storage. OBBBA (signed 3-4 July 2025) gave EOR and utilization the same $85/t as dedicated storage, up from $60. UK NZT Power (742 MW CCGT, Cansolv, up to 2 Mt/yr) reached FID in Dec 2024 with the first non-recourse CCS debt. The EU-UK ETS linkage is under way.
items.energy: n/a
items.cost: 45Q at $85/t sits above the NETL NGCC cost of capture ($61/t at 85% capacity factor) plus $10/t transport and storage, but below most first-of-a-kind realized costs
items.trl_and_scale: In July 2025, 77 facilities were operating with 64 Mtpa of capacity (up 25% year on year), about 0.17% of 37.4 Gt of fossil CO2. A further 47 facilities (44 Mtpa) are in construction, and 513 Mtpa is in the total pipeline. GCCSI says gigatonne goals will not be met even if the whole pipeline is built.
items.potential: Policy is now durable in the US, Norway, the UK and the EU. The pipeline is growing about 30% per year in planned capacity.
items.bottleneck: Even with the full pipeline, capacity is about 1.4% of fossil CO2. Capacity also differs from realized capture (BD3 at 72%, Gorgon at 25-30%).
items.permanence_or_durability: EOR parity raises questions about how much CO2 stays stored
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: wins from EOR parity. S1: opposes EOR credits as subsidizing oil. S7 (US): bipartisan survival of 45Q. S10: first project finance for CCS.

bottlenecks: Capex per tonne, not energy: realized capture capex is $700-2,250 per t/yr of capacity (Petra Nova 2017 about $714; BD3 2014 about $1,100 including the unit rebuild; Klemetsrud 2029 about $2,250). That is about $67-211/t annualised at 8%/25 yr, against an energy cost of only $15-25/t at the BD3 derate and $6-8/t at the thermodynamic floor (my calcs).

Capacity factor and availability: NETL's $61/t (2018$) for NGCC assumes 85% capacity factor. It rises to about $95-109/t at 40% and $134-163/t at 25% (my sensitivity calc, 50-70% fixed-cost share). Petra Nova lost 367 of about 1,095 days to outages, 88 of them from its cogeneration unit.

Subsurface storage and monitoring: Gorgon injected only 1.33 of 5.22 Mt of reservoir CO2 in FY2024-25 (25%, against 80% required) because of reservoir pressure and produced-water handling. At ADM Decatur a monitoring well corroded, fluid migrated into an unauthorized zone, and injection was paused (Sept 2024).

Revenue model fragility: Petra Nova (EOR-dependent) was mothballed in May 2020 when oil prices collapsed. Projects depend on 45Q ($85/t), the EU ETS and state grants (Longship: about NOK 22bn of NOK 34bn).

First-of-a-kind cost escalation: Klemetsrud went from NOK 5.5bn to about 10.5bn and back down to a 9.5bn cap, with start-up delayed from 2026 to 2029. NET Power Permian went from $0.75-0.95bn to $1.7-2.0bn, with start-up in 2029 at the earliest.

Partial capture boundaries: plants capture the cheap concentrated fraction. Quest was designed for about a third of site CO2 (Shell) or 48% (Global Witness), and Brevik covers 50% of plant CO2 because that is what waste heat can serve. Headline capture rates refer to the treated stream.
Scale gap: 64 Mtpa was operating in July 2025, about 0.17% of 37.4 Gt of fossil CO2. The whole 513 Mtpa pipeline is about 1.4%. Realized capture is also below nameplate (BD3 2025: 72%).
open_problems: Flexible, low-capex capture for cycling gas plants. Combine a conventional amine core with one imported mechanism: solvent or thermal storage (from grid balancing) so that regeneration runs on cheap surplus renewable power through an electric reboiler or heat pump. Test it with a capacity-factor-aware cost model against NETL Rev 4A.

A waste-heat-matching atlas. The Brevik model sizes capture to the available low-grade heat, which caps it at 50%. Systematically pair industrial waste heat (and cheap heat pumps) with capture regeneration across cement, steel, refineries and incinerators, and compute the extra capture fraction achievable before new fuel is needed.

Capex compression: process intensification such as rotating packed beds, structured sorbents and modular factory-built absorbers. Because thermodynamic headroom is only about 3x, every dollar of solvent research and development should be checked against the capex lever.

Storage-side engineering: co-optimizing brine production and pressure management (the Gorgon failure mode), monitoring-well integrity (ADM), and shared ship-based storage hubs for small coastal emitters (Northern Lights).

A whole-facility capture-fraction accounting standard. It would end the S1-versus-S3 disputes (Quest: 'a third by design' against '48%') and let buyers of low-carbon cement and hydrogen verify claims.

Rank and prioritize the 'cheap tonnes' first: gas processing, ethanol, ammonia and SMR process streams at about $15-35/t (IEA 2019). Build a global inventory of high-concentration streams within reach of storage. The size of this inventory was not computed here.

Very dilute industrial streams (aluminium smelters at about 1% CO2): check whether electrochemical or membrane-hybrid approaches can beat amines on capex. The thermodynamic floor is only 0.30 GJ/t, so this too is a capex problem.
Revenue de-risking: contracts for difference (as in the UK), CO2 offtake contracts, and premiums for green cement or steel, to replace EOR exposure to oil prices.

key_claims.claim: Point-source amine capture is already about 27-40% second-law efficient, and capex dominates its cost. Boundary Dam 3 (coal, Cansolv) captured 721,239 t in 2025 (72% of its 1 Mt/yr design; Q4 availability 99.3%; 2,826 t/d while online; 7.33 Mt cumulative since 2014) at a net derate of 160 to 110 MW. That derate implies about 1.3-1.5 GJ_e/t, against a verifier floor of about 0.42 GJ/t for separation plus compression. Better solvents can save at most about $10-15/t; capex, capacity factor and storage are the levers.

NETL Rev 4A (Oct 2022, modelled, 2018$): NGCC F-class 90% capture costs $61/t captured at an 85% capacity factor, almost unchanged at 95% capture. Capture adds 100-104% to H-class NGCC overnight cost. The cost therefore depends heavily on capacity factor, reaching about $95-109/t at 40% (my sensitivity calc), which matters as gas plants cycle around renewables.

surprises: The biggest flagship shortfalls were mostly not capture-chemistry failures. Gorgon was limited by storage and brine handling, ADM Decatur by monitoring-well corrosion, and Petra Nova by its second-hand gas cogeneration unit and oil prices. Petra Nova's capture averaged 92.4% while running.

Thermodynamics makes high capture rates nearly free. The marginal minimum work from 90% to 99% is only 0.28 GJ/t for coal flue and 0.43 GJ/t even for a 1% stream, and NETL finds 95% capture costs almost the same as 90%. Low real capture fractions are a matter of design and economic choice, not physics.

Point-source capture (about 30-40% second-law efficient) is already 3-8x closer to its thermodynamic floor than DAC (about 5-10%). An idea engine hunting energy efficiency at point sources is fishing in a small pond.

The 2025 OBBBA raised the EOR and utilization credit to the same $85/t as dedicated storage. This aligns oil and gas (S3) with capture but is likely to deepen S1 opposition, since it subsidizes oil production.

After 11 years, BD3's 2025 output was among its best yet still 72% of nameplate. The emissions intensity of 348 t/GWh implies only about 76-80% capture while running (my back-calculation), against a 90% design.
Shell itself says Quest was designed to capture only about a third of site CO2. The Global Witness-versus-Shell fight is over accounting boundaries, not measurement.

Boundary Dam 3 (coal, Cansolv) captured 721,239 t in 2025 (72% of its 1 Mt/yr design; Q4 availability 99.3%; 2,826 t/d while online; 7.33 Mt cumulative since 2014) at a net derate of 160 to 110 MW. That derate implies about 1.3-1.5 GJ_e/t, against a verifier floor of about 0.42 GJ/t for separation plus compression. Better solvents can save at most about $10-15/t; capex, capacity factor and storage are the levers.
verifs.corrected_claim: SaskPower's Q4 2025 BD3 update (primary source) reports that the CCS facility captured 721,239 t of CO2 in calendar 2025. That is about 72% of the commonly cited 1 Mt/yr nameplate (Wikipedia; the SaskPower post does not give a design figure). In Q4 2025 the facility captured 232,826 t, was available 99.3% of the time, and averaged 2,826 t/d while online. Cumulative capture since 2014 is 7,327,868 t (about 7.33 Mt). Those capture numbers are measured. The MW and energy figures are not in the source. BD3 is about 160 MW gross. SaskPower states about 115 MW net; Wikipedia gives 110 MW, down from 139 MW net before the retrofit. That 45-50 MW gross-to-net gap is not a pure capture derate: it also covers the station's normal auxiliary load, which every coal unit has, and SO2 capture, since Cansolv captures SO2 and CO2 together. The full 45-50 MW at 2,826-3,240 t/d works out to about 1.2-1.5 GJ_e/t, and that is an upper bound on the electricity used by CO2 capture plus compression. The CO2-only share is lower, roughly 1.0-1.3 GJ_e/t if 10-15 MW of normal auxiliary load is excluded. The ~0.42 GJ/t floor is the project's own modelled estimate (verifier): roughly 0.15-0.17 GJ/t minimum separation work at 90% capture from about 12% CO2, plus about 0.3 GJ/t isothermal compression to around 150 bar. The second-law efficiency of 27-40% and the cap of about $10-15/t on solvent savings are derived estimates, not from the source.
verifs.caveats:
1. The SaskPower source only supports the capture numbers: 721,239 t in 2025, 232,826 t in Q4, 99.3% availability, 2,826 t/d while online, and 7,327,868 t cumulative. It contains no design capacity, no MW figures and no energy-penalty data. The 1 Mt/yr nameplate and 160/110 MW come from Wikipedia and general literature. SaskPower's own project page gives 115 MW net, not 110.
2. 99.3% and 2,826 t/d are Q4 2025 figures only, not full-year 2025. Full-year capture averaged only about 1,976 t/d (721,239 / 365), so annual availability was well below 99.3%. The 72% is a capacity factor against nameplate, not availability.
3. "160 to 110 MW" compares gross output with net output, so it is not a capture derate. A non-capture coal unit also loses about 7-10% to auxiliaries, and BD3's figure also includes SO2 capture. The 139→110 MW pre/post comparison is not a clean capture derate either, because the turbine was replaced (139 MW net before vs a new 160 MW gross unit after). So 1.3-1.5 GJ_e/t overstates the electricity attributable to CO2 capture. The resulting 27-40% second-law estimate (0.42 / 1.0-1.5) is a rough, modelled bound. It depends on that attribution and on whether steam extraction is counted as electricity-equivalent.
4. BD3 has historically run below design: about 65-70% capture rate and many outages in earlier years. A single strong quarter should not be used as typical performance.
5. "Capex dominates" and "better solvents save at most $10-15/t" are not supported by this source. They need their own citations, for example the NETL/IEAGHG cost breakdowns.

verifs.claim: NETL Rev 4A (Oct 2022, modelled, 2018$): NGCC F-class 90% capture costs $61/t captured at an 85% capacity factor, almost unchanged at 95% capture. Capture adds 100-104% to H-class NGCC overnight cost. The cost therefore depends heavily on capacity factor, reaching about $95-109/t at 40% (my sensitivity calc), which matters as gas plants cycle around renewables.
verifs.corrected_claim: NETL Bituminous Baseline Rev 4A (DOE/NETL 2023/4320, dated 14 Oct 2022; a modelled greenfield techno-economic study, not measured plant data; real 2018$; 85% capacity factor; Shell CANSOLV solvent) puts the cost of CO2 captured for an F-class NGCC at 90% capture at $60.7/t, about $61/t. This excludes CO2 transport and storage. At 95% capture the F-class figure is $59.9/t, so slightly lower and effectively unchanged. The H-class figures are $55.9/t (90%) and $55.2/t (95%). Cost of CO2 avoided, which includes transport and storage, is higher: about $81/t for F-class and $75/t for H-class. Capture raises H-class total overnight cost per kW net by 100% at 90% capture ($970 to $1,936/kW) and by 104% at 95% ($970 to $1,980/kW). For F-class the increase is 115-120%. NETL reports only an LCOE-vs-capacity-factor sensitivity, not a cost-of-capture one. Scaling the capital and fixed LCOE components by 85/CF in NETL's own LCOE breakdown gives about $99-110/t captured at 40% CF: H-class 95% about $99, H-class 90% about $100, F-class 95% about $108, F-class 90% about $110. That is roughly $72-79/t at 60% CF. The claimed range of $95-109/t at 40% is therefore slightly low at the bottom end.
verifs.caveats:
The figures were checked against the full Rev 4A report as well as the newsletter. Downloaded from netl.doe.gov/projects/files/CostandPerformanceBaselineforFossilEnergyPlantsVolume1BituminousCoalandNaturalGastoElectricity_101422.pdf: Exhibit ES-8 for the costs, Exhibit ES-15 for 97% capture, Section 5 text on TOC and cost of capture, and Section 2.5.6.

1. **What the newsletter supports.** The cited SSAE newsletter (Nov 2022) supports only the $61/t figure, "relatively unchanged" at 95%, 2018$ and 85% CF. The 100-104% TOC increase comes from the report itself, Exhibit ES-8. Section 5 states "The TOC penalty for adding 90 percent CO2 capture in the H-frame case is 100 percent and is 115 percent in the F-frame case."

2. **Cost captured vs cost avoided.** $61/t is cost captured with transport and storage excluded, measured against the matching no-capture NGCC. It is not cost avoided, which is $75-81/t including transport and storage. Comparing it with DAC or carbon prices needs that distinction.

3. **The TOC increase is per kW net.** Part of it reflects the roughly 12% net output lost to capture (727 to 645 MW for F-class), not just the cost of the capture equipment.

4. **Rev 4A assumes the same CF with and without capture.** It assumes 85% for both (Sec 2.5.6). It also says its CF curves assume lower CF does not lower capital or operating costs. A simple 1/CF scaling, mine and the user's, ignores:
   - the part-load heat-rate penalty
   - cycling and start-up wear
   - solvent and capture-unit turndown limits

   These push the real cost at low CF higher, so the 40% numbers are a rough lower bound, not NETL figures. Treat them as the user's own derived calculation.

5. **Age and scope.** Costs are in 2018$, before the 2021-23 capital cost inflation. Applying them today means escalating them; current EPC costs are materially higher. The study models nth-of-a-kind greenfield plants. Retrofits and first-of-a-kind plants cost more.

6. **Very high capture rates.** NETL notes that rates of 95% and above lack operating experience. The 97% cases appear only in an appendix: $60.2/t F-class and $55.5/t H-class.

title: Direct air capture and ocean CO2 removal

items.name: Climeworks Mammoth and Orca: delivered net removal against nameplate (solid amine TVSA, Iceland, geothermal power, Carbfix storage)
items.mechanism: An amine-functionalised solid sorbent adsorbs CO2 from fan-driven air. It is regenerated at about 80-100 C under vacuum, and the CO2 is mineralised underground by Carbfix.
items.energy: Nominal company-stated Gen2 figures (secondary source) are 2,000 kWh_th/t of low-grade heat plus 650 kWh_e/t, or 9.54 GJ/t. That is 4.9% second-law efficiency on an energy basis and 12.3% on an exergy basis (OptiLex calculation). For Mammoth, CEO Wurzbacher said up to 5,000-6,000 kWh/t (reported May 2025 by Heimildin). That is 18-21.6 GJ/t, about 2.2-2.6% efficiency on an energy basis.
items.cost: Climeworks website about $1,000/t (2025, cited by Redd Monitor). Operating cost per tonne at Mammoth fell by more than 50% over the year to H1 2026; the absolute figure was not disclosed. 2030 target is $250-350/t captured and $400-600/t net (Gen3 announcement, June 2024; a claim).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 7-8, first commercial scale. Mammoth nameplate is 36,000 t/yr (started May 2024). Measured net removal was 119 t in H1 2025 (0.66% of nameplate annualised) and 675 t in H1 2026 (3.75%). Puro audit periods give Mammoth 278.3 net CORCs for Mar-Aug 2025 (1.55% annualised) and Orca 357.6 for May-Aug 2025 (about 27% of its 4,000 t/yr). Only 12 of 72 planned collector containers were operating in 2025.
items.permanence_or_durability: Mineralisation in basalt (Carbfix), effectively permanent (more than 10,000 yr).
items.bottleneck: Real-world sorbent capacity and cycling in cold, humid air, plus mechanical reliability. Upgraded containers capture more than twice the original configuration, but the plant still runs below 4% of nameplate.
items.potential: Proves the integrated chain end to end. Throughput per unit of capex is roughly 25x below design, so cost per tonne depends almost entirely on raising utilisation.
items.stakeholder_positions: S1/S8 critics point out that company emissions (1,700 t in 2023) exceeded removals (Heimildin). S10 buyers (Microsoft and others) are still contracting. S7 Iceland is supportive through its geothermal and Carbfix ecosystem.

items.name: Where the gap to the 0.47 GJ/t floor is lost: exergy accounting for DAC
items.mechanism: Second-law analysis divides the minimum work (separation 0.465 GJ/t at 75% capture, plus 0.28 GJ/t isothermal compression to 150 bar) by the exergy actually consumed. The breakdown attributes the destroyed exergy to each component.
items.energy:
Long-Innes and Struchtrup (Cell Rep Phys Sci, 2022) analyse Carbon Engineering's 1 Mt/yr design. It uses 273.2 MW of work potential, destroys 252 MW, and has a second-law efficiency of 7.8%. The losses are:
- chemical exergy dissipated as low-grade heat in the contactor and elsewhere: 39.4%
- calciner: 25.0%
- CCGT: 16.4%
- steam turbine: 4.4%
- air separation unit: 4.1%
- compression: 3.9%
- fans: only 3.7%
- water knockout: 3.1%
The paper's separation floor is 20.48 kJ/mol (465 MJ/t), which matches OptiLex's verifier. OptiLex calculation for Climeworks nominal Gen2: 3.79 GJ/t of exergy, of which electricity is 62% (the 100 C heat has a Carnot factor of only 0.20). The Gen3 claim of half the energy would put exergy efficiency at about 25%.
items.cost: Not costed. Energy at the floor costs only about $6/t at $50/MWh.
items.trl_and_scale: Analysis of a design (Keith et al., Joule 2018: 8.81 GJ gas/t, or 5.25 GJ gas + 366 kWh/t, CO2 delivered at 15 MPa, modelled levelised cost $94-232/t).
items.bottleneck: Strong sorbents (KOH/CaCO3 loop, amines at about 75 kJ/mol) bind CO2 with 3.5-9x more enthalpy than the roughly 20 kJ/mol free-energy floor. Most of that binding energy is then thrown away as heat. Fans are not the main loss in liquid systems.
items.potential: Raising second-law efficiency from about 8% to 25% would cut DAC energy roughly 3x, to about 2 GJ/t. At that level 1 Gt/yr needs about 0.3% of world primary energy.
items.stakeholder_positions: S2 scientists cite these numbers. S3 (Oxy, owner of Carbon Engineering) argues gas-fired designs can be decarbonised with CCS.

items.name: Temperature-swing regeneration heat budget: sensible heat and water co-desorption dominate
items.mechanism: Each cycle heats sorbent, support and structure from about 25 to 100 C and desorbs co-adsorbed water. Both cost far more than the CO2 heat of adsorption.
items.energy: OptiLex illustrative model (assumed cp 1.2 J/gK, deltaT 75 K, adsorption heat 75 kJ/mol, water at 44 kJ/mol) gives 3.7 GJ_th/t in the best case: working capacity 2 mmol/g, no extra heated mass, 1 mol H2O per mol CO2. It gives 19 GJ_th/t in the worst case: 0.5 mmol/g, 3x heated mass, 5 H2O/CO2. The sensible-heat term alone is 45-540 kJ/mol CO2. The CO2 heat of adsorption alone (about 75 kJ/mol) is 3.7x the 20.5 kJ/mol floor. Literature TVSA minimum specific energy ranges from 6.25 to 30.4 MJ_th/kg, as returned in a search result whose source paper was not identified. Moisture-swing resins report about 32 kJ/mol sorption heat (Lackner, AIChE talk).
items.cost: Heat at about $20/MWh_th adds roughly $40/t for 2,000 kWh_th/t.
items.trl_and_scale: Physics of the mechanism; the parameters are assumptions, not measured plant data.
items.permanence_or_durability: Oxidative degradation of amine sorbents during hot, humid, O2-containing regeneration cuts capacity. TEA models suggest viable costs need very long sorbent lifetimes, with figures from 10,000 cycles to 90% capacity up to hundreds of thousands of cycles (USPTO/AIChE 2025 summaries).
items.bottleneck: Working capacity, the thermal mass of the structure, and H2O/CO2 selectivity under humid conditions. Sorbent lifetime is linked to regeneration temperature.
items.potential: Non-thermal swings (moisture, electrochemical, pH) avoid the sensible-heat term entirely, which is the largest lever an idea engine can test.
items.stakeholder_positions: S2 consensus that regeneration takes 70-90% of DAC energy. Materials ML datasets such as Open DAC 2025 (Meta and Georgia Tech) target sorbent discovery.

items.name: Cost structure: capital and utilisation, not thermodynamics, set the price; implications for curtailed-power and intermittent DAC
items.mechanism: Levelised cost per tonne = annualised capex / (nameplate x capacity factor) + energy + O&M + storage. Running only on curtailed power cuts the capacity factor.
items.energy: Energy cost at $50/MWh is $6/t at the floor, $57/t for Gen2 with heat priced at 25% of electricity, and $132/t for Gen2 if all energy were bought as electricity (OptiLex calculation).
items.cost: Stratos has about $1.3bn total project cost for a 500 kt/yr design (BlackRock $550M JV, reported Nov 2023), or about $2,600 per t/yr. At a 10% capital recovery factor (CRF) the capital charge is $274/t at 95% capacity factor (CF), $433/t at 60% and $867/t at 30% (OptiLex calculation). Oxy's 2023 cost estimate for Stratos was $400-500/t with an Nth-plant target of $150/t. Young et al. (One Earth, 2023) model about $230-540/t at Gt scale and conclude stated targets are unlikely to be met.
items.trl_and_scale: Analysis of announced and modelled capex; no audited plant cost per tonne is public.
items.bottleneck: Capex per t/yr of capacity multiplied by utilisation. Mammoth's 3.75% utilisation makes its effective capital charge per tonne enormous.
items.potential: Ideas that store the swing rather than electricity (charge sorbent or heat when power is cheap, regenerate later) could decouple capex from intermittency. Passive or slow contactors with cheap capex per tonne-year also qualify.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5 utilities like DAC as flexible load. S10 investors focus on capex risk. S1 sceptics cite cost.

items.name: 1PointFive Stratos (Oxy; KOH liquid solvent / Carbon Engineering design), Texas
items.mechanism: KOH solution captures CO2 as carbonate. It is causticised to CaCO3 and calcined at about 900 C, and the CO2 is compressed for Class VI storage (and, under 45Q, EOR parity).
items.energy: No measured data. Design basis is Keith 2018 (8.81 GJ/t gas-only). The calcination heat floor alone is 178 kJ/mol = 4.04 GJ/t.
items.cost: About $1.3bn project. 45Q pays $180/t for DAC (OBBBA, July 2025, with parity for utilisation/EOR). Bain bought 9,000 t over 3 years.
items.trl_and_scale: Phase 1 commissioning was delayed by a 'non-process component' issue (May 2026). Oxy said the core technology performed as expected and later guided to operations toward end-2026. Design capacity is 500 kt/yr (about 14x Mammoth). No delivered tonnes as of 2026-10.
items.permanence_or_durability: Geologic storage. Parity for EOR under 45Q raises a durability and additionality question for S1.
items.bottleneck: Commissioning and reliability of a first-of-a-kind chemical-plant-scale unit, plus calciner heat demand.
items.potential: The only near-term 100 kt-scale DAC test. Its first-year utilisation will be the most decision-relevant measured number of 2027.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 Oxy positions DAC as a long-term business (CEO Hollub has spoken of carbon management, including 'net-zero oil'). S1 NGOs object to EOR use. S6 Permian workers benefit. S7 the US federal government kept 45Q at $180.

items.name: US policy and offtake market for DAC: prices paid, hubs and 45Q
items.mechanism: Revenue comes from voluntary offtakes (Frontier, Microsoft, Google), plus the 45Q tax credit, plus DOE hub grants.
items.energy: n/a
items.cost:
Prices paid or contracted for DAC removal:
- Frontier: average $715/t (range $394-1,818)
- Frontier–Heirloom: $990/t
- Frontier–Phlair: $30.6M for 47,000 t ($651/t, electrochemical DAC, 2027-30)
- Microsoft–Heirloom: about $200M for 315,000 t (about $635/t)
- Google–Holocene: 100,000 t at $100/t (2024; very likely relies on 45Q $180/t, unverified)
- OPIS indicative 2026 DAC price: EUR 350-500+/t
Frontier and Microsoft bought more than 80% of DAC volumes in 2025. Durable CDR deliveries across all pathways passed a cumulative 1 Mt in 2025 (CDR.fyi).
items.trl_and_scale: Policy is enacted: OBBBA, 3 July 2025, sets $180/t for DAC and $85/t for point sources. The DOE DAC hubs are uncertain. Project Cypress was awarded about $550M and South Texas about $500M, with only about $50M disbursed each. Both appeared on a leaked termination list (Oct 2025). DOE later said no decision had been made, and in March 2026 they remain in limbo.
items.bottleneck: Demand is concentrated in about 3 buyers. Public procurement is uncertain. Buyer prices of $100-990/t are confounded by whether they include 45Q.
items.potential: 45Q at $180 plus a voluntary price of about $100-400 makes US DAC at about $300-550/t bankable if utilisation is high.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 favours 45Q parity for EOR. S1 opposes EOR. S7 the US government is ambivalent on hubs but kept 45Q. S10 tech buyers are the main payers.

items.name: Direct ocean capture (DOC): Captura (Equinor-validated) and the BPMED energy floor
items.mechanism: Bipolar membrane electrodialysis (BPMED) splits seawater into acid and base. Acidified seawater releases DIC as CO2 gas, which is captured. The decarbonised water returns to the sea and re-absorbs atmospheric CO2.
items.energy:
Captura has disclosed no energy figure. Lab BPMED (Digdaya et al., Nat Commun 2020) measured 155.4 kJ/mol = 0.98 kWh/kg (3.53 GJ/t) at 71% capture efficiency, an exergy efficiency of about 13% (OptiLex calculation). A 2025 study reports 161.2 kJ/mol at 100 A/m2.

OptiLex calculation: seawater equilibrated with air has the same CO2 chemical potential, so the DOC floor is about the same as DAC's. It is 0.44 GJ/t when removing 1% of DIC, 0.47 at 10% and 0.53 at 30% (Revelle factor about 10). The '150x concentration' advantage is volumetric: about 12,000 m3 of seawater per tonne versus 1.76 million m3 of air. Pumping costs 0.17-0.86 GJ/t at 10-50 kPa head.
items.cost: Not disclosed. Series B was only $12.5M (June 2026), led by Equinor Ventures, with Aramco Ventures, Eni Next, Maersk, National Grid and Hitachi participating.
items.trl_and_scale: The Kona, Hawaii pilot (nominal 1,000 t/yr) ran a 1-year qualification against 20 metrics with Equinor, which declared it commercially ready in November 2025. A 30,000-50,000 t/yr first commercial plant is in design. TRL about 6-7.
items.permanence_or_durability: The captured CO2 needs geologic storage. Durability of the ocean re-uptake depends on air-sea equilibration time (weeks to months) and needs MRV.
items.bottleneck: Electrodialysis electricity (about 3.5 GJ/t in the lab), membrane capex and fouling, seawater pretreatment, and MRV of re-uptake.
items.potential: Co-location with existing seawater intakes (desalination, power-plant cooling, LNG) removes the pumping and intake capex. This fits the 'conventional core plus one imported mechanism' pattern.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 oil majors (Equinor, Aramco, Eni) are the investors. S5 is engaged through National Grid. S1/S11 coastal groups are wary of marine discharge effects.

items.name: Equatic: electrolytic seawater CDR with co-produced hydrogen
items.mechanism: Seawater electrolysis produces alkalinity (Mg/Ca hydroxides and carbonates) that mineralises or stores CO2 as bicarbonate, with H2 as a co-product.
items.energy: No public kWh/t figure. Electrolysis energy is partly recovered as H2 (3,600 t H2 per 109,500 t CO2 planned, about 33 kg H2 per t CO2).
items.cost: Equatic-1 Singapore costs about US$20M for a 3,650 t/yr design, about $5,500 per t/yr of capacity.
items.trl_and_scale: Equatic-1 at Tuas, with PUB: starts at 1 t/day, then 10 t/day (3,650 t/yr) plus 105 t/yr H2, targeted Q1 2026 (operational data not found). The Quebec plant with Deep Sky (109,500 t/yr) is targeted for 2026-27 (claim).
items.permanence_or_durability: Mineral carbonates plus dissolved bicarbonate, stable for more than 10,000 yr if alkalinity is retained.
items.bottleneck: Electricity per tonne, chlorine/oxygen evolution selectivity at the anode, and MRV.
items.potential: The H2 co-product creates an industrial (S4) revenue line.
items.stakeholder_positions: S7 Singapore PUB is a partner. S10 Temasek Trust is an investor. S4 hydrogen offtakers are potentially interested.

items.name: Ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) trials and the first verified credits
items.mechanism: Adding mineral or electrochemical alkalinity shifts seawater carbonate chemistry so the ocean absorbs extra atmospheric CO2 as bicarbonate. No CO2 separation step is needed, so the 0.47 GJ/t floor does not apply; the energy goes into making alkalinity.
items.energy: Mineral OAE energy is mining, grinding and processing; electrochemical OAE (Ebb, BPMED) is about 3.5 GJ/t class (lab analogue). Planetary's Tufts Cove project (Halifax) dosed 1,103.2 t of 'alkalinity' from industrial by-products and earned 625.6 verified t CO2 (Isometric, 16 June 2025). That is 0.57 t CO2 per t, about 47% of the ideal 1.21 if the mass is Mg(OH)2 (OptiLex calculation; the unit is ambiguous).
items.cost: Not disclosed. Microsoft–Ebb covers up to 350,000 t over 10 years, starting with 1,333 t. Google–Ebb signed an initial offtake in Dec 2025.
items.trl_and_scale: Field trials. LOC-NESS (WHOI, Aug 2025, the first EPA-permitted OAE trial) released about 65,000 L of NaOH with a rhodamine tracer over about 1 km2, in a 6-hour dispersal in the Gulf of Maine. The patch was tracked for about 5 days and showed no significant biological differences; the uptake tonnage is not yet published (findings presented Feb 2026). Planetary's 625.6 t are the first independently verified marine CDR credits.
items.permanence_or_durability: Dissolved bicarbonate lasts 10,000-100,000 yr if no secondary precipitation occurs. MRV uses hybrid measurement plus ROMS ocean modelling, so the credited uptake is partly modelled.
items.bottleneck: MRV of the delayed and diluted uptake is the binding constraint, not energy. Others are the supply of clean alkalinity, permitting, and public acceptance.
items.potential: Using existing outfalls (power-plant cooling water, wastewater) as the dosing infrastructure is a conventional core plus one import, with low capex.
items.stakeholder_positions: S11 coastal communities and fishers are cautious (permit hearings). S2 ocean scientists support measured trials. S5 utilities provide outfalls. S10 tech buyers are purchasing.

items.name: Non-thermal swings: electro-swing, moisture swing and hybrid DAC (Verdox, RepAir, Mission Zero, Avnos, Phlair)
items.mechanism: Release of CO2 is driven by electrode redox potential, humidity, or electrochemically generated pH instead of a temperature swing, which avoids the sensible-heat and binding-enthalpy losses.
items.energy:
Claimed figures:
- Verdox: 1.5 GJ/t 'regardless of concentration'. That would be 31% second-law efficiency in air (OptiLex calculation); unverified.
- RepAir: under 1 MWh/t (3.6 GJ/t, about 13%).
- Moisture-swing resins: about 32 kJ/mol sorption heat. Vacuum moisture swing modelled electric demand is 1-15 MJ/kg, dominated by vapour flow.
- Avnos HDAC: more than 50% lower energy than other DAC (claim). It produces 5 t water per t CO2 instead of consuming 5-10 t.
items.cost: Phlair (electrochemical): Frontier offtake at about $651/t.
items.trl_and_scale:
Pilots:
- Avnos: Bakersfield pilot of about 30 t/yr. Project Cedar (3,000 t/yr, $17M project finance from Shell and Mitsubishi) is targeted for end-2026.
- Mission Zero and Airhive: units at Deep Sky Alpha (Alberta), the first cross-technology DAC test-bed, operational Aug 2025. Its 3,000 t/yr site hosts up to 10 vendors and is solar-powered.
- Verdox: still pre-commercial.
items.permanence_or_durability: Depends on storage. Electrode and redox-carrier degradation from O2 sensitivity of quinone-type carriers is an open durability risk.
items.bottleneck: There is no independently measured energy per tonne for any non-thermal swing at more than 100 t scale. Oxygen interference and electrode capex per tonne-year are the risks.
items.potential: If even 3 GJ/t electric holds at scale, 1 Gt/yr would need about 2.8% of world electricity. Deep Sky Alpha's side-by-side data is the best near-term test of these claims.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 Shell and S4 Mitsubishi back Avnos. S7 Canada and Alberta host Deep Sky. S11 the water co-product appeals in arid regions.

items.name: Heirloom: passive limestone-looping DAC (Tracy CA; Louisiana)
items.mechanism: CaO from calcined limestone is spread in thin trays and passively re-carbonates in ambient air (no fans), then is re-calcined in an electric kiln to release pure CO2.
items.energy: The CaCO3 decomposition enthalpy of 178 kJ/mol sets a heat floor of 4.04 GJ/t (OptiLex calculation). That limits second-law efficiency to about 11.5% (electric heat) or 15% (exergy basis) without heat recovery, even with zero fan work. No measured plant energy has been disclosed.
items.cost: 'High hundreds of dollars' per tonne (2024 company statement), with a target below $100/t by 2035. Frontier pays $990/t, and Microsoft about $200M for 315,000 t.
items.trl_and_scale: Tracy, CA: 1,000 t/yr capacity since Nov 2023. Delivered tonnage has not been reported publicly. Louisiana: a 17,000 t/yr plant was planned for 2026, and Cypress (Heirloom part 80-120 kt/yr) was reported stalled in March 2026.
items.permanence_or_durability: CO2 is stored geologically or in concrete (CarbonCure).
items.bottleneck: Calcination heat is set by thermochemistry, not by engineering. Slow carbonation kinetics means large land area and tray-handling capex.
items.potential: Passive contacting removes fan work entirely. Recovering heat from the hot CaO and CO2 is the main lever left for efficiency.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 cement and lime know-how transfers. S6 Louisiana workers benefit. S1 groups are mixed on Gulf siting.

items.name: Fan and contactor work: an electricity floor that heat integration cannot remove
items.mechanism: About 1.76 million m3 of air must pass through the contactor per tonne at 75% capture (2.65 million at 50%). Fan work scales with pressure drop divided by capture fraction.
items.energy: OptiLex verifier, at 60% fan efficiency: 75% capture costs 0.09, 0.29, 0.88 and 2.94 GJ/t at 30, 100, 300 and 1,000 Pa; 50% capture costs 0.13-4.41 GJ/t over the same range. Climeworks' stated 650 kWh_e/t (2.34 GJ/t) would equal about 800 Pa at 75% capture if it were all fan work. In practice it also covers vacuum, controls and conditioning. Carbon Engineering's design uses 9.2 MW of fans for 111.9 t/h (about 0.30 GJ/t, 3.7% of losses).
items.cost: At $50/MWh: about $4/t (100 Pa) to $41/t (1,000 Pa).
items.trl_and_scale: Physics floor checked against design data.
items.bottleneck: Packed beds have a high pressure drop. Structured, low-pressure-drop contactors trade off against slower kinetics and more capex per tonne.
items.potential: Natural-draft or wind-driven contactors, existing cooling-tower and HVAC airflows, or passive trays (Heirloom) take fan work to about zero.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5 and S4 operators of cooling towers and HVAC already move this much air.

items.name: DAC with waste heat or co-location (data centres, industry, geothermal)
items.mechanism: Free or low-cost low-grade heat supplies the TVSA regeneration duty, and shared sites cut electricity, emissions and permitting cost.
items.energy: Exergy factor of 100 C heat is 0.20 (OptiLex calculation), so free waste heat removes most of the energy cost but only about 38% of Gen2 exergy. Electricity (62%) remains. Typical air-cooled data-centre exhaust (about 30-45 C) is too cold for amine TSA without heat pumps; direct liquid cooling at higher temperature is better.
items.cost: Saves up to about $40/t (2,000 kWh_th at $20/MWh_th) in heat cost; does not touch capex.
items.trl_and_scale: Fang et al. (CityU HK, arXiv, May 2026), a modelling study. It finds data-centre waste heat can flip DAC from net-positive to net-negative in carbon-intensive US grids, and several states exceed a removal ratio of 1 by 2030. No measured deployment yet. Orca and Mammoth already use geothermal heat at Hellisheiði.
items.bottleneck: Heat temperature mismatch, and siting near storage. Data centres seldom sit above Class VI storage.
items.potential: Pairing with the AI build-out gives S10/S5 a reason to host DAC. The value is mainly accounting and cost, not a thermodynamic breakthrough.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5 utilities and S10 hyperscalers are interested (Microsoft and Google are major DAC buyers). S11 communities are already sensitive to data-centre loads.

items.name: Global scale gap and the energy budget at Gt scale
items.mechanism: Arithmetic of deployed capacity against need, and of energy at the measured, claimed and floor intensities.
items.energy:
OptiLex calculation for 1 Gt/yr:
- at the floor (0.47 GJ/t): 0.5 EJ, 0.08% of primary energy
- at 3.5 GJ/t: 0.56% of primary, or 3.2% of world electricity if electric
- at 6 GJ/t: 0.97% of primary
- at 10 GJ/t: 1.6% of primary, or 9.3% of world electricity
- at 20 GJ/t (Mammoth CEO range): 3.2% of primary, or 18.5% of world electricity
items.cost: Young et al. 2023 model $230-540/t at Gt scale. At $300/t, 1 Gt/yr costs about $300bn/yr.
items.trl_and_scale: IEA: 27 DAC plants commissioned, capturing almost 0.01 Mt/yr. That is about 3.7 million times smaller than fossil CO2 (37.4 Gt). The NZE scenario needs more than 85 Mt in 2030 and about 980 Mt in 2050. The IEA pipeline is 5.5 Mt/yr in advanced development plus 38.7 Mt/yr at an early stage.
items.bottleneck: Manufacturing scale-up rate and capital. Energy is a second-order constraint below 10 GJ/t at 1 Gt/yr.
items.potential: DAC realistically serves residual emissions (about 1-3 Gt/yr by 2050), not bulk fossil abatement.
items.stakeholder_positions: S1 fears DAC is a 'moral hazard' delaying cuts. S3 sees it as a licence to operate. S8 justice advocates question who pays.

bottlenecks: Realised utilisation. Mammoth delivered 675 t net in H1 2026, which annualises to 1,350 t (3.75% of its 36,000 t/yr nameplate), up from 0.66% in H1 2025. Orca runs at about 27% of its 4,000 t/yr nameplate. Capex per tonne therefore scales about 25x above design.

Capital charge. Stratos cost about $2,600 per t/yr of capacity. At a 10% capital recovery factor that is $274/t at 95% capacity factor and $867/t at 30%. Running DAC only on curtailed power roughly triples the capital cost per tonne, while energy at the thermodynamic floor costs only about $6/t at $50/MWh.

Regeneration enthalpy far above the floor. Binding energy is 75 kJ/mol for amines and 178 kJ/mol for calcination, against a 20.5 kJ/mol free-energy floor. Sensible heat of the sorbent bed adds 45-540 kJ/mol and water co-desorption 44-220 kJ/mol (OptiLex model). The result is 4-19 GJ_th/t for temperature-swing sorbents.

Exergy share of electricity. For Climeworks Gen2 nominal figures, electricity for fans, vacuum and compression is about 62% of exergy input (2.34 of 3.79 GJ/t). Free waste heat therefore leaves second-law efficiency below about 20%.

Sorbent oxidative degradation. TEA models need lifetimes from 10,000 cycles (to 90% capacity) up to hundreds of thousands of cycles. No public field-lifetime data exist for any commercial DAC sorbent.

No independent measured energy per tonne for any DAC or DOC plant above 1 kt/yr. All figures are company-stated, CEO remarks or design models. The one primary exergy analysis (7.8%) covers a design, not an operating plant.

Demand concentration and policy risk. Frontier and Microsoft bought more than 80% of 2025 DAC volume. DOE hubs (about $1.05bn awarded, about $100M paid) were in limbo as of March 2026. 45Q at $180/t (OBBBA 2025) is the only firm public support.

Ocean CDR MRV. Re-uptake after OAE or DOC is delayed and dilute. Credited tonnes such as Planetary's 625.6 t are partly modelled (ROMS). LOC-NESS has not published an uptake tonnage. Permitting and S11 coastal acceptance limit scale.
open_problems: Find a sorbent and swing combination whose release enthalpy approaches the roughly 20 kJ/mol free-energy floor while kinetics stay fast. Moisture swing at about 32 kJ/mol and electro- or pH-swing look promising. Then check every claimed GJ/t against measured side-by-side data, for example from the Deep Sky Alpha test-bed.

Store the swing rather than electricity. Load sorbent continuously with passive contactors, and regenerate in batches when power is curtailed. This decouples a cheap contactor from an expensive regeneration capex, so both can run at a high capacity factor. Mechanism to import: thermal and chemical storage from CSP and calcium looping.

Recover the binding and sensible heat, which is 39% of losses in the Carbon Engineering design. Options are counter-current solid heat exchange for calciners and sorbent beds, and heat pumps lifting 30-45 C waste heat to 90-100 C. The question is the exergy cost of each against what it saves.

Co-locate direct ocean capture or OAE with existing seawater flows (desalination brine and intakes, power-plant once-through cooling, LNG regasification water). This removes pumping, about 0.17-0.86 GJ/t, and intake capex. It is a conventional core plus one imported mechanism, and S5/S4 asset owners gain revenue.

Use existing high-volume airflows: cooling towers, building HVAC, mine ventilation, natural-draft towers. These provide contactor airflow at zero marginal fan work, given that fan cost runs from 0.09 GJ/t at 30 Pa to 2.94 GJ/t at 1,000 Pa.
Develop low-cost, measurement-heavy MRV for ocean CDR: autonomous pCO2 and tracer sensing to shrink the modelled share of credited uptake. This is a precondition for S2 and S1 to trust OAE at scale.

Build a DAC failure-mode database from Mammoth's ramp: humidity, cold, sorbent and mechanical issues. Use it to predict utilisation of new designs before they are built. Utilisation, not energy, drives today's cost.

key_claims.claim: The best-documented operating DAC plant is still below 4% of nameplate. Climeworks Mammoth (36,000 t/yr design) delivered 675 t net CO2 removal in H1 2026, up from 119 t in H1 2025, after sorbent and mechanical upgrades. That annualises to about 1,350 t/yr (3.75%). Operating cost per tonne fell more than 50%, but the absolute cost was not disclosed. Measured, net of lifecycle emissions, 2025-2026. The source is Bloomberg via EnergyConnects, not Climeworks' own release.

A primary exergy analysis of Carbon Engineering's 1 Mt/yr KOH DAC design (Long-Innes and Struchtrup, Cell Reports Physical Science, 2022) finds a second-law efficiency of 7.8%: 252 of 273.2 MW is destroyed. The largest loss is chemical exergy dissipated as low-grade heat (39.4%), then the calciner (25%) and the CCGT (16.4%); fans are only 3.7%. The paper's separation floor is 20.48 kJ/mol (465 MJ/t) at 74.3% capture, which matches OptiLex's verifier. The result is modelled and covers a design, not an operating plant.

surprises: Electricity, not heat, dominates the exergy budget. For Climeworks' stated Gen2 figures (2,000 kWh_th at 100 C plus 650 kWh_e), second-law efficiency is 4.9% on an energy basis but 12.3% on an exergy basis, and electricity is 62% of the exergy. Free waste heat cuts cost but not the bulk of the thermodynamic gap.

Direct ocean capture's '150x higher concentration' does not lower the thermodynamic floor. Seawater equilibrated with air has the same CO2 chemical potential, so the DOC floor is 0.44-0.53 GJ/t against 0.47 for air (OptiLex calculation). The advantage is only volumetric: about 12,000 m3 of seawater per tonne against about 1.76 million m3 of air.

In the Carbon Engineering design, fans are only 3.7% of losses. Strong-sorbent chemistry wastes far more: the CO2 heat of adsorption alone (about 75 kJ/mol for amines) is 3.7x the 20.5 kJ/mol separation floor, and calcination (178 kJ/mol) is 8.7x.

At the thermodynamic floor, energy would cost only about $6/t (at $50/MWh), while DAC sells at $394-1,818/t (Frontier). DAC cost is a capital-utilisation problem, not a thermodynamic one, and Mammoth's 3.75% utilisation is the binding number.

Buyer prices span 10x: Google–Holocene at $100/t versus Frontier–Heirloom at $990/t. The low price very likely sits on top of the $180/t US 45Q credit, a confound when it is compared with non-US prices.

Oil and gas majors are the main backers of DAC and ocean CDR: Oxy (Stratos, Carbon Engineering and Holocene acquisitions), Equinor, Aramco and Eni (Captura), and Shell (Avnos). Meanwhile Climeworks' 2023 company emissions (1,700 t) exceeded its removals. Both facts matter for selling to S1 versus S3.
The first verified marine CDR credits (Planetary, 625.6 t, June 2025) came from dosing an existing power-plant outfall. Infrastructure reuse came before any novel ocean hardware.

verifs.claim: The best-documented operating DAC plant is still below 4% of nameplate. Climeworks Mammoth (36,000 t/yr design) delivered 675 t net CO2 removal in H1 2026, up from 119 t in H1 2025, after sorbent and mechanical upgrades. That annualises to about 1,350 t/yr (3.75%). Operating cost per tonne fell more than 50%, but the absolute cost was not disclosed. Measured, net of lifecycle emissions, 2025-2026. The source is Bloomberg via EnergyConnects, not Climeworks' own release.
verifs.corrected_claim: Climeworks says its Mammoth plant in Iceland "removed 675 tons" of CO2 in H1 2026, "almost six times as much as a year earlier." That implies roughly 113-120 t in H1 2025; the cited source gives no exact figure. Mammoth's stated capacity is "as much as 36,000 tons a year." Doubling H1 gives about 1,350 t/yr, or about 3.75% of that capacity. Climeworks attributes the gain to plant-design upgrades and better filter material (sorbent). It says operating cost per tonne fell by more than 50%, without disclosing the absolute cost. These are company-reported figures, not independently verified. The source does not say whether they are gross capture or net of lifecycle emissions. Source: Bloomberg (Akshat Rathi and Alastair Marsh, 10 Sep 2026), republished by EnergyConnects, citing a Climeworks statement.
verifs.caveats:
I read the full EnergyConnects article text (HTTP 200). The Climeworks primary release and the Bloomberg original both returned 403, so I could not check either one.

1. **The "119 t in H1 2025" figure is not in the cited source.** The article only says "almost six times as much as a year earlier." 119 t would be consistent with that (5.7x), but it needs its own primary source or should be dropped.

2. **"Net of lifecycle emissions" is not supported.** The article says "removed" and never says net, gross or lifecycle. Two consequences:
   - If the 675 t is net, comparing it with a 36,000 t gross-capture nameplate understates utilisation compared with a gross basis.
   - If it is gross, the net figure is lower.
   State the basis as unknown.

3. **"Measured" overstates it.** These are company-reported numbers with no third-party verification in the source.

4. **The arithmetic is correct:** 675 x 2 = 1,350 t/yr, and 1,350 / 36,000 = 3.75%. But doubling H1 assumes flat performance through the year, and the improvement trend could change that.

5. **"Best-documented operating DAC plant" is editorial framing.** The source calls Mammoth "the world's largest direct air capture plant."

6. **"Sorbent and mechanical upgrades" is a fair paraphrase.** The source says "upgrades to the plant design and improvements to the filter material."

7. **The 36,000 t/yr is the source's "as much as" stated capacity.** The article does not say how many collector units were installed in either period. That matters for whether the low utilisation reflects per-unit performance or an incomplete build-out.

8. **Correct framing for the strategic point:** the cost-per-tonne fall is relative only. The source gives no absolute $/t, so it cannot support a cost comparison with other carbon-removal methods.

verifs.claim: A primary exergy analysis of Carbon Engineering's 1 Mt/yr KOH DAC design (Long-Innes and Struchtrup, Cell Reports Physical Science, 2022) finds a second-law efficiency of 7.8%: 252 of 273.2 MW is destroyed. The largest loss is chemical exergy dissipated as low-grade heat (39.4%), then the calciner (25%) and the CCGT (16.4%); fans are only 3.7%. The paper's separation floor is 20.48 kJ/mol (465 MJ/t) at 74.3% capture, which matches OptiLex's verifier. The result is modelled and covers a design, not an operating plant.
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the paper's full text, the open-access PDF in UVic's repository (hdl.handle.net/1828/13820). That PDF carries the published Cell Reports Physical Science 3, 100791 (16 March 2022) layout. The Semantic Scholar and Crossref abstracts match it. Every number in the claim appears verbatim: 273.2 MW in, 252 MW lost, 7.8% efficiency (highlights, abstract and Eq. 7), and the Table 1 shares of 39.4%, 25.0%, 16.4% and 3.7%. The text gives 20.48 kJ/mol-CO2 (465 MJ/t) for separation from air at 391 ppm, 21 °C, for a 74.3% reduction (X_f = 0.257 X_i), matching CE's capture fraction.

Context that changes how the claim should be used:

(1) The percentages are shares of the 252 MW lost from the natural gas exergy. They exclude 6 MW of evaporation in the air contactor. As shares of the 258 MW total loss they are 38.5%, 24.4%, 16.1% and 3.6%.

(2) The 39.4% item is labelled "Chemical exergy dissipation (ext. to calciner) + other". It is a residual (99.3 MW = 252 − 152.7 MW accounted for component by component). The authors say they do not analyse its chemical mechanisms in detail. It should be called a residual attributed mainly to dissipation of chemical exergy as low-grade heat in the contactor, pellet reactor and slaker, not a directly computed loss.

(3) The 7.8% figure uses a reversible work of 21.20 MW, which covers separation plus compression to 151 bar, so it is not the separation floor alone. The authors read it as about 13x the theoretical minimum and cite Sabatino et al. at 7.6–7.9% for KOH DAC. Fans (9.2 MW) are treated as a total loss.

(4) Scope: this is CE's all-natural-gas "configuration A" from published design data (Keith et al. 2018), at 391 ppm and T0 = 294 K. It is a model of a design, not plant measurements, as the claim already says.

(5) Match with the verifier: climate/physics.py min_separation_work(391e-6, 0.743, purity≈1, T=294.15) returns 20.49 kJ/mol (465.5 MJ/t), which reproduces the paper. With the defaults (420 ppm, 0.75, 99% purity, 298 K) it gives 20.47 kJ/mol. That is a near-coincidence of different inputs, not the paper's own conditions. The paper's flue-gas comparison (15% CO2) is 5.87 kJ/mol; the verifier gives 5.79, a small difference probably from different purity or mixing assumptions.

(6) The publisher pages (ScienceDirect and cell.com) were blocked by a captcha or a 403, so the repository copy was used.

title: Mineralization, enhanced weathering, biochar, BECCS, soils

items.name: Fermentation (ethanol) BECCS with geological storage
items.mechanism: Fermentation off-gas is already more than 98% CO2, so the separation work is close to zero. The only real energy cost is dehydration and compression. My verifier script gives 0.30 GJ/t for ideal isothermal compression from 1 to 150 bar, or about 0.42 GJ/t (118 kWh/t) at 70% efficiency. Stoichiometry gives 0.955 t of CO2 per t of ethanol. The CO2 goes into saline aquifers (ADM Decatur in the Mt Simon sandstone; Red Trail in North Dakota) or is used for EOR.
items.cost: Compression and dehydration cost about $17/t CO2 (modelled from NETL cases). The Great Plains Institute modelled capture plus transport from NE/KS plants at $35–42/t without credits (2017) and about $14/t net after 45Q (2018). The 45Q credit for storage is $85/t. Red Trail Energy issued 157k removal credits on Puro.earth, the largest issuance by a technology-based removal project at the time.
items.energy: Separation floor is about 0 (task physics). Compression is about 0.3–0.42 GJ/t (my calculation). That is roughly 1/20 to 1/30 of real DAC at 5–10 GJ/t.
items.permanence_or_durability: Saline-aquifer storage. Measured caveat: in 2024 ADM Decatur leaked an estimated 3,000–8,000 t of CO2 into an unauthorised zone because a monitoring well corroded. EPA issued a notice of violation, injection stopped for about a year, and it restarted on 29 Aug 2025 under an administrative order.
items.potential: ADM Decatur has stored about 4.5 Mt cumulatively over roughly 10 years (company/NETL figure), with about 1 Mt/yr capacity. The US ceiling is about 43–46 Mt CO2/yr (my calculation from 15–16 bn gal of ethanol per year). That is a hard cap set by ethanol volume, worth about $3.6–3.9 bn/yr of 45Q at $85/t.
items.bottleneck: Pipelines and permits. South Dakota banned eminent domain for CO2 pipelines (signed 6 Mar 2025). That stalled Summit's $9 bn, 2,500-mile network serving 57 ethanol plants, and Iowa's permit depends on South Dakota's. Well integrity and monitoring transparency are a second constraint (ADM did not report the leak to EPA for about 3 months).
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: gains a storage and EOR business. S6/S7 in the Midwest: supportive, because it keeps corn ethanol viable under low-carbon fuel standards. S11 landowners: strongly opposed to pipelines, enough to change a state law. S1: split, and some groups use the ADM leak as an anti-CCS argument. S9: neutral.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9. Commercial at the Mt/yr scale (ADM since 2011/2017; Red Trail since 2022).

items.name: Agricultural enhanced rock weathering (basalt on cropland)
items.mechanism: Finely ground Ca/Mg silicate rock is spread on cropland. Its dissolution turns soil CO2 into bicarbonate, which is carried to the ocean. The weathering reaction itself does the chemical work, so the energy inputs are quarrying, grinding and transport rather than separation work.
items.cost: Credits trade at about €185–300/t (market compilations, 2025). Modelled extraction cost is $80–180/t at Gt scale (Beerling et al. 2020, Nature 583:242). ERW was under 2% of 2025 durable CDR contracts. Mati Carbon delivered 492.4 t under Isometric's v1.2 ERW protocol, the first issuance under it.
items.energy: My Bond-law calculation assumes a work index of 20 kWh/t and a 1 cm feed. Grinding to P80 = 100 µm takes about 18 kWh/t of rock, or about 1.2 GJe per t of field CDR (about 3.7 GJe per durable t if only about 1/3 reaches the ocean). Grinding to 10 µm takes about 61 kWh/t of rock, or about 4.2 GJe/t field. At 0.4 kg/kWh of grid electricity, that grinding cancels about 47% of field CDR. Trucking at an assumed 0.1 kg CO2 per t-km cancels about 9.5% of field CDR at 50 km and 38% at 200 km.
items.permanence_or_durability: Durable (more than 10,000 years) once the bicarbonate reaches the ocean. However, experts estimate only about 27–39% of the carbon fixed in the field becomes durable removal (Midwest, pH 5.5–6, 20-year horizon). Losses come from secondary carbonates and clays, deep-soil and river degassing, and ocean re-equilibration.
items.potential: Measured: 10.5 ± 3.8 t CO2/ha over 4 years from 50 t/ha/yr of basalt, Illinois 2016–2020. This is a conservative, soil-based, time-integrated CDR potential, and maize and soybean yields rose 12–16% (Beerling et al. 2024, PNAS). It equals about 0.05 t CO2 per t of rock, roughly 17% of basalt's theoretical ~0.3 t/t (my calculation; the 4-year figure understates later weathering of the same rock). Other field results: Minnesota, 3 years at 10 t/acre, gave no detectable basalt CDR because the grains were coarse and metamorphic (steel slag did show a signal; Frontiers 2025). SE Scotland gave 0.33–0.53 t/ha after 1.5 years. Reviews of trials since 2022 give about 0.01–2 t CO2/ha/yr. Global potential: the 2026 expert elicitation puts the most likely basalt removal at 0.7 (mean) / 0.4 (median) Gt CO2e/yr, against the modelled 0.5–2 Gt/yr from Beerling 2020.
items.bottleneck: Two bottlenecks. First, MRV: experts put measurement error at about 100% of the removal itself, and above 100% in the deep-soil and coastal stages. Second, tonnage: about 19 Gt of rock per Gt CO2 at field level, or 49–71 Gt per durable Gt after downstream losses (my calculation). For comparison, US annual crushed stone is 1.6 Gt and construction aggregate 2.5 Gt.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (quarries, steel slag producers): a new market for waste fines. S9/S6 rural: yield and liming co-benefits. S2: split over MRV. S1: cautious about credit mis-selling (Frontier's buyer principles demand full accounting of loss pathways). S8: Indian smallholder projects (Mati) bring income, but also raise MRV and equity scrutiny.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 6–7. Credits issued at the hundreds-to-thousands of tonnes scale. Terradot acquired Eion in Feb 2026 and holds about 300 kt of offtakes, including 12 kt from Microsoft for 2026–2029.

items.name: In-situ basalt mineralization (Carbfix model; Coda Terminal)
items.mechanism: CO2 is dissolved in water, roughly 25 t of water per t of CO2, and injected into reactive basalt. Calcium, magnesium and iron leached from the rock precipitate it as carbonates, so it is stored as mineral rather than as buoyant free-phase CO2.
items.cost: Reported at about $25–30/t (about €20/t) for capture plus injection at Hellisheiði. That figure applies to a geothermal gas stream that already contains H2S; it does not include DAC or shipping.
items.energy: Low for the injection step. Dissolving CO2 in water at depth avoids having to compress it to the supercritical state, at the cost of large water pumping volumes.
items.permanence_or_durability: Matter et al. 2016 (Science 352:1312) found more than 95% of injected CO2 mineralized within 2 years. This was a pilot-scale injection of a few hundred tonnes in 2012. Leakage risk after mineralization is essentially zero.
items.potential: Hellisheiði's Steingerður plant (opened June 2025) bound more than 120,000 t of CO2 and over 50,000 t of H2S between 1 Jul 2025 and 30 Jun 2026. That is mostly geothermal (geogenic) CO2, so it is an emissions reduction, not a removal. Coda Terminal received a €115 m EU Innovation Fund grant and plans 3 Mt/yr of shipped European CO2 by about 2031–32, with start-up slipping from 2025 to 2027. Global basalt and ultramafic storage capacity is vast (Gt to Tt).
items.bottleneck: Water: 25 t/t means 2.5 km³/yr per 0.1 Gt and 25 km³/yr per Gt (my calculation). Carbfix validated seawater injection in 2021, which may ease this. Geography: storage requires young basalt near the coast. Local acceptance: the Hafnarfjörður master-plan changes for Coda drew strong resident opposition.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (cement and other hard-to-abate emitters in northern Europe): a storage outlet that avoids buoyant-CO2 liability. S7 Iceland: revenue, but local politics are contested. S11: Hafnarfjörður residents are opposed. S1: generally favourable on permanence.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 8–9 for geothermal gas at the 10⁵ t/yr scale. TRL about 6–7 for imported, shipped CO2.

items.name: In-situ peridotite mineralization (44.01, Oman)
items.mechanism: CO2 dissolved in water is injected into mantle peridotite (olivine and serpentine), which is far more reactive than basalt. In the Oman pilot the CO2 came from an ammonia plant.
items.cost: Not disclosed at commercial scale.
items.energy: Similar to Carbfix: dissolution and pumping energy, with negligible separation work for a concentrated source.
