items.permanence_or_durability: Mass balance suggests about 88% of the injected CO2 mineralised within 45 days (Nature 2025, Samail ophiolite pilot). That is much faster than the roughly 2 years seen in basalt.
items.potential: Ophiolites in Oman and the UAE have theoretical capacity in the Tt range. The pilot itself was small, on the scale of tonnes to hundreds of tonnes.
items.bottleneck: Scale-up from a single pilot well. Pore clogging and permeability loss from carbonate precipitation over multi-year injection is unknown. The rock is far from most CO2 sources unless it is paired with DAC or Gulf industry.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3/S7 Gulf states: a way to keep producing hydrocarbons and ammonia with a storage offset. S4 (Gulf ammonia and steel): supportive. S1: welcomes the permanence but is wary of it being used as cover for continued extraction.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 5–6. Pilot scale only.

items.name: Biochar carbon removal
items.mechanism: Biomass is pyrolysed. About 40–50% of its carbon is retained as aromatic char that is applied to soil or materials, and the rest becomes pyrolysis energy.
items.cost: Average reported prices of about $177–250/t, with many developers selling below $100/t (2025 market compilations, not primary).
items.energy: Energy-positive: the pyrolysis gas and oil can supply process heat or power.
items.permanence_or_durability: Contested. The Woolf et al. 2021 decay model gives roughly a century-scale persistence factor. The Sanei et al. 2024 'inertinite' model says char with random reflectance Ro ≥ 2% (76% of commercial samples) persists over millennia. A GCB Bioenergy commentary challenges the inertinite model, and an Oct 2025 workshop of five standards bodies (Puro, Isometric, CSI, Rainbow, Verra) has not resolved it.
items.potential: My calculation: 2.6–3.3 t CO2 per t of biochar (70–90% C) before the permanence discount, or 0.55–0.82 t CO2 per t of dry biomass. That means 1.2–1.8 Gt of dry biomass per Gt CO2/yr.
items.bottleneck: Sustainable residue supply (1.2–1.8 Gt biomass per Gt), unresolved permanence, and weak agronomic pull in temperate regions. Jeffery et al. 2017 (ERL) found +25% average yield in the tropics but about zero in temperate zones.
items.stakeholder_positions: S8: a tropical smallholder co-benefit, since that is where the yield gains are. S4/S5: forestry, sawmill and agricultural residue processors gain revenue. S1: generally positive. S2: split on permanence. S9: neutral.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 8–9. Biochar was 86% of durable CDR deliveries in 2024 (CDR.fyi). 1.6 Mt was sold in H1 2025, and 3.04 Mt was contracted from Q1 2022 to Q2 2025.

items.name: Power and CHP BECCS (Drax, Ørsted Kalundborg, Stockholm Exergi)
items.mechanism: Post-combustion amine capture on biomass-fired boilers, with offshore storage in the North Sea (Northern Lights; the UK East Coast cluster).
items.cost: Drax: Ember estimates about £30 bn in subsidy for full conversion (2023 prices), about £591 m per unit. The UK government uses about £200/t as a proxy, while the Climate Change Committee estimates average BECCS cost at £344/t in 2030 (2023 prices). BioCCS purchase value in 2025 was about $5.3 bn (CDR.fyi via secondary source).
items.energy: Flue gas is about 12–15% CO2, so the minimum work is about 0.16 GJ/t. Real amine capture uses about 2.5–3.5 GJ/t of heat (literature range), which is a direct power penalty and requires burning more wood for the same electricity.
items.permanence_or_durability: Geological storage, so durable. Net removal depends on biomass supply-chain accounting.
items.potential: Ørsted: 430 kt/yr (280 kt from Asnæs, 150 kt from Avedøre), slated to start in early 2026, with 3.67 Mt sold to Microsoft. Stockholm Exergi: 800 kt/yr, planned for 2028. Drax: about 8 Mt/yr planned, delayed from 2027 to about 2030. The UK targets at least 5 Mt/yr of engineered removals by 2030.
items.bottleneck: Cost and legitimacy of the biomass supply. In Aug 2024 Drax made a £25 m redress payment after Ofgem found inaccurate data on where its pellets came from. Its new unabated contract for difference (2027–2031) is £109.90/MWh (2012 prices) at a 27% load factor. Measured removals at full scale: none yet.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5 utilities: a strong lifeline for biomass assets. S6: Yorkshire jobs. S7: needs BECCS to hit its removal targets. S1/S8: many NGOs strongly oppose it over forest sourcing in North America and the Baltics. S9: bill-payer exposure. S10: depends on subsidy contracts.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 7–8. First Mt-scale plants are under construction or commissioning in 2026, and BECCS was about 75% of durable CDR contracted in 2025.

items.name: CO2 mineralization in fresh concrete (CarbonCure)
items.mechanism: Captured CO2 is injected into ready-mix concrete, where it forms nano-CaCO3. That raises strength enough to cut cement content, which is where most of the claimed saving comes from.
items.cost: Sold as cost-neutral or cost-saving to concrete producers through the cement reduction.
items.energy: Negligible at the plant. It uses merchant CO2, which is often fermentation- or ammonia-derived.
items.permanence_or_durability: The mineralized CO2 is permanent, but it is a small fraction of the claimed total.
items.potential: More than 500,000 t of CO2 'saved' across 7.5 million truckloads and more than 46 million m³ of concrete. The combined ready-mix and reclaimed-water products save 12–22 kg CO2/m³. By the company's own figure, each tonne mineralized enables about 50 t avoided through cement optimisation, so only about 2% of the claim is stored CO2.
items.bottleneck: It is mainly an efficiency or avoidance product, so its removal scale is tiny. It is limited by how much cement reduction specifications allow.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (cement and concrete): strongly positive, since it saves money with no disruption. S9: neutral to positive. S1: mildly positive, though some NGOs dispute the 'removal' framing.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9, in hundreds of plants.

items.name: Passive and accelerated carbonation of ultramafic mine tailings
items.mechanism: Freshly milled ultramafic (serpentine, brucite-rich) tailings react with atmospheric CO2 and precipitate hydromagnesite. The rate is limited by how fast CO2 dissolves in the tailings water.
items.cost: Passive capture costs nothing extra. Accelerated versions (adding CO2 or acid leaching, as BHP and Anglo American are trialling with Isometric) have no published cost.
items.energy: Uses rock that has already been milled for ore recovery, so the grinding energy is a sunk cost.
items.potential: Mt Keith nickel mine, Western Australia: about 39,800 t CO2/yr captured passively, about 11% of the mine's emissions (about 360 kt/yr by my calculation). At least 80% of the stored carbon comes from the modern atmosphere (Wilson et al. 2014, IJGGC 25:121), and stable isotopes show the rate is kinetically limited by CO2 dissolution. Global potential is Mt/yr scale, limited by ultramafic mine output.
items.bottleneck: Slow CO2 transfer into the water, and MRV across a heterogeneous tailings facility.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 mining (BHP, Anglo American): positive, as it offsets their Scope 1 emissions and could make nickel mines carbon-neutral. S11: may improve tailings stability by cementing it. S1: positive.
items.trl_and_scale: Passive carbonation already happens at commercial scale. Accelerated carbonation is TRL 5–6.

items.name: Soil organic carbon (regenerative practices)
items.mechanism: Changed practices such as cover crops, reduced tillage and grazing management increase how much carbon soils retain.
items.cost: Credits are generally cheap ($10–50/t typical for legacy offsets, not verified here). MRV dominates the cost.
items.energy: Negligible.
items.permanence_or_durability: Reversible. Carbon is lost if practices stop or the climate warms, so it is not durable CDR.
items.potential: Bradford et al. 2023 (Geoderma), using 45 intensively sampled fields, found that an accrual of 3 Mg C/ha per 10 years is consistently detectable. That needs about 30 fields at about 1.2 ha per sample, and individual-field estimates stay inaccurate. 3 Mg C/ha per 10 years is 1.1 t CO2/ha/yr (my calculation). At typical practice rates of 0.1–0.5 Mg C/ha/yr (my assumption), reaching a detectable change takes 6–30 years.
items.bottleneck: Detection versus reversal. Measurement is feasible only at project scale with dense sampling, so most protocols use models such as DayCent-CR. Durability is not guaranteed.
items.stakeholder_positions: S9/S6 farmers: positive about the co-benefits. S1/S2: sceptical of offset claims. S10: wary of reversal risk.
items.trl_and_scale: Practices are TRL 9. Robust, measured credits are early stage.

items.name: ERW using on-site quarry fines and industrial alkaline wastes (steel slag)
items.mechanism: Use rock fines that the aggregate industry already produces, or reactive slag, either on farms within a short distance or weathered on-site at the quarry. This removes most of the grinding and trucking penalty.
items.cost: Feedstock is often a waste material at close to zero cost. Haulage dominates.
items.energy: No added grinding. My calculation puts trucking at 9.5% of field CDR at 50 km and 38% at 200 km.
items.permanence_or_durability: Same as agricultural ERW, with the same downstream loss pathways.
items.potential: Minnesota, 2021–2024: 2 t/acre of steel slag gave a measurable porewater alkalinity signal, while 10 t/acre of coarse basalt gave none. Aberdeenshire Council has hauled more than 15,600 t of quarry dust onto farms. Quarry-site weathering of mafic fines has been proposed in the literature.
items.bottleneck: Grain size and mineralogy of available fines vary roughly tenfold. Slag carries metal-contamination risk, which experts rate as having the highest damage potential at field scale.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (quarries, steelmakers): turns a disposal cost into revenue. S11: concerned about metals and dust. S9: liming value.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 6. Thousands of tonnes deployed.

bottlenecks: Enhanced weathering MRV: the 2026 expert elicitation (24 experts) estimates measurement error at about 100% of the removal itself, and above 100% in the deep-soil and coastal stages. Only about 27–39% of carbon fixed in the field is expected to become durable removal. A 3-year Minnesota basalt trial could not detect any removal.

Enhanced weathering tonnage and logistics: about 19 Gt of rock per Gt CO2 at field level, or 49–71 Gt per durable Gt after downstream losses (my calculation from Beerling 2024 and the elicitation's efficiency). US crushed stone is 1.6 Gt/yr. Trucking 200 km cancels about 38% of field CDR, and grinding to 10 µm on a 0.4 kg/kWh grid cancels about 47%.

Carbfix water: about 25 t of water per t CO2, which is about 25 km³/yr per Gt. It also needs young reactive basalt near a coast and local consent, which is contested at Hafnarfjörður for Coda Terminal.

Fermentation CCS has a hard volume cap of about 43–46 Mt/yr in the US, set by ethanol output, and is gated by pipeline law. South Dakota's eminent-domain ban (Mar 2025) stalled Summit's 57-plant, 2,500-mile network. Monitoring wells are a second weak point, as ADM's 3,000–8,000 t leak showed.

Biomass supply and its legitimacy for biochar and BECCS: 1.2–1.8 Gt of dry biomass per Gt CO2 for biochar. UK power BECCS is estimated at £30 bn in subsidy for Drax and £344/t in 2030 by the Climate Change Committee, and Drax made a £25 m Ofgem redress over sourcing data.

Biochar permanence is unresolved: the Woolf century-scale decay model and the Sanei inertinite model (Ro ≥ 2%, millennial) differ by orders of magnitude, and five standards bodies have not reconciled them as of Oct 2025.
Soil carbon detection: about 30 fields with dense sampling (about 1.2 ha per sample) are needed to detect 3 Mg C/ha per 10 years (1.1 t CO2/ha/yr), and the stored carbon is reversible.

Demand is concentrated: durable CDR is bought mainly by voluntary buyers, especially Microsoft (for example 3.67 Mt from Ørsted, 3.6 Mt from C2X in Dec 2025). Without compliance demand, prices of $150–400/t limit scale.
open_problems: A cheap, low-uncertainty ERW MRV design. Combine solid-phase mass balance, porewater measurements, ion-exchange resins and isotopes, and reuse decades of agricultural liming data, which the elicitation experts recommended. The target is uncertainty below 30% at under $20/t of MRV cost.

'Conventional core plus one import': farmers already spread aglime, which can act as a CO2 source in acidic, nitrogen-fertilised soils. Replace part of it with basalt or quarry fines that provide the same acid neutralisation, credit only the difference, and keep the farmer's routine unchanged. Formulating this as a dose-substitution problem is tractable.

An optimisation over siting: match quarry fines and steel slag to acidic cropland within about 50 km, choosing particle size (P80) to maximise net CDR after grinding and haulage emissions. My calculation shows haulage beyond about 200 km or grinding to 10 µm on a fossil grid erases 40% or more of field CDR.

Accelerate carbonation of ultramafic tailings at mines, where the rate is limited by CO2 dissolution (Mt Keith already passively captures about 11% of its emissions). Supply concentrated CO2 from co-located fermentation, ammonia or power sources. This turns a passive sink into a point-source mineralization sink with near-zero separation work.

Avoid pipeline law for ethanol CO2: put Class VI wells on-site or nearby, move CO2 by rail or truck, or mineralize it locally in basalt or slag. This could reach the about 45 Mt/yr US fermentation pool without eminent-domain fights.
Design a decisive biochar persistence test: accelerated ageing calibrated against archaeological or natural chars, to settle Woolf versus inertinite and unlock pricing.
Seawater-based Carbfix injection to remove the 25 t/t freshwater bottleneck, and pairing with coastal cement and lime plants (flue gas around 25% CO2, separation floor about 0.11 GJ/t).

Downstream loss accounting for ERW, covering secondary carbonate and clay formation, river degassing and ocean re-equilibration. Field-to-ocean efficiency is the single largest multiplier in ERW economics, at 27–39% with wide spread.

key_claims.claim: A 2026 formal expert elicitation (24 experts, Communications Earth & Environment 7:376) put the most likely global CDR from agricultural ERW with basalt at 0.7 (mean) / 0.4 (median) Gt CO2e/yr, including lifecycle emissions. That is well below the modelled 0.5–2 Gt/yr (Beerling 2020) and the 2–4 Gt/yr assumed in integrated assessment models for 2050. The experts estimated field-to-ocean efficiency at about 27–39% (Midwest, pH 5.5–6) and measurement error at about 100% of the removal, and some judged that basalt, lime and olivine could be net sources depending on lifecycle.

In the best realized ERW field result, a replicated trial in the US Corn Belt (Illinois, 2016–2020), basalt applied at 50 t/ha/yr for 4 years gave a conservative, soil-based, time-integrated CDR potential of 10.5 ± 3.8 t CO2/ha. Maize and soybean yields rose 12–16% (P < 0.05), with no rise in trace metals in grain. That is a farmer-side co-benefit that pays independently of carbon credits. The figure is field-level 'potential' and does not include downstream losses.

surprises: Carbfix's headline volume of more than 120,000 t CO2 bound in rock (Jul 2025–Jun 2026) comes from geothermal, geogenic CO2 at Hellisheiði. It is an emissions reduction, not atmospheric removal, even though the mineralization itself is proven (more than 95% within 2 years in the 2012 pilot of a few hundred tonnes).

CarbonCure's 'more than 500,000 t saved' is mostly avoided cement: by the company's own ratio, each tonne mineralized enables about 50 t avoided, so only about 2% is stored CO2. It is an efficiency product that happens to use CO2.

For ERW, haulage distance and over-fine grinding, not the chemistry, decide whether net removal is positive. Trucking 200 km costs about 38% of field CDR, and grinding to 10 µm on a 0.4 kg/kWh grid costs about 47% (my calculation). Pre-crushed quarry fines on nearby farms avoid both penalties.
In Oman, peridotite mineralised about 88% of injected CO2 in 45 days (Nature 2025 pilot), an order of magnitude faster than basalt.
A large nickel mine (Mt Keith) already passively captures about 39,800 t CO2/yr from air in its tailings, about 11% of its own emissions, with no intervention, and the rate is limited by CO2 supply.
Biochar delivered 86% of all durable CDR in 2024, yet BECCS took about 75% of 2025 contracted volume. Deliveries and contracts point to opposite 'winners'.

Biochar's yield co-benefit is essentially zero in temperate agriculture (Jeffery 2017 meta-analysis: +25% in the tropics, about 0 in temperate zones). The farmer co-benefit therefore argues for deploying biochar in the Global South (S8).

Of all these routes, fermentation CCS has the strongest physics (separation work about 0, about 0.4 GJ/t to compress). It is blocked by property-rights politics, not technology: South Dakota's 2025 eminent-domain ban came from landowner (S11) and conservative coalitions, not climate opponents.

verifs.claim: A 2026 formal expert elicitation (24 experts, Communications Earth & Environment 7:376) put the most likely global CDR from agricultural ERW with basalt at 0.7 (mean) / 0.4 (median) Gt CO2e/yr, including lifecycle emissions. That is well below the modelled 0.5–2 Gt/yr (Beerling 2020) and the 2–4 Gt/yr assumed in integrated assessment models for 2050. The experts estimated field-to-ocean efficiency at about 27–39% (Midwest, pH 5.5–6) and measurement error at about 100% of the removal, and some judged that basalt, lime and olivine could be net sources depending on lifecycle.
verifs.corrected_claim: A 2026 formal expert elicitation (Buma et al., Communications Earth & Environment 7:376, published 12 March 2026; 20 experts, screened to exclude anyone with financial ties to commercial ERW firms) put the most likely global CDR from agricultural ERW with basalt at 0.7 (mean) / 0.4 (median) Gt CO2e/yr, net of lifecycle emissions including N2O. Basalt had the highest estimate of the six feedstocks. The experts put basalt's maximum possible CDR at 2.1/2.0 Gt CO2e/yr. Across feedstocks, the most likely values averaged 0.2–0.7 Gt CO2e/yr (medians 0.01–0.4). These figures sit at or below the low end of the modelled 0.5–2 Gt CO2/yr (Beerling et al. 2020): the median is below that range, the mean is inside it. They are well below the 2–4 Gt CO2/yr by 2050 that early integrated assessment models assumed. For the US Midwest at soil pH 5.5–6, the experts put field-to-ocean durable-storage efficiency at about 27% (lime) to 39% (wollastonite), with about 70% confidence in those ranges. They put measurement error at about 100% of the removal, and above 100% for the deep-soil and coastal-ocean stages. The authors note that lime, basalt and olivine could be net carbon sources, depending on lifecycle emissions and CDR efficacy.
verifs.caveats:
Primary source checked: the full open-access article text at nature.com.
(1) The expert count is wrong. The Methods say 20 experts took part ("Ultimately, 20 experts gave consent to participate"). The figure of 24 probably comes from the author list or the number of affiliations.
(2) "Well below the modelled 0.5–2 Gt/yr" overstates the gap. The basalt mean of 0.7 falls inside Beerling 2020's range, and only the median of 0.4 falls below it. The paper itself does not quote Beerling 2020 as 0.5–2. It cites a broader 0.5 to >4 Gt CO2e/yr range from several modelling studies (Beerling 2020 is among them). The 0.5–2 figure is accurate to Beerling 2020 itself.
(3) The figures measure different things. The elicited "most likely" value assumes widespread, maximum deployment of each feedstock on its own, with no target year. Feedstock values cannot be added together. The IAM 2–4 Gt/yr is specifically a 2050 assumption.
(4) The 27–39% efficiency is a hypothetical: enough material to fix 10 t of carbon per hectare, a maximum of 20 years per stage and at least 100 years of ocean retention. It excludes soil-organic-carbon feedbacks. The paper is internally inconsistent here: the figure caption says "10 tons of carbon", while the Methods wording says "10 tons CO2". The range runs from lime to wollastonite. Basalt falls in between and is not separately stated in the main text.
(5) The net-source point is an expert judgment of possibility. Individual most-likely estimates went no lower than −0.1 Gt CO2e/yr. Minimum estimates went down to −2.0, which was the survey's lowest option.
(6) This is expert judgment, not field measurement. Confidence that the true value lies within the ranges was low: 74%/75% (mean/median) for basalt, roughly 2:1 to 3:1 odds. The authors' bottom line is still "strong potential CDR at broad scales" with large uncertainty, not a negative verdict on ERW.

verifs.claim: In the best realized ERW field result, a replicated trial in the US Corn Belt (Illinois, 2016–2020), basalt applied at 50 t/ha/yr for 4 years gave a conservative, soil-based, time-integrated CDR potential of 10.5 ± 3.8 t CO2/ha. Maize and soybean yields rose 12–16% (P < 0.05), with no rise in trace metals in grain. That is a farmer-side co-benefit that pays independently of carbon credits. The figure is field-level 'potential' and does not include downstream losses.
verifs.corrected_claim: The paper is Beerling et al., PNAS 121(9), published 22 Feb 2024 (PMC10907306). It reports a replicated enhanced-weathering (ERW) field trial at the University of Illinois Energy Farm near Urbana, Illinois, on a maize–soybean rotation from 2016 to 2020. Crushed metabasalt was spread each fall at 50 t/ha/yr for 4 years, 200 t/ha in total. The authors estimate a conservative, time-integrated cumulative carbon dioxide removal (CDR) potential of 10.5 ± 3.8 t CO2/ha. They get this figure from soil cation-loss accounting (Ca and Mg). It is not measured removal. Cation retention in the soil and changes in CDR efficiency downstream are not directly accounted for. The figure is roughly 16% of the theoretical maximum of about 65 t CO2/ha for the rock applied. Grain yields rose significantly (P < 0.05) only in single years: maize by 12% in 2020 and soybean by 16% in 2019. Maize gains appeared only in years that followed soybean. Trace metals did not rise significantly in grain or in soil exchangeable pools. The paper extrapolates gross yield value across the Corn Belt but does not net out the cost of buying and spreading the basalt. So the claim that the co-benefit "pays independently of carbon credits" is an inference the paper does not support.
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the abstract and full text (Europe PMC, PMC10907306); the PNAS page returned 403.

What matches the paper: 50 t/ha/yr over 4 years, 2016–2020, the replicated Illinois Energy Farm design, 10.5 ± 3.8 t CO2/ha as a conservative, time-integrated "CDR potential", 12–16% yield gains at P < 0.05, and no significant rise in trace metals.

Errors and missing context that change how the claim can be used:

1. **The yield range is not a sustained effect.** "12–16%" combines two single-year results: maize +12% in 2020 and soybean +16% in 2019. The paper says significant maize gains came only in years after soybean, which suggests an interaction with nitrogen. It is not shown that the gain holds every year.

2. **"Pays independently of carbon credits" is our inference, not the paper's finding.** The authors put the yield gain at about $7–11B for maize and $10B for soybean across the Corn Belt. That is gross crop value at Feb 2023 prices, assuming 60 Mha. Basalt purchase, transport and spreading of 50 t/ha/yr are not subtracted. The paper does say basalt could replace agricultural lime, which costs about $25/t, and that is a real offset. Even so, the farmer's net economics are not shown.

3. **This is not measured, net CDR.** The 10.5 figure comes from soil cation accounting. The paper states that temporary retention of cations on soil exchange sites before drainage and changes in CDR efficiency downstream are "not directly accounted for". It also does not subtract mining, grinding and transport emissions. The claim's "does not include downstream losses" is correct, but net of operations the figure would be lower.

4. **Efficiency is low.** The rock delivered about 2.6 t CO2/ha/yr on average; the text cites about 3.4 t/ha/yr for one rate. The theoretical maximum is 16.2 t CO2 per 50 t of rock. The feedstock was a coarse by-product metabasalt (p80 267 µm) with only about 11% fast-weathering minerals. That points to room for improvement, but also shows realized performance is far below the stoichiometric ceiling.

5. **"Best realized ERW field result" cannot be verified.** It is our own superlative and the paper makes no such claim. Present it as "a leading, peer-reviewed multi-year field result" unless it is compared against other field trials, such as the UK/Malaysia trials, Eion and other MRV datasets, and wollastonite trials.

6. **Scope.** The result covers one site, one feedstock and one rotation over 4 years, on hand-harvested 10 × 10 m subplots plus larger blocks. The authors lead the Leverhulme Centre, which advocates for ERW. Extrapolating to the whole Corn Belt is their modelling, not something they observed.

title: Non-CO2 greenhouse gases: methane, N2O, F-gases

items.name: Oil and gas methane abatement (LDAR, electric pneumatics and pumps, vapour recovery, associated-gas use, ending routine flaring)
items.mechanism: Stop leaks and venting at upstream sites. The captured methane is sold as gas, so the gas revenue pays for the abatement.
items.energy: Energy-positive: about 100 bcm/yr of gas is recoverable from leaks, plus about 100 bcm/yr more by ending non-emergency flaring (IEA GMT 2026). My calculation: 100 bcm is about 68 Mt CH4, worth about $12bn/yr at $3.5/MMBtu or about $39bn/yr at $11/MMBtu.
items.cost: IEA GMT 2026 (modelled, 2025 average energy prices): more than 35 Mt of fossil CH4/yr avoidable at no net cost, out of about 85 Mt abatable with existing technology. Total fossil methane in 2025 was 124 Mt (oil 45, coal 43, gas 36). GMT 2025 put upstream oil and gas alone at about 30 Mt at no net cost. My calculation: the gas credit is $184/t CH4 at Henry Hub $3.5/MMBtu, which is $6/t CO2e (GWP100) or $2/t (GWP20). At $11/MMBtu (EU TTF or Asian LNG) it is $579/t CH4, which is $19/t CO2e (GWP100). The same leak repair therefore pays about 3x less for a US producer than for an LNG-linked or EU-market producer, and less again where domestic gas prices are subsidised.
items.potential: 35 Mt CH4 is 1.04 Gt CO2e (GWP100) or 2.9 Gt CO2e (GWP20), about 2.8% of fossil CO2 on GWP100. Removing the same tonnage by DAC at 6 GJ/t would take 6.3 EJ/yr, about 1% of world primary energy. IEA says current policies deliver only about a 20% cut by 2030 (26% by 2035), against the Global Methane Pledge's 30%.
items.bottleneck: The barrier is incentives and MRV, not technology. The 10 largest emitting countries produce about 70% of fossil methane (IEA 2026). National oil companies and low-price domestic markets capture little of the gas value. Abatement also needs midstream infrastructure, without which recovered gas has nowhere to go.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 profits directly from gas sales; OGCI and OGMP 2.0 members have targets covering more than half of global oil and gas production (IEA). S7 gains energy security (the EU frames this as LNG supply). S1, S2 and S11 support it, with local VOC and air-quality co-benefits. S9 is neutral to slightly positive. This is the clearest 'all parties win' lever in this dimension.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9, deployed. Realized outcome: Permian methane intensity fell from 5.2% to 3.2% over 2019–2023 (TROPOMI inversion, ES&T Dec 2025). In New Mexico, under state rules, it fell from 4.5% to 2.1%.
items.permanence_or_durability: Avoided emissions are permanent per tonne, but the benefit lasts only while equipment and LDAR programmes are maintained.

items.name: EU Methane Regulation (2024/1787) import MRV and methane-intensity requirements
items.mechanism: Market-access standard. From 1 Jan 2027, importers of oil, gas and coal must show producer-level MRV equivalent to EU rules for contracts signed or renewed from 4 Aug 2024. Methane-intensity limits apply from 2030, with fines of up to 20% of annual turnover. The rule reaches producers in exporting countries, including the US, Qatar, Norway and Algeria.
items.cost: Compliance cost falls on exporters. An industry-commissioned estimate (modelled, 2026) said about 43% of EU gas imports and 87% of crude imports could be non-compliant in 2027.
items.potential: It is the only enacted lever that prices methane intensity across borders for about 1/3 of global LNG trade into Europe. Domestically it also bans venting and flaring from coal drainage stations (2025) and from ventilation shafts (2027, with exceptions). Coal mines emitting more than 3 t CH4 per kt of coal may not vent VAM from 2031.
items.bottleneck: Implementation capacity. As of mid-2026 there were no accredited verifiers and the equivalence implementing acts were missing. 17 of 27 member states asked for amendments. In July 2026 the Commission chose non-binding recommendations not to apply penalties for a period, instead of amending the law. The 2027 MRV obligation formally stands.
items.stakeholder_positions: S1 and NGOs (joint CSO letter, June 2026) oppose delay. S3 and EU industry groups (Eurogas, FuelsEurope, Cefic) asked for a 3-year postponement. S7 is split between climate goals and supply security. US exporters object to the equivalence test.
items.trl_and_scale: Policy enacted Aug 2024; importer phase starts 2027; penalties softened by guidance in 2026.
items.permanence_or_durability: Legal durability is uncertain because enforcement was softened by guidance in 2026.

items.name: US methane policy: Waste Emissions Charge and EPA OOOOb/c (rolled back or delayed)
items.mechanism: Fee per tonne of excess methane under the IRA ($900/t for 2024 emissions, $1,200 for 2025, $1,500 for 2026 onward), plus performance standards for new and existing sources.
items.cost: The fee was set at $900–1,500/t CH4. My conversion: $30–50/t CO2e (GWP100). It was projected to raise $7.2bn over 2025–2034.
items.potential: The Congressional Review Act repealed the implementing rule (House 220-206, Feb 26 2025; Senate 52-47, Feb 28 2025). The OBBBA (signed Jul 4 2025) moved the first assessed year to 2034 and rescinded the remaining Methane Emissions Reduction Program funds. EPA extended OOOOb/c deadlines (final rule Nov 26 2025); zero-bleed process controllers are now due no earlier than 22 Jan 2027, and a further reconsideration was planned for 2026.
items.bottleneck: Political durability: the statute survives but has no teeth before 2034. US drivers are now gas value, state rules (New Mexico), buyer requirements and EU import MRV.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 (Western Energy Alliance, API) supported repeal of the fee. Some majors had earlier backed federal methane regulation. S1 (Sierra Club) and S6 unions (BlueGreen Alliance) opposed repeal.
items.trl_and_scale: Policy reversed or delayed in 2025.
items.permanence_or_durability: Low: shown to be reversible within a single political cycle.

items.name: Industrial N2O abatement (adipic acid and nitric acid plants)
items.mechanism: Catalytic or thermal decomposition of N2O in the off-gas. Adipic acid off-gas is 30–50 mol% N2O. Nitric acid plants use secondary catalysts in the burner or tertiary catalysts on the tail gas.
items.cost: $0.25–4/t CO2e in 2026 USD: above $1/t for single systems achieving about 90%, and $4/t for redundant systems above 90% (NRDC Jul 2026, citing sector analyses). Older EU estimates: €0.3–1/t for direct decomposition and €1.3–2/t for SCR. Credits from Ascend's US plant sell at $13/t. NRDC states there is no abatement at ≤$0, so it is pure cost and needs a mandate or price. My calculation: abating China's adipic-acid N2O (about 76 Mt CO2e, AR5) costs $19–304M/yr, against about $40bn/yr for 100 Mt of DAC at $400/t.
items.potential: More than 100 Mt CO2e/yr of industrial N2O is unabated, mostly Chinese adipic acid, which is about 94% of global adipic-acid N2O. NRDC projects industrial N2O could grow to 0.25–0.5 Gt CO2e by 2050. One study found China's industrial N2O to be 2x the GAINS model and more than 6x EDGAR.
items.bottleneck: There is no revenue stream, so it needs regulation or durable finance. The history of gamed credits (CDM) makes buyers wary. China's 11+ adipic acid plants have unknown abatement status, and capacity is still growing (2 new plants in 2023).
items.stakeholder_positions: S4: cost is negligible per tonne of product, so nylon makers' resistance is mainly about rules, not money. S7 China: sovereignty over MRV. S1 and S2 strongly support. S10: voluntary market buyers are burned by CDM history.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9. Adipic plants have achieved more than 90% abatement since the late 1990s, and more than 1 in 6 nitric acid plants have abatement installed.
items.permanence_or_durability: Durable only while abatement is operated. CDM-era units were switched off when credit prices collapsed.

items.name: Coal mine methane: drainage-gas use and ventilation air methane (VAM) oxidation
items.mechanism: Drainage gas (more than about 30% CH4) is used for power, heat or pipeline gas. VAM (about 0.2–1% CH4 in very large air flows) is destroyed in regenerative thermal oxidisers, which run self-sustaining (autothermal) from the methane's own heat of combustion.
items.energy: My calculation: autothermal operation needs at least about 0.18% CH4 with a 95%-effective regenerator and a 1,000°C bed, falling to 0.11% at 97% effectiveness. This matches the literature minimum of about 0.2%. At 0.3% CH4 the adiabatic temperature rise is only 83 K.
items.cost: MATEC 2025 design case (engineering estimate, 360,000 m3/h, 0.326% CH4): capex €9.52M, opex €0.87M/yr, 7,236 t CH4/yr destroyed. My annualisation (8–10% discount rate, 15–20 yr life): €254–293/t CH4, which is €8.5–9.8/t CO2e (GWP100) or €3.1–3.6/t (GWP20). The IEA/Ember aggregate ($2.5bn capex to cut 9.5 Mt CH4/yr) implies capex 5x lower per t CH4/yr than the MATEC case. This discrepancy is unresolved.
items.potential: IEA: coal methane was 43 Mt in 2025. Proven options cut 54–63%. VAM is 70–80% of underground-mine emissions. VAM oxidation alone could cut about 24% of coal mine methane (9.5 Mt). Most drainage abatement is available at no net cost (Ember 2026).
items.bottleneck: VAM yields no saleable product, so it needs regulation or a carbon price. RTOs for VAM have been adopted at only about 7 coal sites globally. Coal mine methane MRV is poor: per Ember, only 23 of 73 coal-producing countries report it. Concentration is variable, and mine operators are cautious about anything that could ignite methane in mine air.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4/S5 coal operators bear the cost; per Ember, halving coal mine methane costs about 16% of annual coal-industry profits. S6 miners: no job loss and possible safety co-benefits. S7: China's coal mine methane standards and the EU 2031 VAM ban. S1 is wary of anything that prolongs coal.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 8–9 for RTO, but only a handful of commercial VAM sites.

items.name: Enteric methane: 3-NOP (Bovaer) feed additive
items.mechanism: 3-NOP inhibits methyl-coenzyme M reductase, the enzyme rumen microbes use in the last step of making methane.
items.cost: About $93–105 per cow per year (dsm-firmenich, 2022); the Scottish plant targets $58–64. My calculation, for a cow emitting 350–450 g CH4/day with a 26–30% cut and biogenic GWP 27: $44–117/t CO2e (GWP100), or $15–40/t (GWP20). Compare Denmark's livestock tax (enacted Nov 2024): 300 DKK/t (about $46) marginal from 2030, effective 120 DKK after a 60% deduction, rising to 750/300 DKK in 2035, with revenue recycled to farming.
items.potential: Kebreab et al. meta-analysis (14 dairy experiments): CH4 production -32.7% at 70.5 mg/kg DM. Another meta-analysis found yield -26.4% at 60 mg/kg. The effect weakens as dietary fibre (NDF) rises (-0.63 percentage points per +10 g/kg NDF), so it is weaker in forage- or grazing-based systems, where most cattle methane occurs.
items.bottleneck: Social licence and cost. Denmark mandated 80 days/yr for conventional farms with more than 50 cows from 2025. In autumn 2025 there were more than 200 complaints to the dairy board; in a SEGES survey, 434 of 644 respondents reported yield drops. Norway's Tine paused use. Aarhus University (May 2026; 73 herds, about 27,650 cows; observational) found no evidence of effects on yield, mortality, mastitis or digestive disorders, but trust is damaged. There is also no delivery method for grazing animals.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4/agri processors (Arla and others) buy it as Scope 3 insetting. Farmers (S6-like) resist cost and perceived risk. S9 faces about 1 cent per litre of milk. S1 is supportive but some groups oppose it as 'techno-fix' for animal agriculture.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9: approved in the EU, US (2024) and elsewhere. National-scale mandate in Denmark only.
items.permanence_or_durability: Methane is avoided only while the additive is fed; there is no cumulative stock effect.

items.name: Enteric methane: Asparagopsis seaweed and bromoform products
items.mechanism: Bromoform from red seaweed inhibits methanogenesis in the rumen.
items.cost: No reliable public $/t; supply is constrained (aquaculture scale-up).
items.potential: Whole A. armata at 0.5% of diet cut methane 95.6%, against 59.6% for an equal dose of pure bromoform. This was a short-term trial funded by CH4 Global, the grower. An Adelaide University study (April 2026) found large cuts in grazing beef cows with no harm to calves.
items.bottleneck: Bromoform is ozone-depleting and a possible carcinogen, raising residue and regulatory concerns. Durability of the effect over months is unresolved. Supply chain, delivery to grazing herds, and long-term animal health data are lacking.
items.stakeholder_positions: S1 is enthusiastic but ozone- and residue-wary. Meat and dairy firms are interested for Scope 3. Regulators are cautious.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 6–7 (field trials; small commercial feedlot use in Australia).

items.name: Waste and landfill methane (open dumps to sanitary landfills, organics diversion, gas capture)
items.mechanism: Divert organic waste to composting or digestion, cover and cap sites, and collect landfill gas for flaring, power or renewable natural gas (RNG).
items.cost: Not quantified here. US landfill-gas RNG earns D3 RINs, so it profits where policy exists.
items.potential: Nature Climate Change 2025 (satellite survey of 151 sites on six continents): satellite estimates do not correlate with reported or modelled facility emissions. Open-dump emissions are underestimated 5.3x in EDGAR v8. Converting dumps and diverting organics cuts emissions by 80% (60–89%), worth 760 (570–850) Mt CO2e/yr (modelled).
items.bottleneck: Municipal finance and governance in the Global South, where open dumps are. MRV is weak (inventories are wrong by up to 10x at site level).
items.stakeholder_positions: S8 and S11 gain public-health co-benefits (fires, leachate). Municipalities lack capital. RNG producers profit under US and EU policy. Waste pickers (informal workers) are at risk unless included.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 technology; deployment is limited by finance.
items.permanence_or_durability: Durable once infrastructure is in place.

items.name: Rice methane: alternate wetting and drying (AWD) and other water management
items.mechanism: Periodically draining paddies interrupts the anaerobic methanogenesis that occurs in flooded fields.
items.cost: Low direct cost; saves about 30% of water. Credit-funded.
items.potential: Field trials show methane cut by 30–50%, or 1.5–5 t CO2e/ha/season. The first Verra VM0051 project (An Giang, Vietnam, listed 2025) covers 116,000 ha and expects 590,682 t CO2e/yr (modelled).
items.bottleneck: Needs field-level water control and MRV across millions of smallholders. AWD can raise N2O, partly offsetting the gain. Credit integrity: in Feb 2023 Verra suspended the CDM rice methodology AMS-III.AU (37 projects, 4.56M credits issued) over data quality and additionality.
items.stakeholder_positions: S8 smallholders gain water savings and a possible credit income. S7 food-security concerns about yield risk. S1 is wary of credit integrity.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 agronomy; MRV at about TRL 5–6.

items.name: F-gases: Kigali Amendment HFC phasedown and HFC-23 by-product destruction
items.mechanism: Production and consumption caps on HFCs. HFC-23, a by-product of HCFC-22 production, must be destroyed.
items.cost: HFC-23 destruction is very cheap per t CO2e (incineration). Under the AIM Act, US EPA projects $283.9bn of cumulative climate benefits over 2022–2050 (modelled).
items.potential: 172 states plus the EU had ratified Kigali by April 2026. Modelled: up to 0.5°C avoided by 2100. Measured: global HFC-23 emissions were 14.0 ± 0.9 Gg/yr in 2023, 5x higher than reported (Communications Earth & Environment, 2024). My calculation: 14 Gg × GWP 14,600 ≈ 204 Mt CO2e/yr, against about 41 Mt implied by reports. About 40% comes from eastern China.
items.bottleneck: Compliance and verification gap. By-product destruction is not happening to the extent parties report. Atmospheric inversions are the only check.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 chemical producers (Chemours, Honeywell) profit from next-generation refrigerants, so the US industry backed the AIM Act. S7: bipartisan in the US. S9: modest equipment cost increases.
items.trl_and_scale: Policy enacted and in force globally.
items.permanence_or_durability: Durable treaty; enforcement is the weak point.

items.name: Atmospheric methane removal (AMR): atmospheric oxidation enhancement (chlorine or iron-salt aerosol) and closed-system reactors (photocatalysts, Cu-zeolite)
items.mechanism: Open systems add oxidants (Cl atoms from iron-salt aerosol photolysis, Cl2, or H2O2/OH) to the atmosphere to speed up methane's natural sink. Closed systems pass air through reactors with catalysts (for example Cu-zeolite at about 300°C, or photocatalysts) to oxidise methane.
items.energy: Closed systems (my calculation with the OptiLex verifier): the minimum work to concentrate CH4 from 1.93 ppm to 0.5% is 18.9 kJ/mol = 1.18 GJ/t CH4 = 0.044 GJ/t CO2e, which is about 10x below DAC's 0.47 GJ/t floor. So the thermodynamic floor is favourable. Real processes are not: fan work alone (100 Pa pressure drop, 60% fan efficiency, 90% conversion) is 146 GJ/t CH4 at 1.93 ppm (4.9 GJ/t CO2e GWP100) and 28 GJ/t at 10 ppm (barn air). Heating 10-ppm air to 300°C for a Cu-zeolite catalyst costs 554 GJ/t CH4 (18.6 GJ/t CO2e) even with 99% heat recovery, and 5,543 GJ/t at 90% recovery. That is worse than DAC. Thermal catalysis on dilute air is therefore ruled out unless heat recovery exceeds 99.9% or the catalyst works at near-ambient temperature.
items.cost: No credible cost estimates exist. NASEM (Oct 2024) recommends $50–80M/yr of research for 3–5 years.
items.potential: Horowitz, ACP, July 2026 (one global model, 1-year simulations): 1,250 Tg/yr of Cl2 lowers steady-state methane by 14.3%. Iron-salt aerosol needs 565 Tg/yr of particulate iron for only -2.5%. 20% bromine co-release by mass reverses the effect (methane +17.2%). OH falls 8–12%, and PM2.5 rises 0–0.4 µg/m3 globally. My calculation: the Cl2 case is about 13x world chlorine production. It equals cutting about 64 Mt CH4/yr of emissions, about 20 t Cl2 per t CH4/yr. The iron-salt case is about 51 t of iron per t CH4/yr equivalent. Compare 35 Mt CH4/yr of fossil abatement available at no net cost.
items.bottleneck: Scale of reagents, side effects (ozone, PM2.5, halogenated gases, bromine impurity), poorly constrained chlorine-release kinetics, governance of an open-atmosphere intervention, and non-durability: the benefit reverses within about a decade once operation stops (arXiv 2601.17462).
items.stakeholder_positions: S2: NASEM supports research only. S1 is split, with many wary of geoengineering. S3 may favour AMR as a moral hazard ('remove later'). S8: justice concerns over who decides on open-air interventions.
items.trl_and_scale: Open-system approaches are at TRL 2–3 (chamber and models; a 2025 ferric chloride field test was planned by GeoRestoration). Cu-zeolite is at TRL 3–4 (bench, 2 ppm–2%; $2M DOE grant).
items.permanence_or_durability: Not durable: avoided warming lasts only as long as the intervention continues.

items.name: Satellite methane detection and alert-response systems (UNEP IMEO MARS; TROPOMI, GHGSat, EMIT)
items.mechanism: Satellites detect super-emitters and alerts are sent to governments and operators. Pressure for fixes then comes from buyers and regulators.
items.cost: Low per tonne. The value depends entirely on whether anyone responds.
items.potential: More than 3,500 MARS alerts sent across 33 countries. Response rate rose from 1% (2024) to 12% (2025), so about 90% go unanswered (UNEP Eye on Methane, Oct 2025).
items.bottleneck: No enforcement link: detection is now cheap, but response is voluntary. Methods disagree. Permian intensity in 2024 was 0.44% by aircraft plume survey (S&P, 2025) against 3.2% in 2023 by TROPOMI inversion (ES&T 2025). Aircraft miss diffuse and small sources, so headline 'intensity' numbers depend on method.
items.stakeholder_positions: S1 and S2 strongly support. S3 is mixed: it helps cut product loss but exposes companies to liability. S7 governments mostly do not respond.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 detection; response mechanisms are immature.

bottlenecks: The 'no net cost' claim depends on gas price and on who gets the gas revenue. My calculation: recovered gas is worth $184/t CH4 ($6/t CO2e GWP100) at Henry Hub $3.5/MMBtu, against $579/t ($19/t CO2e) at $11/MMBtu (EU/Asian LNG). Producers selling into subsidised domestic markets (many NOCs) capture even less, so IEA's more than 35 Mt/yr at no net cost overstates what private operators see in low-price markets.

Implementation gap: IEA GMT 2026 finds current policies cut fossil methane only about 20% by 2030 and 26% by 2035, against the Global Methane Pledge's 30%. Global energy methane did not fall in 2025 (124 Mt).

The core policy levers are politically reversible. The US fee ($900–1,500/t CH4) was repealed under the CRA in 2025 and delayed to 2034 by the OBBBA. EPA OOOOb/c deadlines were extended. The EU import penalties were softened by non-binding guidance in July 2026, before verifiers or implementing acts existed.

MRV is the binding constraint everywhere, and inventories are wrong by large factors. HFC-23 measured at 5x reported (14.0 Gg in 2023, about 204 Mt CO2e). Open-dump methane is 5.3x EDGAR v8. China's industrial N2O is 2x GAINS and more than 6x EDGAR. Permian intensity is 0.44% (aircraft) against 3.2% (satellite inversion). Only 23 of 73 coal-producing countries report coal mine methane.

Several abatement options have no revenue stream and need a mandate or price: VAM €8.5–9.8/t CO2e (GWP100, my calculation from the MATEC 2025 design case); industrial N2O $0.25–4/t; 3-NOP $44–117/t (my calculation). Past credit schemes were gamed. The CDM adipic-acid case and Verra's 2023 suspension of rice credits (4.56M credits) are why buyers distrust offset funding.

Thermal oxidation thermodynamics: autothermal operation needs at least about 0.11–0.18% CH4 with 95–97% regenerators (my calculation, consistent with the field minimum of about 0.2%). Below that, heating dominates. At 10 ppm (barns), heating to 300°C costs 18.6 GJ/t CO2e even with 99% heat recovery.

Scale of atmospheric oxidation enhancement: about 13x world chlorine production (1,250 Tg/yr Cl2) for -14.3% methane, or 565 Tg/yr of iron for -2.5% (Horowitz 2026, a single model). Trace bromine reverses the effect.

Social licence for agricultural interventions. In Denmark's 2025 3-NOP mandate, more than 200 complaints and a farmer backlash led to Norway's Tine pausing use. A later 73-herd Aarhus study found no harm, but trust was lost first. 3-NOP efficacy also falls in high-fibre and grazing diets, where most cattle methane is.
open_problems: A design for an anti-gaming finance contract for China's adipic-acid N2O, about 76 Mt CO2e/yr. Full abatement costs only $19–304M/yr (my calculation), making these among the cheapest large tonnes available. The conventional core is a contract-for-difference or results-based payment. The imported mechanism is a production-capped baseline (so payments cannot drive extra output) plus atmospheric-inversion verification. This avoids the CDM failure, where credit profits exceeded adipic acid profits and 17–22% of credits were not real reductions.

An EU methane MRV equivalence pathway that exporters can actually comply with by 2027: tiered measurement (OGMP 2.0 Level 5 reconciliation plus satellite and aircraft) mapped onto the EU MR equivalence test, with cheap third-party verification. A credible design would let the EU keep the rule without a supply shock, which would satisfy S1, S3 and S7 at once.

Reconcile the VAM capex discrepancy: the MATEC 2025 design case is €1,316 per t CH4/yr, while the IEA/Ember aggregate implies about $263, a 5x gap. Separately, look for catalytic oxidisers or regenerators that run autothermal at 0.05–0.1% CH4 (needs at least 99% heat-recovery effectiveness or a bed below 500°C, per my threshold calculation).

Low-energy methane concentrators for 10 ppm–0.1% streams (barns, manure storage, abandoned wells). The thermodynamic floor is tiny: 0.92 GJ/t CH4 from 10 ppm to 0.5% (my calculation). The real obstacles are sorbent selectivity for nonpolar CH4 against N2/O2, and pressure drop. Fan work alone at 10 ppm is 28 GJ/t CH4.

Methane inhibitors that work in grazing and high-fibre systems (slow-release boluses, water-delivered additives). Also trust-building rollout design: pre-registered, farm-level monitored pilots before a mandate, as the lesson from Denmark 2025.

Turn satellite detection into action. MARS response is only 12%. Options include automatic linkage of alerts to buyer contracts, insurance (S10) or import MRV, and resolving the aircraft vs satellite intensity disagreement (0.44% vs 3.2% in the Permian).

Price-robust design for oil and gas abatement where gas is cheap or subsidised (Russia, Central Asia, Middle East domestic markets). Options include monetising captured gas via LNG or export routes, or methane-intensity premiums in offtake contracts, so that 'no net cost' holds for the operator and not only at the IEA's global average price.

Whether atmospheric oxidation enhancement can avoid bromine contamination and the 8–12% OH penalty. Any open-air AMR claim must be checked against the Horowitz 2026 scale numbers before being taken seriously.

key_claims.claim: IEA Global Methane Tracker 2026 (modelled): fossil fuel methane was 124 Mt in 2025 (oil 45, coal 43, gas 36). About 85 Mt is abatable with existing technology, and more than 35 Mt at no net cost at average 2025 energy prices (about 1.0 Gt CO2e GWP100 or 2.9 Gt GWP20, by my conversion). About 100 bcm/yr of gas is recoverable from leaks and another 100 bcm from ending non-emergency flaring. Current policies deliver only about a 20% cut by 2030.

Horowitz 2026, ACP 26:9471 (one global chemistry model, 1-year simulations): atmospheric oxidation enhancement needs 1,250 Tg/yr of Cl2 to cut steady-state methane by 14.3%, and iron-salt aerosol needs 565 Tg/yr of iron for only 2.5%. 20% bromine co-release raises methane by 17.2%. OH falls 8–12%. The Cl2 case is about 13x world chlorine production (my calculation), so atmospheric methane removal cannot substitute for source abatement on any near-term horizon.

surprises: The thermodynamic floor for concentrating ambient methane (0.044 GJ/t CO2e GWP100, my calculation) is about 10x below the DAC floor per t CO2e. Air methane removal is not ruled out by thermodynamics. It fails on engineering: fan work is about 100x the floor, and heating dilute air is about 10,000x the floor.
HFC-23 emissions measured in 2023 were 5x what parties reported, about 204 Mt CO2e/yr (my GWP conversion), even though Kigali obliges by-product destruction.

CDM credits for adipic-acid N2O were more profitable than adipic acid itself. Plants raised output, 17–22% of credits did not represent real reductions, and abatement was switched off when credit prices collapsed. The cheapest climate tonnes became a cautionary tale about finance design, not technology.

After the 2025 farmer backlash in Denmark, Aarhus University's 73-herd study (May 2026) found no effect of Bovaer on yield, mortality or health, but Norway's dairy monopoly had already paused use. Perception moved policy faster than evidence.
Permian methane intensity depends on the method: 0.44% (aircraft plume survey, 2024) against 3.2% (TROPOMI inversion, 2023). Headline 'success' numbers can differ by about 7x.

'No net cost' methane abatement is worth about 3x less to a US producer selling at Henry Hub than to an LNG-linked one: $6 against $19 per t CO2e of gas value (my calculation). This undercuts a single global 'free abatement' framing.
A 20% bromine impurity flips iron-salt or chlorine methane removal from cooling to warming (methane +17.2%).

verifs.claim: IEA Global Methane Tracker 2026 (modelled): fossil fuel methane was 124 Mt in 2025 (oil 45, coal 43, gas 36). About 85 Mt is abatable with existing technology, and more than 35 Mt at no net cost at average 2025 energy prices (about 1.0 Gt CO2e GWP100 or 2.9 Gt GWP20, by my conversion). About 100 bcm/yr of gas is recoverable from leaks and another 100 bcm from ending non-emergency flaring. Current policies deliver only about a 20% cut by 2030.
verifs.corrected_claim: IEA Global Methane Tracker 2026 (published 4 May 2026): the IEA estimates fossil fuel methane at 124 Mt a year in 2025 (oil 45, coal 43, gas 36). This is an IEA estimate "based on measured, satellite, and inferred data", with high stated uncertainty, not a direct measurement. Fossil fuels are about 35% of anthropogenic methane, and bioenergy adds another 20 Mt. About 70% of fossil methane, nearly 85 Mt, can be abated with existing technology: about three-quarters of oil and gas emissions and about half of coal emissions. More than 35 Mt (about 30%) could be avoided at no net cost at average 2025 energy prices, because the captured gas is worth more than the abatement costs. That is roughly 1.0 Gt CO2e at GWP100 or 2.9 Gt CO2e at GWP20 (my conversion, not the IEA's). Nearly 30 Mt of the no-net-cost potential is in upstream oil and gas. The IEA says nearly 100 bcm/yr of gas could be made available through a global effort to cut methane from oil and gas operations, and a further 100 bcm by eliminating non-emergency flaring. The IEA adds that not all of this can be recovered, it would take time to deploy, and only about 15 bcm is available in the near term. The "current policies deliver only about a 20% cut by 2030" figure does not appear in the cited key-findings page and could not be verified; remove it or source it separately.
verifs.caveats:
How it was checked: iea.org is behind a Cloudflare bot check that blocked WebFetch, curl and the browser pane, so I did not try to get past it. Instead I read the Wayback Machine snapshot of the key-findings page from 2 Sep 2026, plus snapshots of the "Understanding methane emissions" and "Strategies to speed action" chapters. All figures except the 20% one match that text word for word: 124/45/43/36 Mt, nearly 85 Mt (about 70%) abatable, more than 35 Mt at no net cost on 2025 prices, nearly 100 + 100 bcm.

Problems found:
(1) The "only about 20% cut by 2030 under current policies" claim is not on the key-findings page or the two other chapters I could read. The "Policy trends" chapter was not archived, so it may be there, but it is unverified. The 20% figures that do appear in the report are unrelated: 20% of LNG trade disrupted, 20% of oil and gas methane from downstream, and less than 20% of production covered by company pledges in 2021. The policy statements the page does make are different: tried-and-tested policies applied globally would cut oil and gas methane by more than half, and more than 75% with data-dependent policies added. The Global Methane Pledge target is -30% by 2030.
(2) "Recoverable from leaks" is a loose paraphrase. The IEA's 100 bcm comes from cutting methane from oil and gas operations generally (venting, equipment, leaks). The IEA says not all of it can be recovered and that only about 15 bcm is available quickly.
(3) "Modelled" is fair, but the IEA labels the 124 Mt figure an estimate built from measured, satellite and inferred data. Measured data coverage is limited or absent for several top-10 emitters, including Russia, Venezuela and Indonesia.

Context for using this: the "no net cost" figure depends on gas prices, and the IEA says the economics improve in 2026 because of the Middle East conflict. It is also an economy-wide cost-curve result, not a guarantee for any single operator; the barriers to capturing it are institutional and policy-related, not thermodynamic. For coal, abatement often means destroying the methane through flaring or oxidation rather than selling it, so the no-net-cost share is concentrated in oil and gas (about 30 of the 35+ Mt). The CO2e conversion is the user's own. It is consistent with AR6 GWP100 of about 29.8 and GWP20 of about 82.5 for fossil methane, but the IEA did not publish it.

verifs.claim: Horowitz 2026, ACP 26:9471 (one global chemistry model, 1-year simulations): atmospheric oxidation enhancement needs 1,250 Tg/yr of Cl2 to cut steady-state methane by 14.3%, and iron-salt aerosol needs 565 Tg/yr of iron for only 2.5%. 20% bromine co-release raises methane by 17.2%. OH falls 8–12%. The Cl2 case is about 13x world chlorine production (my calculation), so atmospheric methane removal cannot substitute for source abatement on any near-term horizon.
verifs.corrected_claim:
Horowitz (2026), ACP 26, 9471–9491, sole author, published 7 July 2026. The study uses one model, GEOS-Chem 13.2.1 at 4°x5°, with a 1-year simulation (2019) after a 1-year spin-up. Steady-state methane is extrapolated with a methane feedback factor; it is not simulated directly.

Results:
- **Cl2:** 1,250 Tg/yr of Cl2 emitted over the oceans cuts steady-state methane by 14.3% (methane lifetime about −11%).
- **Iron-salt aerosol:** 565 Tg/yr of particulate iron gives −1.7% alone (Results section and Table S5). The Conclusions put the same case at −2.5%. Adding 1,250 Tg/yr of chloride gives −5.4%. Depending on what is emitted, iron/chloride scenarios range from −5.4% to +3.2%.
- **Bromine:** 20% bromine contamination of the Cl2 release raises steady-state methane by 17.2%.
- **Tropospheric OH (Table 2):** −27.7% in the Cl2 case, −47.1% with bromine, −2.1% for iron alone, −8.6% for iron plus chloride. OH rises in the H2O2 cases.
- **Chlorine supply:** the paper says 1,250 Tg/yr is about 20x the current manufacture of Cl2, which it takes as 58 Tg/yr from the World Chlorine Council (2024). It is also about 20x the current natural tropospheric source of gas-phase inorganic chlorine (54 Tg/yr).

Conclusion: in this model, atmospheric methane removal needs emissions an order of magnitude or more beyond today's chlorine industry, so it cannot substitute for source abatement on a near-term horizon. That last step is our inference, not a statement in the paper.
verifs.caveats:
1. **The "OH falls 8–12%" figure is wrong.** For the 1,250 Tg Cl2 case, Table 2 shows OH −27.7% (−47.1% with bromine). The 8.6% figure belongs to the Iron_Chloride case only. The "12%" in the paper is a different number: how much past model-version changes in nitrogen chemistry have shifted the simulated OH burden.

2. **The iron figure is inconsistent within the paper.** The Results section gives −1.7% for 565 Tg/yr iron alone. The Conclusions say 2.5%, probably measured against a different baseline (standard model vs standard + Chen et al.). Cite the range 1.7–5.4%, not "only 2.5%". The 5.4% also needs 1,250 Tg/yr of chloride.

3. **The chlorine-supply multiple depends on the denominator.** The paper's own figure is ~20x, against 58 Tg/yr Cl2 manufacture. The "13x" in the claim implies about 95 Mt/yr, which is closer to commonly quoted industry capacity. I could not check that figure because the web-search budget was used up. Use the paper's ~20x, or give the denominator explicitly.

4. **Model-dependent result.** For the same 1,250 Tg Cl2, Li et al. 2023b found −45% methane by 2050 (−50% lifetime), compared with −14% here. The difference comes from the model framework, RCP8.5 emissions and a longer run. Meidan et al. 2024 (CESM, a different chlorine-release mechanism) found −20% after 10 years from 200 Tg/yr iron. These are rival model estimates of the same quantity, so treat them as model uncertainty, not settled numbers.

5. **Only 1 year was simulated.** The author says this is too short to assess stratospheric ozone impacts. Steady-state values are extrapolations.

6. **Other findings worth noting:** all methods raise surface PM, with some regional exceedances of air-quality standards. Cl-based methods lower ozone pollution and can raise ozone-depleting substances. H2O2 at the same 1,250 Tg/yr gives only −4.6%.

7. **The source-abatement conclusion is our inference.** The paper does not discuss AOE as a substitute for abatement.

title: Heavy industry decarbonization that reuses incumbent assets

items.name: Make the green premium visible per end product, not per tonne (lead markets, buyer clubs, embodied-carbon standards)
items.mechanism: Decarbonized steel and cement cost 20-80% more per tonne, but the premium is under about 1% per car or building. A mandate or standard on embodied carbon in end products, plus pooled procurement, moves the cost to the end buyer, who barely notices it. Incumbents keep their plants and charge for the green version.
items.cost: Global Efficiency Intelligence (2024, modelled, $5/kg H2): H2-DRI-EAF premium about $231/t in Japan, $225/t in China, $186/t in the EU. That is $208 per car in Japan, under 1% of a $28k car. Energy Transitions Commission, Mission Possible (2018, modelled): about $180 per car for green steel. My calculation (heavy_industry.py): 0.9-1.2 t of steel per car at $186-235/t gives $167-246 per car, or 0.56-0.82% of a $30k car. The same premium is 9-14% of a 6% carmaker EBIT margin, so the cost is small for consumers but material for OEM profits. Cement CCS at about €100-150/t CO2 adds €54-81 per tonne of cement, about 0.4-1.2% of a €2,000/m2 build cost (my calculation, assumed 0.15-0.3 t cement per m2).
items.energy: n/a (a demand-side mechanism)
items.trl_and_scale: The market exists but is thin. Fastmarkets assessed the EU green flat-steel premium at €100-170/t in early 2026, firming to €150-200/t by Q2 2026, with a slow, narrow buyer pool (Eurometal, 2026). That market premium roughly equals the modelled premium.
items.potential: Covers the roughly 2.4 Gt (cement, IEA 2024) and roughly 2.6 Gt (steel) of direct CO2 in the long run, if demand-side rules spread beyond the EU.
items.bottleneck: There is no common definition of green steel or cement, and buyers lack willingness to pay at volume. The cost sits in the OEM's margin, not the consumer's price.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (inferred) prefer it because they keep their plants and market share and get paid for the premium. S9 face less than 1% end-price impact. S1 and S2 support embodied-carbon rules. OEMs resist absorbing the premium in their margin (inferred from margin arithmetic, not a documented position).
items.permanence_or_durability: Depends on policy durability (CBAM, procurement rules).

items.name: Gas-first DRI that switches to hydrogen later (reuses gas supply chains; DRI off-gas is a near-pure CO2 point source)
items.mechanism: Replace blast furnaces with shaft-furnace DRI and an EAF that can run on reformed natural gas now and on H2 later. That cuts about 50% at once without waiting for cheap H2, and keeps steel sites, workers and gas demand. DRI process-gas CO2 removal yields a concentrated stream that can be stored.
items.cost: Thyssenkrupp Duisburg DRI: about €3bn, about two-thirds from German and NRW public funding. The EU Commission approved an amendment letting it start without H2, and its H2 tender was put on hold over price. My calculation: each $1/kg of H2 adds about $55/t of steel (55 kg H2/t). The $5 vs $1.5/kg gap is worth about $190/t.
items.energy: Gas-DRI cuts CO2 by more than 50% vs blast furnaces (Thyssenkrupp claim). H2-DRI needs about 2.9 MWh/t for electrolysis plus about 0.7 MWh/t, so about 3.6 MWh/t. The Fe2O3 dissociation enthalpy floor is 7.38 GJ/t = 2.05 MWh/t (my calculation), so H2-DRI is already within about 1.8x of the floor. H2 use (~55 kg/t) is about equal to stoichiometric demand (54 kg/t).
items.trl_and_scale: Gas DRI is TRL 9 (a mature global technology). Measured precedent for capture: Al Reyadah (Abu Dhabi, ADNOC/Masdar) has captured up to 0.8 Mt/yr CO2 from Emirates Steel DRI since November 2016, used for EOR.
items.potential: If all of the EU's ~70 Mt of blast-furnace hot metal moved to H2-DRI, it would need about 250 TWh/yr, about 9% of EU electricity. All ~1,350 Mt of global blast-furnace output would need about 4,800 TWh, about 16% of world electricity (my calculation).
items.bottleneck: The price of H2 (about $55/t of steel per $/kg) and of gas and power in Europe. Storage for gas-DRI CO2 is only available near CO2 networks.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 gain gas demand and a CO2-storage business. S4 and S6 keep sites (the Thyssenkrupp Duisburg workforce). S1 criticize gas lock-in: the Swedish EPA withheld part of Stegra's state aid because the plant will run on natural gas at first.
items.permanence_or_durability: Uses geological storage when CCS is attached; Al Reyadah stores via EOR, where net storage accounting is disputed.

items.name: Retrofit CCS on existing cement kilns (Brevik / evoZero model)
items.mechanism: Amine capture with heat integration is bolted onto a 100-year-old kiln. CO2 is liquefied, shipped and stored offshore under the North Sea (Northern Lights). The plant, quarry and workforce stay, and the low-carbon cement sells at a premium.
items.cost: Capex about €421M. Estimated abatement cost NOK 1,150 (about €100) per tonne CO2 (a modelled estimate from the Longship cost study, not measured). The Norwegian state funded about NOK 8bn of the capture part, within NOK 16.8bn for Longship.
items.energy: Capture capacity was sized to the available waste heat, at 400 kt/yr, about 50% of plant emissions. My calculation: the floor for a 25% CO2 flue at 90% capture is 0.11 GJ/t. Amine reboiler heat of about 3 GJ/t at 120°C is about 0.72 GJ/t of exergy, a second-law efficiency of about 15%, which beats DAC's 5-10%.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 at a single plant. Started June 2025; evoZero delivered from October 2025. The first year's output was pre-sold. evoZero is planned to grow from 100 kt (2025) to 1,350 kt (2030). Northern Lights phase 1 has 1.5 Mt/yr of storage capacity; phase 2 (5 Mt/yr) is under construction.
items.potential: Cement process CO2 was about 1.5 Gt in 2024, plus about 0.9 Gt from combustion (IEA). CCS is the only route for calcination CO2 short of changing the chemistry.
items.bottleneck: Waste heat limits capture to about 50%, and going beyond needs extra heat or electricity. Storage network access is limited, and the subsidy share was large.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4: GCCA calls CCS critical for cement decarbonization. S3 gain a storage business. S1 are mixed on CCS. S11 face CO2 shipping and storage risk (low at Brevik).
items.permanence_or_durability: Saline-aquifer storage 2.6 km below the seabed; permanence over 1,000+ years is typical for well-sited aquifers.

items.name: Calcined clay / LC3 and other clinker substitution (same kilns, less clinker)
items.mechanism: Replace about half the clinker with calcined clay plus limestone. Clay calcines at about 800°C vs 1,450°C for clinker and releases no carbonate CO2. Existing cement plants and kilns can be converted (Cimpor Souselas).
items.cost: Claimed up to 25% cheaper to produce than Portland cement at 50% clinker (an industry/academic claim). LeadIT (September 2026) says it is economically competitive with OPC depending on local conditions.
items.energy: About 20% less energy; CO2 down by up to 40% vs OPC (claimed by producers and the LC3 project; JK Lakshmi launched an LC3 product in February 2026).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 but tiny. In 2023 there were 14 calcination plants with 3.45 Mt/yr of capacity. Six more were due in 2026, and the pipeline would enable about 26 Mt/yr of LC3 cement vs about 4,000 Mt/yr of global cement, under 1% (LeadIT 2026). The global clinker ratio was 0.71 in 2022 (IEA).
items.potential: The largest near-zero-cost lever for cement if it scales: 40% of about 2.4 Gt is roughly 0.9 Gt/yr at full adoption (an upper bound I calculated).
items.bottleneck: Scale-up speed, building standards and contractor acceptance, and finance for new calciners. Venture-stage alternatives are fragile: Sublime Systems paused its Holyoke plant after DOE cancelled its $87M grant in October 2025.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 keep their kilns and lower costs. S8 benefit, since the leaders are Africa and Latin America (Ghana, Cameroon). S9 face neutral or lower prices.

items.name: Green iron trade: make HBI where renewables are cheap, keep the EAF, rolling and finishing at incumbent sites
items.mechanism: H2-DRI electricity sits close to the thermodynamic floor (see item 2), so the cost lever is the electricity price, not process efficiency. Moving only the ironmaking step to high-quality solar and wind regions lowers cost. Downstream steelmaking, its value and most jobs stay in Europe, Japan and Korea.
items.cost: Modelled for Germany (steel, fertilizer and plastics precursors: HBI, ammonia, methanol). Sourcing them from European partners saves €4.1bn/yr (11.2%); global sourcing saves €8.6bn/yr (23.3%). Other reported modelling: HBI imports cut European steel costs 12-15% by 2040.
items.energy: Same 3.6 MWh/t, but at a cheaper and better-matched site.
items.trl_and_scale: HBI trade is mature (gas-based). Green HBI projects are at announcement or FID stage (Brazil Iron/RWE; Vale's project on an EU priority list).
items.potential: A redistribution that keeps value in incumbent countries and lowers the global cost of H2-DRI.
items.bottleneck: S6 lose the ironmaking jobs; energy-security concerns arise over import dependence; and there is no certified green-HBI standard.
items.stakeholder_positions: S8 gain industrialization (Brazil, MENA, Australia). S4 keep downstream steelmaking and their customers. S6 in ironmaking regions lose (inferred). S7 weigh security against cost (the study's own theme).

items.name: Blue ammonia: CCS on existing SMR ammonia plants
items.mechanism: SMR ammonia already produces a nearly pure CO2 stream; dehydrate, compress and store it. The existing plant, jobs and gas supply all stay.
items.cost: The fermentation-like pure stream has a near-zero separation floor (verifier). It is paid by US 45Q at up to $85/t stored.
items.energy: Only compression and dehydration.
items.trl_and_scale: CF Industries Donaldsonville started up in July 2025 with ExxonMobil, at up to 2 Mt/yr CO2. It markets up to 1.7 Mt/yr of low-carbon ammonia. Blue Point (1.4 Mt/yr NH3) is planned for 2029.
items.potential: The cheapest abatement in chemicals. It covers process CO2 but not upstream methane leakage or combustion CO2.
items.bottleneck: Upstream methane leakage sets lifecycle CI. Storage-site controversy (Hydrogen Insight flags a contested storage option). It depends on 45Q durability.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3, S4 and S6 are all in favour: they keep assets and gas demand. S1 are sceptical about methane leakage and lock-in.
items.permanence_or_durability: Geological storage, details to be verified per site.

items.name: Green ammonia via long-term auctioned offtake (India SECI/SIGHT model)
items.mechanism: A government-run 10-year reverse auction aggregates fertilizer-plant demand. Contracted prices came in near grey ammonia prices. Existing fertilizer plants switch their feedstock rather than close.
items.cost: Contracted at Rs 49.75-64.74/kg ($570-745/t) for 10 years. Grey ammonia traded at $400-490/t FOB in early 2026, before the conflict raised prices. Awards are 724 kt/yr across 13 fertilizer units, with about 670 kt/yr confirmed.
items.energy: About 9-10 MWh/t NH3 via electrolysis (literature range, not computed here).
items.trl_and_scale: Contracted, not built: first deliveries 2028 at the earliest, realistically 2029-30. Elsewhere, cancellations: AES Andes INNA in Chile ($10bn, January 2026), Green Ammonia Linz in Austria (September 2025, despite €48.5M of EU funding), Hy2Gen Sauda in Norway (March 2026).
items.potential: Ammonia is about 1-2% of global CO2 (literature). Bid prices show the premium can be about 1.2-1.5x grey under good renewables plus aggregated demand.
items.bottleneck: Delivery risk: auction prices are not yet realized output. Offtake aggregation and finance; IEA cut its 2030 low-emissions H2 outlook from 49 to 37 Mt/yr (GHR 2025).
items.stakeholder_positions: S8 gain domestic supply security (India). S7 improve energy security by cutting LNG imports for fertilizer (inferred). S3 lose gas demand.

items.name: Electrified steam cracking (retrofit of cracker furnaces)
items.mechanism: Replace fired cracker furnaces with resistive heating inside the existing olefins complex. Downstream units and feedstock chains stay the same.
items.cost: Not disclosed. Economics depend on the power price vs the cheap fuel gas it replaces (by-product fuel gas must find another use).
items.energy: 6 MW of renewable power for about 4 t/h of feedstock in the demo, about 1.5 MWh per tonne of feed (my arithmetic from the stated numbers). Claimed potential cut of at least 90% in furnace CO2.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 6-7. BASF/SABIC/Linde demo in Ludwigshafen inaugurated in April 2024, with a planned 2-3 years of operation for data.
items.potential: Covers cracker furnace firing emissions (literature: about 300 Mt/yr globally; not verified here).
items.bottleneck: Firm cheap power at hundreds of MW per cracker, and grid connection. Furnace fuel-gas by-products need a new outlet.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 keep their complexes; S5 gain large new loads.

items.name: SAF through incumbent refineries (HEFA co-processing and refinery conversions) under blend mandates
items.mechanism: Blend mandates (ReFuelEU 2% in 2025, rising to 6% in 2030) produce SAF partly in converted fossil refineries, keeping refinery assets and workers.
items.cost: IATA (December 2025): 1.9 Mt of SAF in 2025, 0.6% of jet fuel. SAF costs about 2x fossil jet, up to 5x in mandated markets per IATA, an interested party blaming supplier margins. Airlines paid a $2.9bn premium. My calculation (assumed 138 kg fuel per transatlantic one-way seat, jet $750/t): +$2-4 per seat at 2%, +$6-12 at 6%, +$103-206 at 100%.
items.energy: HEFA is feedstock-limited, not energy-limited. e-SAF needs large amounts of H2 plus CO2, where the verifier's point-source floors apply.
items.trl_and_scale: HEFA is TRL 9. Output is 0.6% of demand (2025) and was expected to reach 0.8% in 2026.
items.potential: Limited by waste-lipid feedstock. Beyond about 5-10% requires e-SAF or other biomass routes.
items.bottleneck: Feedstock (waste oils) and the market structure of mandated supply.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 refiners gain a new product. Airlines (consumers of fuel) oppose mandate costs (IATA). S1 are split over biofuel sustainability.

items.name: Shipping: dual-fuel methanol and ammonia fleets plus a global fuel standard (IMO Net-Zero Framework)
items.mechanism: A global GHG-intensity fuel standard and carbon price, with dual-fuel ships that can burn fossil or green fuel. Shipowners keep their fleets and fuel suppliers (including oil majors) supply the new fuels.
items.cost: Bio-methanol about $600-850/t vs grey $250-350/t and e-methanol $800-1,200/t (secondary sources). My calculation: green methanol at $700-1,000/t is +$20-36/GJ over VLSFO, about +$316-548 per TEU Asia-Europe, 0.3-0.55% of $100k cargo value. ETC 2018: under 1% on an imported pair of jeans.
items.energy: Methanol carries 19.9 GJ/t vs 41 GJ/t for VLSFO, so about twice the fuel mass.
items.trl_and_scale: Dual-fuel ships are TRL 9. Maersk burns 10-11 Mt/yr fuel-oil equivalent, of which 3% was alternative fuel in 2025; Goldwind green-methanol offtake of 500 kt/yr starts in 2026. IMO adoption was deferred on 17 October 2025 by 57 votes to 49 (Saudi motion), with a vote now due in October 2026, this month.
items.potential: Shipping is about 3% of global CO2 (literature). The binding global rule decides the outcome.
items.bottleneck: Politics (the October 2026 IMO vote) and green-fuel supply.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 and petrostates (Saudi Arabia) blocked or deferred in 2025. Pacific states and S8 (via a fund) and the EU support the framework. Shipowners favour global rules over a patchwork (inferred).

items.name: Electrochemical ironmaking (Electra low-temperature; Boston Metal molten oxide electrolysis)
items.mechanism: Reduce iron ore electrically without H2. Electra's process runs at about 60°C and can use lower-grade ores; its iron feeds incumbent EAFs (Nucor).
items.cost: Electra: $186M Series B, a $50M Breakthrough Energy Catalyst grant and an $8M Colorado tax credit; offtakes with Meta, Nucor and Toyota Tsusho. Costs not public.
items.energy: Bounded below by the Fe2O3 dissociation enthalpy of 2.05 MWh/t Fe (my calculation), so it cannot beat H2-DRI's 3.6 MWh/t by more than about 1.8x.
items.trl_and_scale: Electra's Colorado demonstration plant is due to start in mid-2026 at up to 500 t/yr, about 10^-6 of global iron output. Boston Metal suffered a critical equipment failure in Brazil on 30 January 2026, missed a financing milestone, and laid off 71 people with its Woburn facilities closing in April 2026. This was a scale-up and finance failure, not evidence against MOE chemistry.
items.potential: Long term; could handle low-grade ores that H2-DRI cannot (H2-DRI needs DR-grade pellets).
items.bottleneck: Scale-up capital and engineering, given decade-long timelines.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 incumbents (Nucor) are hedging through offtakes. S10 face high risk.

items.name: Stalled European H2-DRI flagships (evidence on what fails)
items.mechanism: Flagship projects for full H2-DRI conversion. Several have been cancelled or delayed, which shows where incumbents are actually binding.
items.cost: Stegra Boden: total cost above SEK 70bn. It closed a €1.4bn raise in June 2026 (Wallenberg-led), the start date is under review and may slip to 2027, and capacity is 5 Mt/yr at full build. ArcelorMittal halted DRI-EAF at Bremen and Eisenhüttenstadt and cancelled DRI at Dunkirk (2025). It is still going ahead with a €1.2bn EAF at Dunkirk (late 2028 or 2029), relying on scrap and imported metallics.
items.energy: See items 2 and 5.
items.trl_and_scale: First commercial-scale plant (Stegra) not yet operating as of October 2026.
items.potential: n/a
items.bottleneck: Renewable H2 price and availability, and EU gas and power prices. ArcelorMittal cited unfavourable policy and no viable H2 market.
