items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (ArcelorMittal) choose EAF without DRI. S7: the Swedish EPA withheld aid because of the gas start. S10 compare Stegra with Northvolt (Nordsip, October 2025).

items.name: CBAM plus phase-out of free allocation (EU carbon border adjustment)
items.mechanism: From 2026, importers of steel, cement, aluminium, fertilizer, H2 and electricity pay the EU ETS price on embedded emissions, while EU producers' free allowances phase out. This protects incumbents that invest in decarbonization from carbon leakage.
items.cost: Phase-in coefficient is 2.5% in 2026, 5% in 2027 and 10% in 2028, reaching 100% in 2034. My calculation: a 2.0 t CO2/t BF-BOF route at €70-100/EUA faces €140-200/t at full exposure, comparable to the green premium, but only about €4-5/t at 2026's 2.5%.
items.energy: n/a
items.trl_and_scale: Definitive phase started 1 January 2026. Certificates for 2026 imports can be bought from 1 February 2027.
items.potential: Makes the green premium cost-neutral against imports by the early 2030s.
items.bottleneck: The weak phase-in until about 2030. Austria and Germany lobbied to extend free allocation (S&P, October 2025). Export leakage is not covered.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 in the EU are split (they want both protection and free allowances). S8 exporters (India, South Africa) object. S7 in the EU gain fiscal revenue.

bottlenecks: Renewable hydrogen price and supply: every $1/kg of H2 adds about $55/t of steel. The gap between $5/kg and $1.5/kg (about $190/t) is the whole green-steel premium. IEA cut its 2030 low-emissions H2 outlook from 49 to 37 Mt/yr (GHR 2025), and ArcelorMittal, Linz, INNA and Sauda have cancelled.

Firm cheap electricity at scale: converting the EU's ~70 Mt of blast-furnace hot metal to H2-DRI needs about 250 TWh/yr, about 9% of EU electricity. Doing it worldwide needs about 4,800 TWh, about 16% of world electricity (my calculation). H2-DRI is already within about 1.8x of the 2.05 MWh/t Fe enthalpy floor, so efficiency cannot close this gap; only cheap power or relocating ironmaking can.

Cement CCS capture fraction is limited by heat: Brevik captures about 50% (400 kt/yr) because capture was sized to available waste heat, at an estimated ~€100/t (modelled). Going above 90% needs extra heat or power, and storage access (Northern Lights 1.5 Mt/yr, expanding to 5 Mt/yr) is scarce.

Demand-side willingness to pay is thin: the EU green steel premium is €150-200/t (Fastmarkets Q2 2026) with a narrow buyer pool. The premium is under 1% of car price but 9-14% of a 6% OEM margin, so it sits with the OEM, not the consumer.
Scale of the cheap levers: calcined-clay capacity enabling about 26 Mt/yr of cement vs about 4,000 Mt/yr global (<1%); SAF at 1.9 Mt = 0.6% of jet fuel (2025).

Policy timing: CBAM charges only 2.5% of embedded emissions in 2026, rising to 100% in 2034. The IMO Net-Zero Framework vote was deferred to October 2026 (57 to 49). DOE cancelled grants for Sublime and others ($7.5bn, October 2025).

Scale-up finance and engineering risk for new process routes: Boston Metal had an equipment failure, missed a financing milestone and laid off 71 people (February 2026). Stegra faced cost overruns and a delay to possibly 2027.
open_problems: Design a contract that splits a sub-1% end-product premium across the steel, OEM and consumer chain (a 'green premium pass-through' instrument, e.g. a per-car embodied-carbon label plus a pooled buyer club). The aim is to stop the premium landing in the 6% OEM margin. Test it against the actual Fastmarkets premium history.

Cement kiln capture beyond the waste-heat limit: which heat-integration or electrified regeneration options (heat pumps, oxyfuel, calcium looping) raise Brevik-type capture from 50% to 90% at under €100/t? Check each against the verifier's 0.11 GJ/t floor and the 0.72 GJ/t of exergy amine uses today.

An optimal split of ironmaking between incumbent and renewable-rich sites, minimizing cost subject to job retention (S6) and an import-security cap (S7). The arXiv 2510.00918 model gives 11-23% savings without a jobs constraint.

Gas-DRI lock-in: design a contract or regulation that guarantees a gas-to-H2 switch date or CCS on DRI off-gas, so that S1 accept gas-first DRI and S3 keep demand in the meantime. Al Reyadah has done 0.8 Mt/yr since 2016 as precedent.

Supply of calcined clay and SCMs as fly ash and slag decline with coal and blast-furnace closures: map clay deposits against cement plants to find which kilns can convert first (the cheapest abatement, often cost-negative).
Electrochemical iron from low-grade ores that H2-DRI cannot use (H2-DRI needs DR-grade pellets): what electricity price and ore grade make Electra-type routes beat H2-DRI, given the 2.05 MWh/t floor?

Can India's SECI auction (green ammonia at $570-745/t over 10 years) be copied for green HBI or e-methanol in other countries? Separate the contract-design effects (aggregated demand, 10-year term) from site effects (solar resource) before claiming it transfers.
Prediction target with a short feedback loop: the IMO vote this month (October 2026) and Stegra's first-production date are near-term realized outcomes that could calibrate the engine's forecasts.

key_claims.claim: Green steel's modelled premium is about $186-231/t, which is about $167-208 per car (under 1% of car price; GEI 2024, H2 at $5/kg, 0.9 t steel/car). The EU market premium assessed by Fastmarkets in Q2 2026 is €150-200/t, consistent with that. So the per-tonne premium is large, but the per-product premium is under 1%. That premium is still 9-14% of a 6% OEM EBIT margin (my calculation), so the barrier is who absorbs the cost, not consumer affordability.

Retrofitting CCS onto an existing cement kiln works at industrial scale. Brevik (Heidelberg Materials, Norway) has operated since June 2025 at a 400 kt/yr CO2 design (about 50% of the plant, sized by available waste heat). Capex is about €421M and the estimated abatement cost about €100/t CO2 (modelled). The first year of evoZero output was pre-sold.

surprises: H2-DRI has almost no efficiency headroom. H2 use (~55 kg/t) is about the stoichiometric 54 kg/t, and total electricity (~3.6 MWh/t) is within about 1.8x of the 2.05 MWh/t Fe2O3 dissociation-enthalpy floor (my calculation). So green steel is an electricity-price and location problem, and an idea engine looking for a cleverer reduction process is targeting the wrong lever.
Cement point-source capture is already thermodynamically better than DAC, at about 15% second-law efficiency vs 5-10%. Brevik's 50% capture is limited by waste heat, not by separation work.

In India's SECI auction (agreements reported June 2026), green ammonia came in at $570-745/t for 10 years, close to conflict-elevated grey ammonia prices. Meanwhile, comparable projects in Chile, Austria and Norway were cancelled. Contract design (aggregated demand, long tenor) appears to matter as much as technology. Delivery is still unproven: first output 2028-30.
ArcelorMittal is building the EAF but dropped the DRI (Dunkirk €1.2bn EAF, 2028-29; DRI cancelled in France and Germany). Incumbents are electrifying steelmaking but not ironmaking.
The green premium is negligible for consumers but material for OEMs (9-14% of a 6% EBIT margin), which explains the thin buyer pool despite the under-1% end-price effect.

Before its failure, Boston Metal had pivoted its Brazil plant from steel to recovering tin and niobium from mining waste to earn revenue. Its collapse was a financing and equipment event, not evidence against molten oxide electrolysis chemistry.

IATA, an interested party, reports that SAF in mandated EU and UK markets costs up to 5x fossil jet, attributing this to supplier margins rather than production cost. Yet per seat, a 6% blend is only about $6-12 on a transatlantic one-way (my calculation).

verifs.claim: Green steel's modelled premium is about $186-231/t, about $167-208 per car (under 1% of car price; GEI 2024, H2 at $5/kg, 0.9 t steel/car). Fastmarkets' Q2 2026 EU market premium of EUR150-200/t is consistent with this. The per-tonne premium is large but the per-product premium is under 1%, and it is still 9-14% of a 6% OEM EBIT margin, so the barrier is who absorbs the cost, not consumer affordability.
verifs.corrected_claim: Global Efficiency Intelligence (Hasanbeigi et al., "Green Steel Economics", July 2024) models the premium for H2-DRI-EAF steel over BF-BOF steel at $5/kg H2 with no carbon price. Across its seven countries the premium is about $186/t (EU) to $263/t (South Korea), which at the report's assumed 0.9 t of steel per car is about $167-237 per car. That is 1% or less of the average car price in each country. The figures by country are EU $186/t and $167/car; China $225/t and $203/car; US $226/t and $203/car; Brazil $219/t and $197/car; Australia $227/t and $204/car; Japan $231/t and $208/car; South Korea $263/t and $237/car. These are modelled values, not observed market prices. At the GEI average car prices, a $167-237 premium equals about 9% (EU, $30k car) to about 18% (South Korea or China, $22k car) of a 6% EBIT margin, which is an assumption the user supplied. The Fastmarkets EUR150-200/t Q2 2026 figure could not be checked against a primary source.
verifs.caveats:
1) The range leaves out the high end. $186-231/t covers only the EU through Japan. GEI's own country factsheets give South Korea $263/t and $237/car. The web page cited (globalefficiencyintel.com/green-steel-economics) shows only Japan ($231/t, $208/car) and China ($225/t). The $186/$167 figures come from the EU factsheet (factsheet_03_EU_240721.pdf), not from that page. I read the main PDF and five country factsheets (EU, US, Australia, Brazil, South Korea). The China and Japan figures come from the main report and the web page.

2) "Under 1%" is GEI's own wording for every country, but South Korea's numbers ($237 on a $22,000 car) work out to 1.08%. "About 1% or less" is the accurate phrasing. EU: 0.56%; Japan: 0.74% of $28k; China: 0.92% of $22k.

3) These are modelled levelized costs from a financial model of a greenfield plant, with 5% scrap and no carbon price, at $5/kg H2. GEI's own sensitivity runs show the premium disappearing at about $1.3-1.4/kg H2, or at higher H2 prices once a carbon price applies. The premium is therefore very sensitive to the H2 price and is not a fixed number.

4) The 0.9 t/car figure is GEI's assumption ("on average 0.9 ton of steel"). It is not measured. Heavier vehicles such as SUVs, or counting crude steel including yield losses, would raise the per-car figure.

5) The EBIT calculation is the user's own. The 6% margin is not from GEI and needs its own source. "9-14%" holds only for some pairings: EU 167/(0.06x30k)=9.3%, Japan 208/(0.06x28k)=12.4%. Reaching 14% needs about a $25k car. With GEI's own car prices, China and South Korea come out at 15-18%. The point that the barrier is margin absorption rather than consumer affordability still holds, and is stronger with these numbers.

6) I could not verify the Fastmarkets EUR150-200/t Q2 2026 figure. Web search was unavailable (session budget used up), the Fastmarkets URLs I tried returned 404, and the only mention I found is an unsourced comment in local scratch code. Even if the figure is correct, a market premium for "low-carbon" flat steel in Europe largely reflects scrap-EAF and mass-balance products, not H2-DRI-EAF. Calling it "consistent with" GEI's modelled H2-DRI premium compares different products and a market price with a model. At most it is the same order of magnitude (about $175-235/t at roughly 1.17 USD/EUR). It should not be presented as confirming the model until a primary Fastmarkets source is cited.

verifs.claim: Retrofitting CCS onto an existing cement kiln works at industrial scale. Brevik (Heidelberg Materials, Norway) has operated since June 2025 at a 400 kt/yr CO2 design (about 50% of the plant, sized by available waste heat). Capex is about €421M and the estimated abatement cost about €100/t CO2 (modelled). The first year of evoZero output was pre-sold.
verifs.caveats:
Checked against the GCCSI PDF (text extracted), the Heidelberg Materials press release of 18 June 2025, brevikccs.com, and ccsnorway.com, which is the PDF's footnote 4.

1. Most figures match the GCCSI PDF word for word. It gives operation from June 2025 on a retrofit of an operating plant that makes about 1 Mt/yr of cement. It gives capture capacity as "400,000 tpa CO2", with waste-heat availability "chosen as the basis for the capture capacity specified". It gives capex as "~€421 million" and the estimated abatement cost as "NOK 1150 (~€100) per tonne CO2". It says the first year's evoZero production "has already been pre-sold".

2. The "about 50% of the plant" figure is not in the GCCSI PDF. It comes from Heidelberg's 18 June 2025 press release, which says 400 kt is half the plant's emissions. The claim is correct, but cite Heidelberg for that number.

3. 400 kt/yr is design capacity, not measured output. Neither source reports how much CO2 was actually captured or stored in the first year. brevikccs.com says only that the plant "has been in operation since the summer of 2025" (official opening 17–18 June 2025). Heidelberg said subsea injection was due to start in August 2025. "Works at industrial scale" is supported as a commissioned plant, not as a demonstrated annual capture rate.

4. The abatement cost is an estimate with a narrow definition. GCCSI's source (ccsnorway.com) gives NOK 1,150/t as NOK 965/t in 2020 money, restated in 2024 money. It was NOK 842/t at the KS-2 stage, so the estimate has risen over time. It is a 25-year net-present-value figure for Brevik's part of the chain: capture, compression, intermediate storage and development of the CO2 hub. It is not an observed operating cost. €100 is GCCSI's own approximate currency conversion.

5. Capex: GCCSI's footnote for the ~€421M is a secondary source (EnergyWatch news), not company accounts.

6. Funding: the project relied on Norwegian state grants, avoided Norwegian carbon pricing and a green premium on evoZero. Its economics do not carry over directly to plants without those supports.

7. evoZero: with only about 50% of emissions captured, "near-zero" evoZero cement presumably means the captured CO2 is allocated to a subset of the plant's output. The sources checked do not spell this out, so treat that part as inference.

8. Context: the pre-sale shows there is demand at a premium. It does not by itself show that cement CCS is cheap.

items.name: Oil and gas methane abatement at no net cost (leak detection and repair, dry seals, vapour recovery, ending venting)
items.mechanism: Stop methane escaping upstream rather than remove it later. The captured gas is sold, so for a large share of measures the gas revenue pays for the abatement. About 80% of oil and gas methane comes from upstream operations. This is a conventional core (gas handling) with one imported mechanism (satellite and aerial measurement turning invisible leaks into attributable liabilities).
items.energy: Net energy GAIN. My calculation (scratchpad energy_side.py): 35 Mt CH4 recovered is about 1.75 EJ of gas at an LHV of 50 MJ/kg. Removing the same 1.04 Gt CO2e by DAC would cost 0.49 EJ at the thermodynamic floor, or 6.3 EJ at 6 GJ/t.
items.cost: IEA Global Methane Tracker 2026 (2025 data): more than 35 Mt CH4 avoidable at no net cost at average 2025 prices. The IEA says the economics improved in 2026 because higher prices followed the Middle East conflict. That no-net-cost claim fails where gas is stranded: Waha hub (Permian) prices were negative on a record 87 days in 2026 so far and averaged -$2.38/MMBtu (pgjonline, 2026).
items.potential: IEA 2026: 124 Mt CH4 from energy in 2025 (oil 45, coal 43, gas 36). About 85 Mt is avoidable with existing technology, and more than 35 Mt at no net cost. Nearly 100 bcm of gas is recoverable each year from leaks. My calculation: 35 Mt = 1.04 Gt CO2e at GWP100 (2.9 Gt at GWP20). That is 16x the entire global operational CCS capacity of 64 Mtpa.
items.bottleneck: Incentives and attribution, not technology. The US Waste Emissions Charge ($900-1,500/t CH4) was repealed under the CRA (signed 14 Mar 2025), and OBBBA delayed the fee to 2034. The EU Methane Regulation's import MRV-equivalence requirement starts 1 Jan 2027, but the Commission recommends no penalties for 2027-2029. Under policies in force, the IEA projects only about 20% reduction by 2030 against the 30% pledge.
items.permanence_or_durability: Avoided emissions are permanent. Abatement equipment needs ongoing LDAR; leaks recur without monitoring.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9. Measured: Permian methane intensity fell from 0.44% to 0.34% of production in 2025 (S&P aerial data), down nearly two-thirds since 2022. Absolute basin emissions stayed flat because production grew (confound: intensity is not emissions).
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: IEA frames abatement as gas recovered for sale. US independents lobbied for and won the fee repeal; EU-facing LNG exporters need MRV. S1/S2: top priority (methane drives ~30% of warming since pre-industrial per IEA). S7: energy-security framing, nearly 100 bcm recoverable. S8: benefits from cuts by the top 10 emitters (70% of fossil methane). S9: neutral to positive.

items.name: Elimination of routine flaring (gas capture, reinjection, gas-to-power, gas-to-products)
items.mechanism: Route associated gas that is now burned at oil wells to pipelines, reinjection, on-site power or chemicals. This also cuts unburnt methane from flares that burn inefficiently.
items.energy: My calculation: 151 bcm at an assumed 38 MJ/m3 is 5.7 EJ, or about 1,590 TWh of heat. Burned in a CCGT at 50% efficiency, that is about 800 TWh of electricity, roughly 2.7% of world electricity.
items.cost: World Bank (2024 data): $63B of energy wasted, about $0.42/m3 (roughly $12/MMBtu at delivered prices). Capture pays only where there is takeaway capacity. Wellhead value is negative in constrained basins (Waha).
items.potential: 2024 flaring was 151 bcm (+3 bcm; highest since 2007), emitting 389 Mt CO2e including 46 Mt CO2e of unburnt methane (about 2.6 kg CO2e per m3). The IEA puts another ~100 bcm/yr recoverable from ending non-emergency flaring.
items.bottleneck: Location and ownership. Nine countries account for 75% of flaring but under half of oil output, many of them NOCs or conflict zones. Flaring intensity has been flat for 15 years. Countries endorsing Zero Routine Flaring cut intensity 12% since 2012, while non-endorsers rose 25%; this is correlational and endorsers may self-select. Flare-to-compute is tiny so far: Crusoe's reported cumulative 2.5 bcf avoided is 0.047% of one year of global flaring (my calculation).
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 (Norway banned routine flaring in 1971). VIIRS satellite measurement of flaring is global and annual.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3/NOCs: revenue upside but capex on marginal fields. S7: energy security; flared gas equals Africa's annual gas use (World Bank). S8/S11: flaring harms communities in the Niger Delta and Iraq, so ending it is a strong co-benefit. S1: supportive.

items.name: Enhanced geothermal with oil and gas horizontal drilling and fracturing (Fervo Cape Station)
items.mechanism: Conventional core: oilfield horizontal drilling and multi-stage stimulation. Imported into geothermal, it creates engineered reservoirs in hot rock, giving firm 24/7 power that runs on the same rigs, crews and service companies as shale.
items.energy: Firm baseload. The Project Red pilot (3 MW) has generated since 2023 with no premature thermal decline (company-reported). Capacity factor ~90% assumed in my LCOE calculation.
items.cost: S-1/A (2026): Phase I overnight capex about $7,000/kW, long-term NOAK target $3,000/kW. Drilling time per well fell ~75% and per-foot cost ~70% from 2022 to 2025. Binding PPAs total 658 MW at $100-130/MWh (SCE, Shell and others). My modelled LCOE before tax credits: $89-104/MWh at $7,000/kW (7-9% WACC); $38-45/MWh at $3,000/kW. IEA (Dec 2024, modelled) projects next-generation geothermal at about $50/MWh by 2035.
items.potential: Cape site potential about 4.3 GW. 500 MW is under construction; first power is due late 2026 and about 100 MW by early 2027. Google has a 3 GW non-binding framework. IEA: up to 80% of geothermal investment uses skills transferable from oil and gas, and investment could reach $1T by 2035 (modelled).
items.bottleneck: FOAK capex 2.3x the target. Long-term reservoir thermal decline is not yet proven at 100+ MW scale. Interconnection: the median US queue time exceeds 5 years. Geothermal kept its US tax credits under OBBBA (2025) while wind and solar lost theirs.
items.permanence_or_durability: Plant life about 30 years. Durability depends on the reservoir heat-depletion rate, with make-up wells budgeted.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 7-8: a 3 MW pilot operating since 2023 and a 100 MW commercial phase commissioning in 2026-27. Fervo IPO'd in 2026 (ticker FRVO).
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: Shell is an offtaker; oil and gas companies (Devon, Chevron) invested in Fervo or in EGS pilots. S6: Fervo/SUU apprenticeship for oilfield-service workers, at least 22 registrants from 10 service firms (2024; small). S5/S10: utilities and hyperscalers buying firm clean power at $100-130/MWh. S1: broadly supportive; induced seismicity is the local concern (S11). S7 (US): bipartisan support.

items.name: Closed-loop geothermal (Eavor-Loop, Geretsried, Germany)
items.mechanism: Two deep vertical wells joined by multilateral horizontal branches form a sealed radiator. Working fluid circulates without contacting the formation, so no stimulation or fracturing is needed. Heat is extracted by conduction.
items.energy: Design: 8.2 MWe and up to 64 MWth for district heat, across four loops. Loop 1 delivered first grid power on 4 Dec 2025. Measured output per loop not yet published.
items.cost: Not disclosed per kW. Received EU Innovation Fund support. FOAK; first power slipped from H1 2025 to Dec 2025.
items.potential: Siting is not limited to permeable reservoirs. Heat-plus-power suits district heating in Europe.
items.bottleneck: Conductive heat flux into a closed loop is physically limited, so output per km of lateral is low. Economics depend on drilling cost per km; laterals were reportedly drilled in about half the earlier time. Loop 2 drilling was due to start in March 2026.
items.permanence_or_durability: Conductive drawdown over decades is the key unknown.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 7: the first loop of a 4-loop commercial plant is generating.
items.stakeholder_positions: S11: no fracturing, so lower seismic and groundwater concern. S3: uses directional-drilling skills. S7 (Germany/EU): heat security.

items.name: Superdeep geothermal via millimetre-wave drilling (Quaise)
items.mechanism: A gyrotron ablates rock with no downhole bit, aiming at 10-20 km depth and supercritical temperatures. Plants could then be sited at or repowering existing thermal plants.
items.energy: Not yet demonstrated for power. Gyrotron electrical energy per metre drilled is not published.
items.cost: Unknown. Quaise raised $134M (initial close, July 2026).
items.potential: Claimed near-universal siting. Unproven.
items.bottleneck: Depth demonstrated: about 100 m through granite in 2025, approaching 1 km in 2026. A target of 10+ km is 10x beyond that. Borehole stability, debris removal and energy per metre are open.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4-5; pilot plant targeted for as early as 2028 (claim).
items.stakeholder_positions: S5: repowering coal-plant sites would preserve grid connections and jobs (S6, S11). The claim is company-stated so far.

items.name: CO2 transport and storage run by oil majors (depleted fields and saline aquifers: Northern Lights, Porthos, Exxon Gulf Coast)
items.mechanism: Oil companies sell subsurface storage as a service to emitters, reusing reservoir characterisation, offshore operations and pipelines. Storage in depleted gas fields uses known seals and existing wells and data.
items.energy: Compression and transport are small next to capture. Capture energy is set by source concentration: the minimum is 0.11-0.22 GJ/t for kiln or flue gas versus 0.47 GJ/t from air (verifier).
items.cost: Exxon has about 16 Mtpa under contract with six customers (Apr 2025). Northern Lights and Porthos are state-supported; prices are not public.
items.potential: GCCSI 2025: 77 operating facilities with 64 Mtpa capacity, plus 47 under construction (44 Mtpa). My calculation: 64 Mtpa is 0.17% of fossil CO2; with the construction pipeline, 0.29%. Northern Lights first injected in Aug 2025 (1.5 Mtpa), with Phase 2 at 5+ Mtpa from 2028. Porthos (37 Mt total, 2.5 Mtpa) has slipped to 2027.
items.bottleneck: Capacity is nameplate, not tonnes actually stored. Much existing capacity is gas processing or EOR. Performance risk is real and its mechanism still applies: Gorgon stored 1.33 Mt in FY24-25, only 25% of reservoir CO2 removed against an 80% condition (about 5.3 Mt removed; IEEFA), because of pressure and water-management problems. US 45Q survives OBBBA with utilisation parity.
items.permanence_or_durability: Geological storage is ~1,000+ years if well integrity holds. Sleipner (since 1996) is the best measured long-run case.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 for storage; Mt/yr scale per hub.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: a core 'transition' business that reuses assets (Equinor, Shell, TotalEnergies, Exxon). S4: needs it for cement and process emissions. S1: split; many NGOs oppose it as a fossil-life extender, supporting it at most for cement and other process CO2. S11: pipeline-safety concerns (Satartia 2020). S10: wary after Gorgon.

items.name: Gas-fired power with post-combustion CCS (NZT Power UK; Calpine Baytown US)
items.mechanism: A conventional CCGT with an amine capture plant, with CO2 sent to a major's storage hub. Gives dispatchable low-carbon power that keeps gas demand.
items.energy: Verifier: minimum work for 4% CO2 flue gas at 95% capture is 0.22 GJ/t. A typical amine reboiler uses 2.5-3.5 GJ/t of ~120 C heat, which is about 0.6-0.8 GJ/t as exergy. That puts the second-law efficiency at roughly 25-35%, versus 5-10% for DAC. My estimate, modelled.
items.cost: NZT Power plus the Northern Endurance Partnership reached FID in Dec 2024, with about £4B of contracts across two Teesside CCS projects, under a UK dispatchable power agreement. Strike price not public.
items.potential: NZT: 742 MW, up to 2 Mtpa, operation 2028. Calpine Baytown: about 500 MW plus industrial steam, up to 2 Mtpa to Exxon storage, 2027-28. My calculation: 2 Mtpa at a 90% capacity factor is about 85% of gross CO2. At a 50-70% capacity factor, the design captures all of it.
items.bottleneck: FOAK cost and the economics of part-load and cycling. Residual emissions of 5-10% stack CO2 plus upstream methane. No commercial-scale gas-CCS plant has operating data yet. Boundary Dam (coal, 2014) is the nearest analogue; its underperformance mechanisms (solvent degradation, availability) partly apply.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 7-8 for gas-power CCS (first plants in construction).
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 and S5: strongly favoured, since gas demand is preserved. S7: firm power and industrial-cluster jobs (Teesside, S6). S1: largely opposed to new gas lock-in. S9: costs passed through via contracts for difference.

items.name: Interconnection and transmission expansion (cross-cutting enabler)
items.mechanism: Firm clean supply (geothermal, nuclear, gas-CCS, storage) and renewables cannot deliver without grid access. Reusing interconnection rights at retiring fossil sites is a fast-track lever.
items.energy: N/A
items.cost: Not quantified here.
items.potential: LBNL Queued Up 2026 (end-2025 data): about 8,200 active projects, 1,312 GW of generation plus 749 GW of storage. 549 GW have interconnection agreements but are unbuilt. Queued gas rose 86% to 253 GW, while solar fell 19%.
items.bottleneck: Median time from interconnection request to commercial operation exceeded 5 years for projects built in 2025, up from 22 months in 2008. Example: PJM said Crane's (TMI-1) transmission upgrades would take until 2031, so Constellation sought to transfer injection rights from its Eddystone fossil unit to restart in 2027.
items.trl_and_scale: Institutional, not technical.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5: favoured where rate-based. S11: siting opposition. S7: permitting reform contested. S3: gas plants are now the fastest-growing queue entrants.

items.name: Nuclear: restarts and SMRs (Palisades, Crane, Darlington BWRX-300, Linglong One)
items.mechanism: Firm zero-carbon power run by utilities. Restarts reuse existing licensed sites and grid connections; SMRs aim at factory learning.
items.energy: Firm; capacity factor of 90%+ for the existing US fleet.
items.cost: Darlington (OPG, approved 2025): C$20.9B for 4 x 300 MW, about C$17,400/kW or US$12,500/kW. The first unit is C$7.7B, about C$25,700/kW. My modelled LCOE at US$12,500/kW is about $91/MWh at 4% WACC and $133/MWh at 7% (60 years, 93% capacity factor).
items.potential: Darlington unit 1 in service in 2030, the rest mid-2030s. Linglong One (CNNC, 125 MWe) targeted commercial operation in H1 2026 (secondary source; not verified). Palisades restart slipped from Aug 2025 into 2026 and was still pre-restart as of July 2026. Crane is targeting 2027.
items.bottleneck: FOAK capex and the cost of capital (LCOE nearly doubles across WACC scenarios). Schedule slips (Palisades about 1 year). Fuel (HALEU) for advanced designs.
items.trl_and_scale: Restarts TRL 9. BWRX-300 TRL 7 (first unit under construction). ACP100 TRL 8.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5/S7/S10: rising support, with hyperscaler PPAs. S6: union jobs. S1: split. S8: cost concerns. S11: waste and siting.

items.name: Low-emissions hydrogen (electrolytic and gas plus CCS) for industry
items.mechanism: Replace grey hydrogen in refining and ammonia, and use it as a reductant for steel. Blue hydrogen lets gas producers keep their feedstock.
items.energy: Electrolysis uses about 50-55 kWh/kg. Blue hydrogen depends on high capture rates and low upstream methane, which links it to item 1.
items.cost: Not quantified here. The IEA cites persistent cost and offtake barriers.
items.potential: IEA GHR 2025: low-emissions hydrogen grew 10% in 2024 to about 1 Mt in 2025, under 1% of hydrogen production. Announced 2030 output fell from 49 to 37 Mtpa in one year, with electrolysis behind 80%+ of the drop. FID'd plus operating projects reach 4.2 Mtpa by 2030.
items.bottleneck: Offtake willingness to pay, and electricity cost and carbon intensity. Infrastructure. Projects are being cancelled faster than they reach FID.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 8-9 for components; scale is lagging.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: retreating. bp cut transition investment to $1.5-2B/yr in its Feb 2025 reset; Shell said hydrogen, CCS and low-carbon fuels were 'not delivering adequate returns'. S4: needed for steel and ammonia. S1: skeptical of blue hydrogen.

items.name: Oil and gas company capital allocation to transition businesses (the incumbent-participation signal)
items.mechanism: Majors decide whether to redeploy capex and skills into geothermal, storage-as-a-service, methane and CCS, or to return cash.
items.energy: N/A
items.cost: IEA WEI 2025: 2025 is the third year in which oil and gas companies reinvest under 50% of cash flow, with 30% going to buybacks and 23% to dividends. Upstream investment is about $570B (-4%). bp: transition investment $1.5-2B/yr, more than $5B below prior guidance (Feb 2025). Shell: low-carbon target cut to 10% of capex by 2030, from 15-20%.
items.potential: Clean investment was about $2.2T versus $1.1T for fossil fuels globally in 2025. The incumbents' share of clean investment is small.
items.bottleneck: Returns: transition businesses return less than upstream. Investors (S10) reward cash returns. Geothermal and storage-as-a-service are the exceptions that fit the core skill base and earn utility-like PPA returns.
items.trl_and_scale: N/A
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: retreat from renewables and hydrogen but continued CCS and some geothermal stakes. S10: favours payouts. S1: criticises the backsliding.

items.name: Long-duration energy storage (Form Energy iron-air, 100 hours)
items.mechanism: Multi-day storage that firms renewables and could cut the need for gas peakers. Built on cheap iron and air chemistry.
items.energy: Round-trip efficiency is low for iron-air (company targets roughly 40%; not verified here).
items.cost: Not disclosed.
items.potential: First commercial pilot: Great River Energy, Cambridge MN, 1.5 MW / 150 MWh, targeted to operate by late 2025. Operating status not verified in this search.
items.bottleneck: No published field performance yet. Value depends on market design for multi-day adequacy.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 7 (MW-scale pilot).
items.stakeholder_positions: S5: co-op utilities are piloting it. S3: competes with gas peakers. S1: supportive.

bottlenecks: Stranded associated gas: Waha hub (Permian) prices were negative on a record 87 days in 2026 (average -$2.38/MMBtu year to date, record 78 consecutive days). Where captured gas has negative value, the IEA's 'no net cost' methane and flaring economics invert and flaring is rewarded.

Policy retreat on methane in the US: the Waste Emissions Charge ($900-1,500/t CH4) was repealed under the CRA (14 Mar 2025) and OBBBA delayed the fee to 2034. The EU import MRV requirement starts 2027, but the Commission recommends no penalties for 2027-2029. The IEA projects only about 20% methane reduction by 2030 under policies in force, versus the 30% pledge.

Grid access: US median time from interconnection request to commercial operation exceeded 5 years for 2025 builds. 2,061 GW is queued, and 549 GW holds interconnection agreements but is unbuilt (LBNL 2026).

CCS scale and performance: 64 Mtpa operating capacity is 0.17% of fossil CO2 (nameplate, not stored). Gorgon stored only 25% of removed CO2 in FY24-25 against an 80% condition. Porthos slipped to 2027.

EGS first-of-a-kind capex: about $7,000/kW for Fervo Phase I versus the $3,000/kW target. My modelled LCOE is $89-104/MWh now versus about $40/MWh at target, and long-term thermal decline at 100+ MW is unproven.

Incumbent capital allocation: oil and gas companies reinvest under 50% of cash flow, with 53% going to buybacks and dividends (IEA WEI 2025). bp cut transition capex to $1.5-2B/yr; Shell cut its low-carbon target to 10% of capex by 2030.
Nuclear SMR FOAK cost: Darlington is about US$12,500/kW for 4 units and C$25,700/kW for unit 1. My modelled LCOE is $91-133/MWh, highly sensitive to WACC.
Hydrogen offtake: the announced 2030 low-emissions pipeline fell 49 to 37 Mtpa in one year. Output was about 1 Mt in 2025, under 1% of hydrogen production.
open_problems: A stranded-gas sink design problem: find a flexible, relocatable load or product that pays a positive netback for gas at negative-price hubs and remote flares. Candidates are modular gas power with CCS feeding co-located compute or DAC, small-scale ammonia or methanol, and reinjection for pressure support. Score each with executed netback and CO2e arithmetic. Flare-to-compute so far is about 0.05% of one year's flaring.

Satellite plus aerial MRV that meets EU Methane Regulation 'equivalence' for US LNG before 2027. Incumbents (LNG exporters) need this and climate NGOs want it, so it is a rare win-win product. The work is mapping measurement uncertainty to the regulatory methodology due by Aug 2027.

Make methane abatement bankable without a US fee: design an instrument that pays for verified avoided CH4 at the asset level, such as differentiated-gas premia, buyer standards or OGMP 2.0 Level 5 certificates. Check them against the 35 Mt no-net-cost and 85 Mt technical potentials and against measured basin intensity versus absolute emissions.

EGS cost-down path from $7,000/kW to $3,000/kW: decompose capex (wells versus surface plant versus stimulation) and test which oilfield learning curves (pad drilling, rig-days per well, PDC bits) transfer. Quantify thermal-decline risk from Project Red and Cape data once public.

Imported-mechanism combinations at shared subsurface sites: CO2 storage plus geothermal heat from the brine produced for pressure management (the Gorgon failure mechanism); depleted gas fields reused for both storage and heat; retiring coal-plant interconnections reused for geothermal or nuclear, as the Crane/Eddystone transfer did. These need executed reservoir-pressure and heat-balance calculations.
Closed-loop geothermal physics: what heat flux per km of lateral is achievable over 30 years given conductive limits, and does Eavor's measured Loop 1 output support 8.2 MWe from four loops?

Gas-CCS operation: capture-rate and solvent-energy performance at part load and under cycling. Residual stack plus upstream methane per MWh is needed for a fair comparison with geothermal and nuclear.

Workforce matching: quantify which oilfield-service roles map to geothermal, CCS and plugging of abandoned wells by region (S6), and the timing against shale downturns. Evidence so far is the IEA's 80% investment-skill overlap estimate and small apprenticeship numbers (22 registrants).

key_claims.claim: IEA Global Methane Tracker 2026 (2025 data): energy-sector methane was 124 Mt. Over 35 Mt is avoidable at no net cost at 2025 average prices, and about 85 Mt with existing technology. By my calculation (GWP100 29.8), 35 Mt is about 1.04 Gt CO2e, 16x global operational CCS capacity (64 Mtpa), and it yields about 1.75 EJ of saleable gas instead of consuming energy. This is the largest incumbent-compatible, physics-favourable lever, but the economics fail where gas is stranded (Waha). Note: the IEA page returned 403 to my fetch; the numbers come from search snippets of the IEA page and a secondary summary.

Fervo S-1/A (SEC, 2026): drilling time per well fell ~75% and per-foot drilling cost ~70% from 2022 to 2025. Cape Station Phase I is about $7,000/kW overnight capex, targeting $3,000/kW. 658 MW of binding PPAs are signed at $100-130/MWh. First power is due late 2026 and about 100 MW by early 2027, with 500 MW under construction. This is the strongest measured evidence that an oil and gas skill set (horizontal drilling and fracturing) can be redeployed into firm clean power. Verified directly from the filing.

surprises: Avoidable methane dwarfs all capture. The IEA's no-net-cost methane alone (about 1.0 Gt CO2e, GWP100) is 16x the world's entire operating CCS capacity and recovers energy (about 1.75 EJ) rather than consuming it. DAC of the same tonnage would need 6.3 EJ at 6 GJ/t.
Negative gas prices undercut 'free' methane abatement. Waha prices were negative on a record 87 days in 2026, so in the Permian, the largest US basin, recovered gas can be worth less than zero.

Permian methane intensity fell by nearly two-thirds from 2022 to 2025 (0.34% in 2025), yet absolute basin emissions stayed flat because production rose. Headline intensity gains are confounded by output growth.
Flare-to-compute, often cited as the poster child of incumbent-friendly climate tech, has avoided cumulatively only about 0.047% of one year's global flaring (Crusoe's 2.5 bcf versus 151 bcm/yr).
Fervo's FOAK geothermal PPAs ($100-130/MWh) already overlap the modelled LCOE range of the Darlington SMR ($91-133/MWh), at roughly half the capex per kW ($7,000 versus about $12,500).

Gas is now the fastest-growing US interconnection-queue entrant (+86% to 253 GW in 2025), while solar, wind and storage fell 16-19%. Point-source capture on new gas (25-35% second-law efficiency, my estimate) is thermodynamically far better than DAC (5-10%), but locks in upstream methane.

Under OBBBA (July 2025), geothermal and nuclear kept their US tax credits while wind and solar lost theirs, which turns the oil-and-gas-skill technologies into the politically durable US clean options.

verifs.claim: IEA Global Methane Tracker 2026 (2025 data): energy-sector methane was 124 Mt. Over 35 Mt is avoidable at no net cost at 2025 average prices, and about 85 Mt with existing technology. At GWP100 29.8, 35 Mt is about 1.04 Gt CO2e, 16x global operational CCS capacity (64 Mtpa), and it yields about 1.75 EJ of saleable gas instead of consuming energy. This is the largest incumbent-compatible, physics-favourable lever, but the economics fail where gas is stranded (Waha).
verifs.corrected_claim: IEA Global Methane Tracker 2026 (2025 data) estimates methane from fossil fuel operations at 124 Mt/yr: oil 45, coal 43, gas 36. That is not the whole energy sector, because bioenergy adds another 20 Mt, so energy-related methane is about 144 Mt. Nearly 85 Mt (about 70% of fossil methane) can be abated with existing technology, and more than 35 Mt could be avoided at no net cost at average 2025 energy prices. Of that 35 Mt, nearly 30 Mt is upstream oil and gas; the rest is mostly coal. At GWP100 29.8 (AR6, fossil CH4), 35 Mt is about 1.04 Gt CO2e, roughly 16x a 64 Mtpa operational CCS capacity (a figure I could not verify here). Recovered gas comes to about 1.75 EJ at 50 MJ/kg LHV, or about 1.9 EJ at the 55 MJ/kg the IEA itself uses. It is an upper bound, because the coal share and some measures (flaring or destruction rather than capture) produce no saleable gas. IEA says the economics look even better in 2026 because the Middle East conflict is pushing fuel prices up. Economics are weaker where gas is stranded or priced locally far below the average, as at Waha. That point is the author's own; it is not from the IEA.
verifs.caveats:
Primary source checked: the IEA key-findings page, read from the Wayback Machine snapshot of 2026-09-24 (web.archive.org/web/20260924025155/https://www.iea.org/reports/global-methane-tracker-2026/key-findings). The live page returned 403 and a Cloudflare bot check, which I did not try to bypass. The web-search budget was used up, so I could not check secondary sources.

Verified word for word against the page:
- 124 Mt, with the 45/43/36 split and the extra 20 Mt from bioenergy.
- "Around 70% ... nearly 85 Mt" abatable with existing technology.
- "More than 35 Mt could be avoided at no net cost, based on average energy prices in 2025."
- "Nearly 30 Mt" of upstream oil and gas abatable at no net cost.

Caveats that change how the claim can be used:

1. **Wrong label.** The 124 Mt covers fossil-fuel operations only, so calling it "energy-sector" is mislabelled. The total including bioenergy is about 144 Mt.

2. **Modelled, not measured.** The 124 Mt is an IEA estimate "based on measured, satellite, and inferred data". Measured data are limited or absent for most of the top 10 emitters; for Russia, Venezuela and Indonesia there are none. Uncertainty is high, as the IEA itself says.

3. **No-net-cost depends on prices.** The IEA prices recovered gas at average 2025 energy prices, so the "no net cost" result is price-dependent. Where gas is regulated, stranded or has negative prices (Waha), the economics weaken. The IEA's long-standing point that measures already at no net cost go unadopted for non-price reasons (who owns the gas, infrastructure, information) also applies.

4. **The CCS comparison is not like-for-like.** CO2e at GWP100 is a weighted equivalence, while CCS capacity is physical tonnes of CO2. Methane is short-lived: at GWP20 (about 82.5) the same 35 Mt is about 2.9 Gt CO2e, so the choice of metric matters. I did not verify the 64 Mtpa figure for operational CCS capacity; it is plausibly the Global CCS Institute's 2025 number.

5. **The energy figure is a ceiling.** The 1.75 EJ uses a lower-heating-value assumption of 50 MJ/kg, while the IEA uses 55 MJ/kg. It is an upper bound because part of the 35 Mt is coal mine methane and some measures destroy the gas rather than sell it. Electrifying pneumatic devices also uses a small amount of electricity.

6. **The ranking is a judgement.** "Largest incumbent-compatible, physics-favourable lever" is the author's judgement, not an IEA statement. The IEA does call upstream oil and gas abatement "among the most effective ways to reduce methane".

verifs.claim: Fervo S-1/A (SEC, 2026): drilling time per well fell ~75% and per-foot drilling cost ~70% from 2022 to 2025. Cape Station Phase I is about $7,000/kW overnight capex, targeting $3,000/kW. 658 MW of binding PPAs are signed at $100-130/MWh. First power is due late 2026 and about 100 MW by early 2027, with 500 MW under construction. This is the strongest measured evidence that an oil and gas skill set (horizontal drilling and fracturing) can be redeployed into firm clean power. Verified directly from the filing.
verifs.corrected_claim:
Fervo Energy S-1/A, Amendment No. 1 (filed with the SEC 4 May 2026, Reg. No. 333-295165). It reports these figures:
- Drilling: "days spent drilling to total depth per well" fell about 75% from 2022 to 2025, and per-foot drilling cost fell about 70% over the same period. This is self-reported ("Source: Fervo Data"), and it held while the wells got deeper: Project Red wells were about 7,500 ft TVD / 11,000 ft MD; Cape Phase I wells are about 9,000 ft TVD / 14,000 ft MD with laterals of about 5,000 ft.
- Cost: the company's estimate of capex to build one 50 MW GeoBlock was about $7,000/kW as of 31 Dec 2025, covering wellfield, surface facilities and plant. The filing says this "outcompetes" nuclear and SMR overnight capital costs. The long-term goal is an Nth-of-a-kind cost of $3,000/kW.
- Contracts: 658 MW of binding PPAs are signed across the portfolio (SCE, Shell, Clean Power Alliance, Desert Community Energy, Google/NV Energy). They have about 15 years of remaining term and about $7.2B of "potential revenue backlog". The contract prices are not disclosed. The $100-130/MWh range is Rystad's estimate of what clean firm power in general can command, not Fervo's contracted price. The illustrative unit economics assume about $115/MWh.
- Schedule: the company expects first power from the 500 MW Cape Station by late 2026 and about 100 MW operating by early 2027, and describes about 500 MW (Phases I+II) as under construction. These are forward-looking expectations.
verifs.caveats:
1. The PPA price is the material error. The filing never states Fervo's contract prices; "$100-130 per megawatt-hour" is Rystad market commentary. A rough implied average from the backlog is about $7.2B / (658 MW x 8,760 h x ~0.85-0.9 CF x ~15 yr) ≈ $90-100/MWh. That is my own back-of-envelope estimate, not a disclosed figure, and it is sensitive to start dates and capacity factor.

2. "Measured" applies only to the drilling learning curve, and even that is company data from a chart, not audited or independently verified. The $7,000/kW is an estimate of what a GeoBlock costs to build, not a realized figure from a plant in operation, and $3,000/kW is an aspiration. At the filing date no Cape Station power had been delivered. The only operating evidence is the small Project Red pilot.

3. "500 MW under construction" needs context: Phase II capex is about $940M, "a majority of which remains unfunded". Nevada underground-injection permits run on renewed temporary 30-day permits. The first-power date was an expectation as of May 2026, and I could not check whether it has slipped by Oct 2026 because my web search budget was exhausted.

4. The drilling percentages compare 2022 wells with 2025 wells at different depths and lateral lengths, so this is a mixed metric. It also comes from one operator at one or two sites, which makes it a learning-curve anecdote rather than an industry-wide result.

5. The filing does explicitly frame EGS as reusing oil and gas technology, supply chains and workforce. So the "oil and gas skill set redeployed into firm clean power" reading is fair as a strategic framing. But "strongest measured evidence" overstates it: this is a pre-revenue IPO prospectus making promotional, forward-looking claims.
