title: Policy and market mechanisms with broad coalitions

items.name: US 45Q carbon-capture credit survived the 2025 OBBBA rollback and was made more generous for EOR and utilization
items.mechanism: A per-tonne production tax credit for captured and stored CO2: $85/t point-source and $180/t DAC in dedicated geologic storage, transferable for cash. OBBBA (signed 4 Jul 2025) gave EOR and utilization parity with dedicated storage; before, EOR/utilization got at most $60/t. Inflation indexing was kept from 2027 on a 2025 base, and foreign-entity-of-concern limits were added. It is a pull subsidy that pays incumbents to capture rather than taxing them.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3, S4 and S5 support it; EOR parity is a direct win for S3 (Enverus estimated a 40% cut in some E&P costs). S6 unions belong to the Carbon Capture Coalition. Some S1/S2 accept CCS, while fiscal watchdogs (Taxpayers for Common Sense) and most S1 oppose EOR parity because the stored CO2 helps produce more oil. S7 is bipartisan: this is the only major carbon-specific IRA credit the 2025 Congress strengthened.
items.cost: My calculation, a bound rather than a forecast: paying $85/t on all 37.4 Gt of fossil CO2 would cost $3.2 trillion a year. 45Q therefore scales only for niche or concentrated sources, or with very cheap storage.
items.potential: The US runs 33 of about 70 operational CCS projects worldwide, with more than 300 in development (Global CCS Institute, 2025).
items.bottleneck: The fiscal cost per tonne. Parity also weakens the climate value per dollar, since EOR tonnes can raise oil output. Net-lifecycle accounting is unresolved.
items.trl_and_scale: Policy in force since 2008, with IRA (2022) and OBBBA (2025) revisions.
items.permanence_or_durability: Survived two changes of party control; begin-construction rules and transferability preserved.
items.energy: Point-source floor is 0.11-0.22 GJ/t (verifier) against roughly 0.47 GJ/t for air, so the $85 vs $180 split roughly tracks the thermodynamic gap.

items.name: OBBBA as a natural experiment: credits for incumbent constituencies survived, credits for new entrants were cut
items.mechanism: The same 2025 law ended EV credits (Sept 2025), set wind/solar 45Y/48E cliffs (begin construction by about June/July 2026 or in service by end-2027), ended 45V hydrogen at end-2027 rather than 2033, and ended home electrification credits at end-2025. It kept 45Q, kept 45U nuclear (with a bonus) and extended 45Z biofuels to 2031.
items.stakeholder_positions: The surviving credits each have an S3/S4/S6 or farm-state constituency: 45Q (oil and gas), 45Z (agriculture), 45U (utilities and unions). The cut credits mostly benefited new entrants and S9 consumers.
items.bottleneck: A credit's political survival depends on who receives the money, not on abatement per dollar.
items.potential: The design rule is to route climate support through existing high-carbon firms and their workers rather than around them.
items.trl_and_scale: Enacted 4 Jul 2025.

items.name: US methane Waste Emissions Charge: legislated, then repealed and delayed before collecting anything
items.mechanism: The IRA 2022 set a fee on oil and gas facilities above 25,000 tCO2e/yr: $900/t CH4 for 2024, $1,200 for 2025 and $1,500 from 2026. Congress disapproved EPA's implementing rule (40 CFR Part 99) under the Congressional Review Act in Feb-Mar 2025 (Senate 52-47). OBBBA then pushed the first assessment to 2034 emissions at $1,500/t.
items.stakeholder_positions: S1 (Sierra Club) and S2 supported it. Western Energy Alliance and most of S3 opposed it, although some majors had earlier backed direct methane regulation. S7 split along party lines.
items.cost: My calculation: $1,500/t CH4 is about $50/tCO2e at GWP100 (AR6 fossil, 29.8) and $18/tCO2e at GWP20, a moderate carbon price. It still failed politically.
items.bottleneck: A penalty-only design with no compensating revenue for the payers. Fee-type instruments on S3 lost every US vote in 2025.
items.potential: The verifier shows atmospheric methane removal costs about 8.8 GJ/t CO2e (GWP100) in fan work alone, so methane must be cut at concentrated sources. This makes source policy (fees, standards, import MRV) the main lever.
items.trl_and_scale: Statute still on the books with no operative rule; earliest assessment covers 2034 emissions.

items.name: EU ETS: covered emissions halved since 2005, mostly in power, while free allocation shielded industry
items.mechanism: A cap-and-trade system with a Market Stability Reserve. Heavy industry receives free allowances, being phased out against CBAM from 2026.
items.stakeholder_positions: S5 power has adapted. S4 accepted it because of free allocation and now lobbies on CBAM. S1 criticises the windfalls from free allocation. S7: in 2025 member states worried about inflation delayed ETS2 (buildings and road fuel) from 2027 to 2028, with a €45 price-release valve in its first 3 years.
items.potential: Verified emissions: about -50% vs 2005; -5% in 2024 vs 2023 (power -12%, industry roughly flat); -1.3% in 2025 vs 2024. 2030 target -62%. Revenue €43.6bn in 2023, of which €33bn went to member states (Wikipedia citing the Commission).
items.bottleneck: Industry abatement has been close to flat; the confound is that free allocation weakens the marginal signal and fertiliser/cement output swings dominate. Extending pricing to consumers (ETS2) runs into affordability politics.
items.trl_and_scale: In operation since 2005, covering power, industry, aviation and, from 2024-25, maritime (about 72 Mt reported in its first year).
items.permanence_or_durability: 20 years old and survived several price collapses. The consumer extension is the fragile part.

items.name: CBAM: EU border adjustment, simplified before its definitive phase
items.mechanism: Importers of iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, cement, hydrogen and electricity buy certificates matching embedded emissions, which levels the field as free allocation is withdrawn. The Omnibus Regulation (adopted 8 Oct 2025, in force 20 Oct 2025) set a 50 t/yr per-importer mass threshold that exempts about 90% of importers while keeping about 99% of emissions in scope. It also postponed certificate surrender to 2027. The definitive phase began 1 Jan 2026.
items.stakeholder_positions: EU S4 (steel, cement) supports it as protection, as do many S1. S8 trading partners such as India and South Africa have objected that it is unilateral and discriminatory (documented positions, not re-verified this session). S9 effect is small in the EU.
items.bottleneck: MRV of embedded emissions abroad, and the fact that CBAM revenue flows to the EU rather than to exporting countries (a justice gap for S8). Export competitiveness is not covered.
items.potential: It is the enforcement backbone that lets free allocation be phased out without carbon leakage.
items.trl_and_scale: Definitive phase from 2026; first surrender in 2027.

items.name: Carbon contracts for difference (Germany's Klimaschutzverträge)
items.mechanism: Reverse auctions in which firms bid the subsidy they need per tonne avoided. 15-year two-sided contracts pay the gap between the abatement cost and the ETS price, only after verified annual reductions.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 participates: round 1 covered chemicals, paper, glass, metals and sugar, and about 130 firms expressed interest in round 2. The chemical industry association (VCI) welcomed it but called it 'no panacea' and wants lower energy prices as well. S1 is generally supportive because it is pay-for-performance.
items.cost: Round 1 (15 Oct 2024): 15 contracts, up to €2.8bn, 17 Mt CO2e over 15 years. My calculation gives a maximum of about €165/t, an upper bound because the funds are 'unlikely to be fully used'. Round 2 is budgeted at a 'low double-digit billion' euros, including CCS; the programme claims 350 Mt potential by 2045 (modelled).
items.bottleneck: Budget: 17 Mt over 15 years is about 1 Mt/yr, a rounding error against German industrial emissions. It also depends on the federal Climate and Transformation Fund.
items.trl_and_scale: Pilot round awarded; payouts are retrospective.

items.name: Advance market commitments for durable carbon removal (Frontier, Microsoft)
items.mechanism: Corporate buyers pre-commit to buy durable removal (>1,000 years) to pull technologies down the cost curve. Frontier is a $1.8bn AMC to 2040, targeting <$100/t and >0.5 Gt/yr capacity, with members including Stripe, Google, Shopify, Anthropic, JPMorgan and Salesforce.
items.stakeholder_positions: S10 and tech buyers are the demand side. S3 (Occidental/1PointFive) sells into it. S1 is split: supportive of durable removal, wary of offsetting continued emissions. Buyers are drawn by the volunteer moral premium, not by compliance.
items.potential: Microsoft FY2025: 45 Mt contracted with 21 suppliers, more than double FY24 and 9x 2023; about 78 Mt since June 2023 (secondary reporting). Durable CDR contracts were 29.6 Mt in 2025, 42.5 Mt cumulative (ClimeFi via secondary). In 2024 about 8 Mt was purchased but only 318.6 kt delivered (CDR.fyi 2024 review).
items.bottleneck: Delivery and buyer concentration. About 1.2% of contracted durable CDR had been delivered by end-2025 (about 0.5 Mt, my calculation). At the 2024 delivery rate the backlog would take about 130 years. Microsoft was about 90% of 2025 durable volume, a single-buyer market.
items.energy: DAC floor about 0.47 GJ/t; real 5-10+ GJ/t (verifier).
items.trl_and_scale: Commercial pilots; contracted volumes are tens of Mt, delivered volumes under 1 Mt/yr.

items.name: Montreal Protocol, Kigali Amendment and the US AIM Act: the clearest example of a policy backed by industry and NGOs together
items.mechanism: A scheduled phasedown of a gas class (HFCs) with predictable timelines, Multilateral Fund payments to developing countries, and trade measures against non-parties. Industry backed it because incumbent chemical makers own the patented substitutes (HFOs), so the phasedown creates their market.
items.stakeholder_positions: AIM Act (Dec 2020): bipartisan (Kennedy R / Carper D), endorsed by the US Chamber of Commerce, AHRI, the Alliance for Responsible Atmospheric Policy and NRDC. S8 was brought in through slower schedules and Multilateral Fund money.
items.potential: Kigali adopted 15 Oct 2016, in force 1 Jan 2019; ratified by 172 states plus the EU as of Apr 2026. Developed countries reach 15% of baseline by 2036; Group 1 developing countries 20% by 2045; high-ambient-temperature countries 2047. Modelled: more than 80 Gt CO2e avoided by 2050 and up to 0.5 C of warming by 2100. The AIM Act cuts US production and import by 85% over 15 years.
items.bottleneck: The template needs a substitute that the incumbents themselves sell. For CO2 from fossil fuels no drop-in substitute exists, except that stored carbon can be produced by the same firms, which is the takeback logic.
items.trl_and_scale: Global, near-universal.

items.name: Carbon takeback obligation (Allen, Jenkins et al., Joule 2021), with a partial EU precedent in the NZIA storage obligation
items.mechanism: Fossil producers and importers must store a rising fraction of the CO2 from the carbon they sell, reaching 100% at net zero. This makes the extractor responsible for the fix, as in extended producer responsibility, without a tax on consumers. The EU Net-Zero Industry Act (Reg. 2024/1735) sets a 50 Mt/yr CO2 injection-capacity objective by 2030 and obliges EU oil and gas licence holders to contribute pro rata. This is from my own knowledge; the primary text was not retrievable this session.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 benefits relative to a carbon tax because it keeps its business and earns a storage revenue line, as with Equinor/Northern Lights. S1 is wary of fossil lock-in and moral hazard. S9 pays through product prices. S2 (Oxford Net Zero) backs it as a backstop.
items.cost: The paper's modelling finds the cost to the world economy no higher than global carbon-price scenarios of similar ambition. My bound: 10% of CO2 stored at $80-150/t adds $3.4-6.5 per barrel; 100% adds $34-64/bbl, or $3-5.6 trillion a year on today's 37.4 Gt. Only the early fractions are cheap.
items.bottleneck: Storage build-out rate. The NZIA's 50 Mt is about 4-5% of EU ETS stationary emissions (my calculation, assuming about 1.1 Gt). Late-stage fractions need DAC or BECCS for diffuse emissions at 10-20x the thermodynamic floor.
items.energy: Point-source floor 0.11-0.22 GJ/t; the 50 Mt objective at the floor needs only about 5.5-11 PJ. The real constraint is capex and storage, not thermodynamics.
items.trl_and_scale: Concept modelled; first partial legal form (NZIA) adopted 2024.

items.name: Visible consumer carbon prices lose and invisible industrial prices survive (Canada 2025), with a counter-case where visible spending defended a price (Washington 2024)
items.mechanism: Canada: PM Carney signed a directive on 14 Mar 2025 removing the consumer fuel charge from 1 Apr 2025, despite rebates such as an average $422 in Saskatchewan in 2019, and kept the industrial output-based pricing system. Washington: 61.95% of voters rejected Initiative 2117, which would have repealed the Climate Commitment Act cap-and-invest, in Nov 2024. The CCA had raised about $1.8bn in 2023 for visible local projects.
items.stakeholder_positions: S9 and opposition parties won 'Axe the Tax' in Canada; even the NDP withdrew support. In Washington, S6 (SEIU), S1 and some businesses funded the No campaign.
items.bottleneck: The visibility and salience of costs to S9. The confound: Washington leans Democratic, and Canada's rebate was poorly perceived (households credited the cost, not the cheque).
items.potential: Pricing should sit upstream or industrial, and revenue should be spent visibly and locally rather than as dispersed rebates.
items.trl_and_scale: Enacted and electoral outcomes.

bottlenecks: Fiscal ceiling on pull subsidies: paying 45Q's $85/t on all 37.4 Gt of fossil CO2 would cost about $3.2tn/yr (my calculation). Subsidies only scale for concentrated or cheap tonnes, so the rest must be funded by producers or consumers.

Removal delivery gap: about 1.2% of the roughly 42.5 Mt of contracted durable CDR was delivered by end-2025 (about 0.5 Mt). At the 2024 delivery rate (318.6 kt/yr) the backlog would take about 130 years.
Buyer concentration: Microsoft was about 90% of 2025 durable CDR purchase volume (45 Mt in FY25), so the removal market has a single point of failure.

Political fragility of fees on incumbents: the US methane fee (about $50/tCO2e at GWP100) was repealed by CRA and delayed to 2034, and Canada's consumer carbon price was removed on 1 Apr 2025. Every penalty-only instrument facing S3 or S9 lost in 2025.

Industrial abatement lag under the ETS: covered emissions are down about 50% since 2005, but industry was roughly flat in 2024. Free allocation dulls the signal, and CBAM is needed to remove it, which hurts S8 exporters.
CCfD budget scale: Germany's round 1 buys about 1 Mt/yr for €2.8bn (at most about €165/t). Billions per Mt/yr does not scale to Gt without carbon-price convergence.

Storage build-out: the EU's NZIA objective of 50 Mt/yr injection by 2030 is only about 4-5% of ETS stationary emissions. Takeback-style obligations are bounded by storage permitting and capex, not by thermodynamics (point-source floor 0.11-0.22 GJ/t).
open_problems: Design a carbon takeback obligation ramp (stored fraction over time) indexed to observed storage cost and capacity, so that S3's cost stays below its avoided carbon-tax exposure while S1 gets a binding net-zero end point. Test it with explicit $/bbl incidence (10% stored is about $3-7/bbl).

Close the net-emissions accounting gap from 45Q's EOR parity: what share of EOR tonnes are additional storage net of the extra oil they produce, under different oil-market elasticities? The idea engine could build a verifiable lifecycle calculator that turns parity into 'net-negative EOR only'.

Transfer the Kigali template, where incumbents own the substitute and the phase-down creates their market, to CO2 and methane. Which fossil-adjacent products (stored carbon, low-methane certified LNG, green iron) could incumbents own so that a phasedown raises their revenue?

Compliance demand for removals that reduces dependence on one buyer: design an ETS or CBAM-linked integration of durable CDR (the EU's 2026 ETS review is the venue) with quality tiers and a price floor and ceiling.
Recycle CBAM revenue to S8 exporters, Multilateral-Fund style, conditional on their industrial decarbonization, to turn S8 opposition into support. Quantify transfer sizes per exporter.
A methane import standard with MRV (satellite plus OGMP-style reporting) that US LNG exporters can meet cheaply, replacing the politically dead domestic fee with market-access pull.

Make carbon-price revenue visible and local (the Washington pattern) rather than dispersed rebates (the Canadian failure). Run a design or experimental test of which revenue framing survives S9 salience.

key_claims.claim: In the 2025 rollback (OBBBA, signed 4 Jul 2025), US carbon-capture support survived and expanded. 45Q kept $85/t point-source and $180/t DAC, and gave EOR and utilization parity (up from $60/t). In the same law, wind/solar, EV, hydrogen and home-electrification credits were cut. Instruments that pay incumbents to abate are the politically durable class.

Penalty instruments facing high-carbon industry failed politically: the IRA methane Waste Emissions Charge ($900-1,500/t CH4) had its implementing rule disapproved by Congress under the CRA in early 2025, and OBBBA delayed the first assessment to 2034 emissions.

surprises: 45Q became more generous for enhanced oil recovery under the same 2025 law that cut most other IRA clean-energy credits. Carbon capture is the rare climate instrument that S3, S6 unions and parts of S1 all lobby for.
The durable CDR market is effectively one buyer: Microsoft was about 90% of 2025 volume, and contracted tonnes run about 80x ahead of delivered tonnes.
Washington voters kept cap-and-invest 62-38 in Nov 2024, four months before Canada abolished its consumer carbon price. Whether revenue is visible may matter more than the price level.
The repealed US methane fee was only about $50/tCO2e at GWP100 ($18 at GWP20), a moderate price that still could not survive.
The CBAM simplification exempts about 90% of importers while keeping about 99% of embedded emissions in scope, a near-free administrative win that could be reused for other border or MRV mechanisms.

The EU has already written a partial carbon takeback obligation into law: NZIA obliges oil and gas producers to supply 50 Mt/yr of CO2 injection capacity by 2030. This is my own knowledge; the primary text was not retrieved this session.
Germany's first carbon contracts for difference averaged at most about €165/t but buy only about 1 Mt/yr, well short of industrial scale.

verifs.claim: In the 2025 rollback (OBBBA, signed 4 Jul 2025), US carbon-capture support survived and expanded. 45Q kept $85/t point-source and $180/t DAC, and gave EOR and utilization parity (up from $60/t). In the same law, wind/solar, EV, hydrogen and home-electrification credits were cut. Instruments that pay incumbents to abate are the politically durable class.
verifs.corrected_claim:
OBBBA (H.R. 1, signed 4 Jul 2025), Sec. 70522, titled "Restrictions on carbon oxide sequestration credit", kept the 45Q values for geologic storage. Those are $17/t base, or $85/t with prevailing-wage and apprenticeship, for point-source capture, and $36/$180 per tonne for DAC. It raised EOR and utilization to the same rates. Before, the full-wage rates were $60/t for point-source and $130/t for DAC; now both earn $85/$180. Parity applies only to facilities or equipment placed in service after 4 Jul 2025. Inflation indexing starts in 2027 on a 2025 base. The same section adds foreign-entity-of-concern bars (taxable years after enactment) and keeps transferability. Elsewhere the law ends or curtails these credits:
- **EV credits 30D, 25E, 45W:** end for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025.
- **Home credits 25C and 25D:** end for expenditures or property placed in service after 31 Dec 2025.
- **Hydrogen 45V:** the begin-construction deadline moves from 2033 to 1 Jan 2028.
- **Wind and solar under 45Y/48E:** cut off for facilities placed in service after 31 Dec 2027, subject to a begin-construction safe harbour.
CCS was one of several technologies that survived with an incumbent constituency; others were 45Z clean fuels (extended), 45U nuclear, and geothermal, hydro and storage. That pattern fits the view that subsidies aligned with incumbents last longer politically, but it is one law. It does not show that "paying incumbents to abate" is a durable class.
verifs.caveats:
1. **What the cited source does and doesn't support.** The cited GCCSI page confirms $85/$180, utilization/EOR parity, signing on 4 Jul 2025, 2027 inflation indexing, transferability and the FEOC restrictions. It does NOT give the prior $60/t figure, and it does not mention the other credits being cut. I verified those against the enrolled bill text on govinfo.gov (BILLS-119hr1enr): Sec. 70522 for 45Q, plus Secs. 70501-70513.

2. **"Up from $60/t" is incomplete.** It is right only for point-source utilization/EOR. DAC utilization/EOR rose from $130 to $180.

3. **The headline rates are not automatic.** $85 and $180 apply only with prevailing-wage and apprenticeship; otherwise they are $17 and $36.

4. **"Expanded" mostly means the EOR uplift.** The parity raises the credit for CO2 injected for enhanced oil recovery to the same rate as permanent storage. So much of the expansion subsidizes oil production as well as abatement, which weakens the claim as evidence that "pay to abate" instruments specifically are durable. The section is officially titled "Restrictions…", because of the FEOC bars.

5. **The final sentence is interpretation, not a fact in either source.** It rests on one 2025 law. The confound is that what survived tracks constituency: fossil (CCS/EOR), farm (45Z biofuels, which was extended) and nuclear/geothermal. It does not track an "abatement-payment" mechanism. Wind, solar and hydrogen subsidies also paid producers and were still cut. Also, 45Q's 2033 begin-construction deadline is unchanged, and parity applies only to new placed-in-service assets.

verifs.claim: Penalty instruments facing high-carbon industry failed politically: the IRA methane Waste Emissions Charge ($900-1,500/t CH4) had its implementing rule disapproved by Congress under the CRA in early 2025, and OBBBA delayed the first assessment to 2034 emissions.
verifs.caveats:
I could not read the cited IEA page because it returned HTTP 403, so I checked each fact against primary sources instead.

- **Charge amounts and start date.** The statute is 42 U.S.C. 7436, via Cornell LII. Subsection (c) sets the charge per metric ton of methane at $900 for 2024 emissions, $1,200 for 2025 and $1,500 for 2026 onward. Subsection (g), as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 (OBBBA, signed 4 July 2025), now says the charge is imposed "beginning with respect to emissions reported for calendar year 2034". Before the amendment it read 2024. So the first payment would fall due around 2035.
- **CRA disapproval.** EPA's WEC page says the President signed the joint resolution disapproving the final WEC rule on 14 March 2025, which is H.J.Res.35. I could not load the congress.gov page (403), so the resolution number is not confirmed here. EPA removed the rule from the CFR on 12 May 2025, and no 2024 WEC filings were collected.

Context that affects how the claim is used:
1. **The CRA vote killed the rule, not the charge.** The statutory charge still exists. The CRA bars EPA from issuing a "substantially the same" rule without new authorization, and OBBBA's delay then pushed the charge back by ten years. "Failed politically" is fair: the charge has never been collected.
2. **The tonnes are methane, not CO2.** At a GWP100 of about 28–30, $1,500/t CH4 works out to roughly $50/t CO2e. Do not compare it directly with CO2 prices.
3. **The charge was narrow.** It covered only oil and gas facilities reporting more than 25,000 t CO2e/yr, and only on methane above set waste-intensity thresholds. It also had exemptions, for example for facilities complying with EPA's methane standards. One US case of a narrow penalty being repealed is weak evidence that penalty instruments fail in general. The EU ETS and other carbon prices have survived, so any general claim needs those counterexamples too.

title: Documented stakeholder positions on climate solutions

items.name: Fossil methane abatement: the widest documented overlap across stakeholders
items.mechanism: Leak detection and repair, ending routine venting and flaring, and vapour recovery at oil, gas and coal sites. Captured methane is sold as gas, so part of the cost pays for itself. This is a point-source fix, consistent with the verifier result that methane removal from ambient air costs about 263 GJ/t CH4 in fan work alone.
items.potential: IPCC AR6 WGIII SPM C.4.5 (2022): fossil-energy CH4 was 6% [4-8%] of global GHG and 32% [22-42%] of global CH4 in 2019, and about 50-80% of it could be avoided with available technology at <USD50/tCO2e (medium confidence). My calculation (stakeholder_overlap.py): about 3.5 GtCO2e/yr (GWP100), so 1.8-2.8 GtCO2e/yr is avoidable. That is 16-26% of global CH4, against a 34% [21-57%] cut needed by 2030 in 1.5C pathways (C.1.2). So fossil abatement alone covers about half to three-quarters of the 2030 methane cut. The 1.8-2.8 Gt/yr is also about 1,000-1,700 times the cumulative durable CDR delivered to date.
items.cost: IPCC: <USD50/tCO2e for 50-80% of the potential, and C.12.1 lists methane among the options costing <USD20/t. Recovered gas is worth about $4.8/tCO2e at $3/MMBtu, $9.5 at $6 and $15.9 at $10 (GWP100; my calculation, LHV 50 GJ/t). So in importing regions, gas sales offset a large share of the abatement cost.
items.energy: Net energy positive: the recovered gas is sold.
items.stakeholder_positions: S2: IPCC C.4.5 as above. S3: OGCI's 12 members (Aramco, BP, Chevron, CNPC, Equinor, Eni, ExxonMobil, Oxy, Petrobras, Repsol, Shell, TotalEnergies) target near-zero methane by 2030. They self-report intensity below 0.20% and a 72% cut in routine flaring since 2017. The OGDC has 55+ companies with about 40% of global oil production, including NOCs (CEO champions from ADNOC, Aramco and TotalEnergies), committed to <0.2% methane intensity and zero routine flaring by 2030. API says it supports cost-effective direct regulation of methane from new and existing sources. S7: the EU Methane Regulation 2024/1787 entered into force 4 Aug 2024; it bans routine venting and flaring, sets LDAR repair windows of 5-15 working days and phases in importer requirements. All parties to COP28 (decision 1/CMA.5 para 28f) called for substantially reducing methane by 2030. Red line for S3: a per-tonne fee. The US Waste Emissions Charge was disapproved under the Congressional Review Act (signed 14 Mar 2025) and removed by EPA on 12 May 2025.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9; deployed commercially. Industry figures are self-reported (OGCI, and API's claimed 42% reduction over 2015-2023); I did not verify them independently.
items.bottleneck: Measurement, reporting and verification, plus enforcement. Industry supports regulation but opposed the US fee, and voluntary intensity claims are self-reported. Measured independently, emissions could be higher than reported; this is a confound to check against satellite data.

items.name: IPCC AR6 WGIII (S2): CCS and CDR are needed, but CCS also preserves fossil assets
items.mechanism: An assessment of modelled pathways that maps the roles of CCS, CDR and fossil fuels.
items.potential: C.4.6: technical geological storage capacity is on the order of 1000 GtCO2, more than needed through 2100 for 1.5C, though regional availability may limit it. CCS is mature for gas processing and EOR, less mature in power, cement and chemicals, where it is a critical option. 'Currently, global rates of CCS deployment are far below those in modelled pathways'. C.11: CDR to counterbalance hard-to-abate residual emissions is 'unavoidable' for net zero. C.3.2: in 1.5C pathways (>50%, no or limited overshoot), coal, oil and gas use fall by about 95%, 60% and 45% by 2050 (medians vs 2019), and unabated use falls by about 100%, 60% and 70%.
items.cost: C.11.1: DACCS USD100-300/tCO2; soil carbon USD-45 to 100/t. C.12.1: options costing <=USD100/t could halve 2019 emissions by 2030, with more than half of that potential at <USD20/t (solar, wind, efficiency, methane).
items.stakeholder_positions: C.4.4 says CCS 'could allow fossil fuels to be used longer, reducing stranded assets' (high confidence). It puts the value of unburned fuels and stranded infrastructure at about USD1-4 trillion (2015-2050, discounted, ~2C). This is the exact mechanism behind S3's support for CCS and S1's fear of mitigation deterrence. The same IPCC text supplies both sides' arguments.
items.trl_and_scale: In 2022 the SPM described CCS deployment as far below pathway rates.
items.permanence_or_durability: Geological storage: 'permanently isolated' if sites are selected and managed appropriately; storage time of 10,000+ years (C.11.1).
items.bottleneck: The deployment-rate gap, and barriers the SPM names as technological, economic, institutional, ecological-environmental and socio-cultural.

items.name: Climate Action Network (S1, 1,300+ NGOs in 120+ countries): explicit red lines on CCS, EOR, subsidies and offsets
items.mechanism: A network position paper (Jan 2021) that sets the conditions NGO coalitions apply to carbon management.
items.stakeholder_positions: Red lines: (3) phase out all public support for fossil-linked technologies 'including CCS'. (4) CAN 'will not support any effort to promote negative emissions or offsets as an alternative to stringent emission reductions'. (5) BECCS is not recognised as proven and is opposed if it causes food or land conflicts. (6) There is 'no definitive evidence' that CCS is the best route for cement, steel or chemicals, and the 'promise of CCS must not delay' action. (7) CAN opposes EOR/EGR. (8) DACCS has 'no place' in scenarios built on early, steep reductions. (9) Storage liability is likely to shift to the public. Implicit opening: CAN's objection to industrial CCS is evidential ('no definitive evidence'), not categorical, and it calls for R&D for these industries. The paper cites <5 MtCO2/yr stored by operating non-EOR CCS (about 2020).
items.potential: This position sets what a solution must avoid to win S1: EOR, offsets substituting for cuts, subsidies flowing to fossil producers, and BECCS on contested land.
items.trl_and_scale: n/a (position paper, 2021; I found no newer CAN CCS position).
items.bottleneck: The paper is dated 2021, before Brevik (2025) and Northern Lights operations. Its evidence claims about industrial CCS may now be partly outdated, but the EOR and mitigation-deterrence objections are about mechanism and still apply.

items.name: COP28 Global Stocktake (decision 1/CMA.5 para 28-29): the only text every government has agreed
items.mechanism: A consensus UNFCCC decision that names the technologies all parties accept.
items.stakeholder_positions: S7 (all parties, Dec 2023): calls for tripling renewables and doubling the efficiency rate by 2030; 'transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner'; accelerating 'renewables, nuclear, abatement and removal technologies such as carbon capture and utilization and storage, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors, and low-carbon hydrogen'; substantially reducing methane by 2030; and phasing out inefficient fossil subsidies. Para 29 recognises that 'transitional fuels' can support energy security. This is the negotiated common ground between petro-states (S3/S7), the EU and small island states (S8). The qualifier 'particularly in hard-to-abate sectors' marks where CCS is legitimate.
items.potential: Its framing (CCS for hard-to-abate sectors, methane by 2030, a just transition) is already accepted diplomatically by nearly 200 parties.
items.trl_and_scale: A non-binding decision text.
items.bottleneck: No binding quantities or enforcement.

items.name: 30-country public survey on CDR and SRM (Baum et al., Nature Communications 2024)
items.mechanism: Nationally representative surveys of public support for ten climate-intervention technologies (SRM, ecosystem CDR, engineered CDR).
items.stakeholder_positions: S9/S8 publics: N=30,284 in 30 countries, at least 1,000 per country, fielded Aug-Dec 2022, online quota samples. Afforestation and reforestation drew the most support and was the only option on which North and South agreed. SRM options and enhanced weathering drew the least. Global South publics were more supportive of every technology but more worried that the technologies undermine mitigation and spread risk unequally. Both North and South rated engineered CDR (DACCS, BECCS) as the highest mitigation-deterrence ('moral hazard') risk. Small-scale field trials had the most support of the three activities. Government funding and information campaigns were the most popular policies; national restrictions and international bans or moratoria were the least popular.
items.potential: Mitigation-deterrence safeguards are what the public demands most. Public consent is not the binding constraint on research or small trials.
items.trl_and_scale: n/a
items.bottleneck: Familiarity was low for everything except afforestation, so stated support is unstable and frame-dependent (a confound). Online samples in the Global South over-represent younger, urban respondents.

items.name: Global willingness to pay for climate action (Andre et al., Nature Climate Change 2024; Gallup World Poll 2021/22)
items.mechanism: A survey measuring willingness to contribute (WTC) 1% of income, and perceptions of others' willingness.
items.stakeholder_positions: S9 and global public: 125 countries (96% of global GHG), N=129,902. 69% are willing to contribute 1% of household income monthly, 86% endorse pro-climate norms and 89% want more political action. People underestimate others' willingness by 26 percentage points (pluralistic ignorance). In a US validation sample, stated WTC predicted 43% higher real donations.
items.potential: Price tolerance exists at about 1% of income, which bounds acceptable consumer cost pass-through for S9 and suggests a cap for any cost-sharing scheme.
items.trl_and_scale: n/a
items.bottleneck: Stated, not revealed, preference for most respondents. Willingness to pay 1% of income is a different measure from acceptance of specific price rises on energy.

items.name: US public energy priorities (Pew Research Center, May 2024)
items.mechanism: A national survey of US adults' energy priorities.
items.stakeholder_positions: S9 (US): N=8,638, 13-19 May 2024. 65% prioritise developing renewables over fossil fuels (34% the reverse); 63% support US carbon neutrality by 2050. Republican support for expanding wind and solar has fallen since 2020. Support for CCS tax credits and nuclear is in the full report but not on the page I fetched, so I did not verify it.
items.potential: Partisan sorting is growing for wind and solar. In the US, cross-partisan acceptance has to come from technologies not coded as 'green' (an inference; unverified here).
items.trl_and_scale: n/a
items.bottleneck: Single country; partisan trends shift over time.

items.name: Solar radiation modification: organised NGO and academic non-use vs public tolerance for research
items.mechanism: Campaigns to block SRM research and deployment, set against survey evidence on what the public accepts.
items.stakeholder_positions: S2/S1/S8: the Solar Geoengineering Non-Use Agreement calls for no public funding, no outdoor experiments, no patents, no deployment and no institutional support. Its site lists 650+ academics in 65 countries, 2,000+ endorsing organisations and 5,345+ citizen signatures (as fetched 2026-10-05). The HOME manifesto (4 Oct 2018, 195 organisations in 45 countries) demands an immediate stop to all open-air geoengineering experiments. The Baum 2024 survey found SRM among the least-supported technologies, but bans and moratoria were also the least-supported policies, and small field trials the most supported.
items.potential: Any solution that relies on SRM fails the 'satisfy as many parties as possible' test. SRM is a hard red line for organised S1 and S8.
items.trl_and_scale: Research stage; not assessed for deployment.
items.bottleneck: Governance and legitimacy, not technology.

items.name: Heavy industry (S4): the cement roadmap relies on CCUS, and the first full-scale cement plant with CCS is operating
items.mechanism: Amine capture of process CO2 from limestone calcination at cement kilns (verifier floor 0.11 GJ/t at 25% CO2), with offshore storage via Northern Lights.
items.potential: GCCA Net Zero Concrete roadmap (2021): CCUS supplies 36% of the reductions (1,370 MtCO2) to net zero by 2050. Its 2030 milestones are a 25% cut in CO2 per m3 of concrete and capture at industrial scale in 10 plants. Heidelberg Materials' Brevik CCS (Norway) was inaugurated in mid-June 2025 as the first industrial-scale CCS at a cement plant; its product is sold as evoZero.
items.cost: Not verified. I recall about 0.4 Mt/yr capture, about half the plant's emissions, and a majority state subsidy, but none of this came from a fetched primary source.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 depends on CCUS for process emissions that fuel switching cannot remove. S1 (CAN) disputes this on evidence but does not oppose it categorically, so process-emission CCS is the narrowest bridge between S1 and S4. Heidelberg credits Brevik's success to 'clear support of the government' and social acceptance in Norway.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 at one site (2025). The other 9 plants in the 2030 milestone are not yet verified.
items.bottleneck: Public funding (which CAN opposes), storage access outside the North Sea, and green-premium demand.

items.name: Durable CDR market: realised money and the delivery gap
items.mechanism: Voluntary advance purchases of durable carbon removal (DAC, BECCS, biomass storage, enhanced weathering and others).
items.potential: CDR.fyi tracker, fetched 2026-10-05, all time: 50.5 Mt contracted vs 1.7 Mt delivered (3.4%). Weighted average price is $337/t, ranging from $61/t (biomass direct storage) to $1,331/t (direct ocean removal). Implied contracted value at the average price is about $17bn (my rough calculation; the average covers only disclosed prices).
items.cost: $337/t on average (DACCS is higher), vs the IPCC's USD100-300/t for DACCS in 2022. Verifier: DAC's thermodynamic floor is 0.47 GJ/t, and real plants use 5-10+ GJ/t.
items.stakeholder_positions: S10/S3 are buyers; Microsoft is reportedly dominant, but I did not verify that on the page. S1 (CAN) objects when removals substitute for reductions. Publics in both North and South rate engineered CDR the highest moral-hazard risk (Baum 2024).
items.trl_and_scale: Delivered volume is about 1.7 Mt in total, versus 37.4 Gt/yr of fossil CO2.
items.permanence_or_durability: Varies by method; geological storage lasts more than 10,000 years.
items.bottleneck: Delivery is about 30 times below contracts, and demand is concentrated in a few buyers.

items.name: Carbon pricing coverage and industry stance
items.mechanism: Emissions trading systems and carbon taxes.
items.potential: World Bank State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2026: about 30% of global GHG covered by 87 implemented instruments, raising more than $107bn for public budgets in 2025. All large middle-income economies have adopted or are planning direct carbon pricing. Carbon credit issuance rose 8% from 2024 to 2025.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3: API supports 'market-based policies' and 'predictable and economically efficient policy frameworks' to cut emissions at least cost. S7 adoption is widening. S1 opposes offsets as a substitute for cuts (CAN 2021). Middle-income adoption suggests S8 governments accept domestic pricing, but I could not verify their documented opposition to border adjustments (CBAM) here.
items.trl_and_scale: Deployed.
items.bottleneck: Price levels: I could not verify the share of emissions priced at Paris-consistent levels, and I recall it is low. There is also leakage and political tolerance of energy-price rises.

items.name: Carbon Capture Coalition (US): a cross-stakeholder alliance of companies, unions and NGOs
items.mechanism: Federal policy advocacy for the 45Q credit and carbon-management infrastructure.
items.stakeholder_positions: Describes itself as a 'nonpartisan collaboration of companies, unions, conservation and environmental policy organizations', which puts S3, S4, S5, S6 and some S1 groups in one coalition. It issued a statement welcoming Treasury's extension of the 45Q safe harbour (14 Aug 2026). The 2025 reconciliation-law changes to 45Q (reported parity for utilisation and EOR) are NOT verified from a primary source; if true, they collide directly with CAN's EOR red line.
items.potential: Shows that CCS can win union and industry support (S6 jobs in high-carbon regions) and bipartisan backing in the US.
items.trl_and_scale: n/a
items.bottleneck: The EOR question splits S1 from this coalition.

bottlenecks: CCS deployment gap: the IPCC (2022) says global CCS deployment rates are 'far below' modelled 1.5-2C pathways. CAN (2021) cited <5 MtCO2/yr stored by operating non-EOR CCS, against an IEA Sustainable Development Scenario need of 760 Mt/yr by 2030 (as cited by CAN).
Durable CDR delivery: CDR.fyi all-time figures are 50.5 Mt contracted vs 1.7 Mt delivered (3.4%) at an average of $337/t. Even contracted volume is about 0.13% of one year of fossil CO2 (37.4 Gt).

Stranded-asset conflict: the IPCC puts unburned fossil fuels and stranded infrastructure at USD1-4 trillion (2015-2050, discounted, ~2C) and says CCS reduces stranded assets. That is why S3 favours CCS and why S1 sees it as mitigation deterrence. The value at stake defines the conflict.

EOR red line: CAN opposes EOR/EGR outright, and the IPCC notes CO2 injection is 'mature' mainly because of gas processing and EOR. Any US incentive parity for EOR (reported for 2025, unverified) deepens the split.

Subsidy red line: CAN wants all public support for CCS phased out, while industrial CCS depends on the state. Brevik's success was credited to government support, and the GCCA roadmap needs CCUS for 36% of its reductions (1,370 MtCO2).

Methane MRV and enforcement: 50-80% of fossil CH4 (1.8-2.8 GtCO2e/yr, my calculation from IPCC C.4.5) is avoidable at <$50/t, yet the US fee was repealed (CRA, Mar 2025). Industry intensity figures (OGCI <0.20%; API -42% for 2015-2023) are self-reported.
Mitigation-deterrence perception: in a 30-country survey (N=30,284, 2022), North and South publics both rate engineered CDR the highest moral-hazard risk, and Global South concern is greater.
SRM legitimacy: 650+ academics and 2,000+ organisations back non-use, and 195 organisations (HOME, 2018) demand a stop to outdoor experiments. That rules SRM out as a consensus solution.
open_problems: Design an eligibility rule for public CCS support that covers process emissions with no substitute (cement calcination, verifier floor 0.11 GJ/t) and excludes EOR and fossil-power life extension. Then test whether CAN-type NGOs would accept it. Process emissions are the one place where CAN's objection is evidential ('no definitive evidence'), not categorical.

Build independent, low-cost methane MRV (satellites, aerial surveys, continuous sensors) that the EU import rules can accept as equivalent, and that NOCs, majors and NGOs all trust. This replaces a fee with a measurement-based market-access condition, which industry says it supports (direct regulation).

Find mechanisms that make the 1.8-2.8 GtCO2e/yr of avoidable fossil methane profitable without a fee: gas-capture finance, LNG offtake premiums for verified low-methane cargoes. Recovered gas is worth $5-16/tCO2e (GWP100) at $3-10/MMBtu.

Find safeguards against mitigation deterrence that make removals acceptable to S1 and S8, for example separate targets for removals and reductions, and like-for-like durability matching for residual emissions only. Their effect on stated acceptance could be tested with survey experiments.
Close the 30-fold gap between contracted and delivered durable CDR. Find what limits delivery: MRV, financing or technology readiness.
Measure and price liability transfer for long-term CO2 storage (CAN point 9) in a way insurers (S10) will underwrite. Insurer positions are under-documented in this pass.
Design benefit-sharing for Global South publics, who are more supportive of climate-intervention technologies but more worried about unequal risks and mitigation deterrence (Baum 2024).
Use the 26-point perception gap (Andre 2024) to raise political tolerance for carbon pricing and methane rules, for example by publicising the true share of supporters, and test it.

By my calculation that is 1.8-2.8 GtCO2e/yr, half to three-quarters of the 34% methane cut needed by 2030 in 1.5C pathways. verifs.claim: IPCC AR6 WGIII SPM C.4.5 (2022): fossil-energy CH4 was 32% of global CH4 and 6% of global GHG in 2019, and about 50-80% of it could be avoided with currently available technologies at <USD50/tCO2e. By my calculation that is 1.8-2.8 GtCO2e/yr, half to three-quarters of the 34% methane cut needed by 2030 in 1.5C pathways. Oil and gas majors and NOCs (OGCI, the 55+ company OGDC with about 40% of oil output, API) publicly back near-zero methane or direct methane regulation, making this the widest-overlap lever across S1-S11.
verifs.caveats:
I checked the claim against the primary SPM PDF and the OGDC website. The API position comes from memory because the API pages returned 404s and the web-search budget had run out.

What the source says:
- **C.4.5 wording.** It refers to "methane emissions from energy supply, primarily fugitive emissions from production and transport of fossil fuels". "Fossil-energy CH4" is a fair shorthand for that.
- **Shares, with their ranges.** That methane was 32% [22–42%] of global CH4, 6% [4–8%] of global GHG, and 18% [13–23%] of energy-supply GHG in 2019. These shares carry high confidence.
- **Abatement figure.** The 50–80% avoidable "with currently available technologies at less than USD50 tCO2-eq-1" is rated medium confidence only.

The arithmetic holds:
- **Avoidable amount.** 2019 net GHG was 59 ± 6.6 GtCO2-eq (GWP100), so 6% is about 3.5 Gt. Avoiding 50–80% of that gives 1.8–2.8 Gt.
- **Share of the 2030 cut.** Global CH4 was 11 ± 3.2 GtCO2-eq in 2019 (SPM Fig. SPM.1). A 34% cut is therefore about 3.7 Gt, and 1.8–2.8 Gt is roughly 47–76% of it. "Half to three-quarters" is fair.
- **Uncertainty.** These figures use central values only. Carrying the [4–8%] range through gives about 1.2–3.8 Gt.

Context for the 34%:
- **Source.** It is SPM C.1.2. It applies to 1.5°C (>50%) pathways with no or limited overshoot, as a cut from modelled 2019 emissions. The model range is [21–57%].
- **Not additive.** The modelled pathways already include fossil CH4 abatement, and the SPM says most models are near their maximum technical potential for CH4. So fossil methane abatement is a way to deliver that cut, not an extra lever on top of it.
- **Metric.** All of this is GWP100. On a 20-year metric, methane's near-term warming share would be about three times larger, which strengthens the case for this lever.
- **Dates.** The numbers describe 2019 and technology as of 2022, and they are modelled or estimated, not measured. Satellite and IEA tracking suggest bottom-up inventories undercount oil and gas methane.

Industry backing:
- **OGDC.** Its website confirms "55+ companies with assets in 100+ countries", "around 40% of global oil production", and "near-zero upstream methane emissions by 2030" (below 0.2% methane intensity). These commitments are voluntary and self-reported.
- **API.** The support for "direct regulation of methane from new and existing sources" dates from API's March 2021 Climate Action Framework. API opposed the IRA methane fee (Waste Emissions Charge) and backed its repeal and delay in 2025. Say that API backs direct regulation but opposes the methane fee; don't present it as unqualified support.
- **OGCI.** It is a much smaller group of about 12 companies, with its Aiming for Zero methane initiative.
- **Public backing is not delivery.** These are stated positions, not evidence that emissions are falling.

"Widest-overlap lever across S1-S11" is the author's own judgment, which no source can confirm.

verifs.claim: Climate Action Network (1,300+ member organisations, Jan 2021) opposes CCS-EOR/EGR, opposes all public support for fossil-linked technologies 'including CCS', will not support negative emissions or offsets 'as an alternative to stringent emission reductions', and holds that DACCS has 'no place' in early-reduction scenarios. These are the red lines any multi-stakeholder solution must respect. Its objection to industrial CCS rests on evidence ('no definitive evidence'), not principle.
verifs.corrected_claim:
Climate Action Network's position paper "Carbon Capture, Storage and Utilisation" (January 2021) describes CAN as having more than 1,300 members in over 120 countries. It takes five positions.

1. It opposes EOR/EGR combined with CCS (position 7: "CAN opposes such an practice").
2. It calls for all government subsidies, loans, grants, tax credits, incentives and financial support for fossil fuels and for technologies that support continued fossil-fuel use, "including CCS", to be "phased out as soon as possible" (position 3).
3. It "cannot and will not support any effort to promote negative emissions or offsets as an alternative to stringent emission reductions", and gives "absolute priority" to natural sequestration (position 4).
4. It says DACCS "has no place in decarbonisation scenarios focusing on early and steep CO2 emissions reductions" because it will not contribute significantly "in the coming years" (position 8).
5. It does not recognise BECCS as proven (position 5).

On industrial CCS, the paper's wording is comparative. CAN "sees no definitive evidence that CCS is the fastest, cheapest, cleanest and most durable way to decarbonise the industrial sectors" (position 6). That objection is evidence-based, but it is not the whole of CAN's opposition. The paper also objects on non-empirical grounds:
- storage liability being shifted to the public (conclusion 9);
- intergenerational equity and justice (conclusion 11);
- diverting resources and entrenching fossil business as usual (conclusion 10);
- a blanket call to phase out public support for CCS (position 3).

So the objection is partly empirical and partly a matter of principle and policy, not purely evidential.
verifs.caveats:
I checked this against the primary PDF, which carries CAN's own branding. The copy used is a reproduction filed as a reference to the Center for Biological Diversity's comment in the Alaska CCUS public scoping record (2024-11-07). Every quoted phrase in the claim appears verbatim in it.

1. **"Evidence, not principle" is the main error.** Position 6's "no definitive evidence" is a comparative test: is CCS the fastest, cheapest, cleanest and most durable route? It is not a claim that CCS has no evidence behind it. Separately, conclusions 2, 9, 10 and 11 object on storage permanence, liability transfer, resource diversion and intergenerational equity. Better data alone would not answer those objections. Conclusion 6 also says industrial emissions can be cut "without CCS". A solution designer should not assume new efficiency evidence would win CAN over on industrial CCS. Liability, permanence and the risk of entrenching fossil fuels would still need to be addressed.

2. **"Opposes all public support" overstates the wording slightly.** The text says such support "should be phased out as soon as possible" and that "CAN opposes government support to the fossil fuel industry". That is still a red line against subsidised CCS. One ambiguity remains: CCS on non-fossil process emissions, such as cement calcination, is not fossil-fuel use, and position 3 does not say clearly whether it covers that.

3. **The negative-emissions and DACCS positions are conditional, not absolute bans.** Negative emissions are rejected "as an alternative to" deep cuts, which leaves room for removal that is additional to cuts. The DACCS exclusion applies to "early and steep" reduction scenarios "in the coming years". Conclusion 8 explicitly allows "future consideration of DACCS" if it addresses energy demand and SDG alignment. That is a conditional opening, not a permanent red line.

4. **Date and scale.** This is a January 2021 position, about 5.75 years before today (2026-10-05). The membership figure is CAN's own self-description at that time. My recollection is that CAN now reports roughly 1,900+ members; I could not verify that, because my web search budget was used up. I also could not check whether CAN has updated its CCS or CDR position since 2021. The paper's technical figures are also dated: CCS project counts, and DACCS energy estimates from Rhodium (2019) and IEA WEO 2019, such as about 2/3 t CO2 emitted per tonne captured on the then-current grid mix. They should not be reused as current numbers.

5. **"Red lines any multi-stakeholder solution must respect" is the claimant's framing, not CAN's.** CAN is one network. Other activist groups may be stricter or more flexible.

title: Frontier climate-tech research 2025-2026 with measured results

items.name: Realized DAC performance: Climeworks Orca and Mammoth (Iceland)
items.mechanism: Solid amine sorbent, temperature-vacuum swing, geothermal heat and power, storage through Carbfix mineralization
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 7-8. Orca: 4,000 t/yr nameplate (2021). Mammoth: 36,000 t/yr nameplate, partially commissioned May 2024
items.energy: CEO statement (2025, via Nikkei) of 5,000-6,000 kWh per tonne at Mammoth = 19.8 GJ/t. That is 43x the 0.465 GJ/t floor, a second-law efficiency of about 2.3% on an energy basis (frontier_calcs.py). Early-operation figure; the heat/electricity split is not disclosed
items.cost: Climeworks website price about $1,000/t (reported May 2025). The 2017 target had been about $100/t by 2025
items.potential: Realized: Mammoth captured 105 t in its first 10 months, per Puro.earth data reported by Heimildin (May 2025). That is 0.35% of pro-rated nameplate (30,000 t). Lifetime capture since 2009 is about 2,400 t, against Climeworks' own corporate footprint of 1,700 tCO2 in 2023. A cited run-rate of about 860 t/yr means the 40,000 t sold to Morgan Stanley would take about 47 years
items.bottleneck: Ramp-up and availability, plus energy intensity 10-40x the floor. Confound: Mammoth was only partially commissioned, so the 0.35% overstates the steady-state shortfall. Even so, delivery lags sales by decades
items.permanence_or_durability: Mineralized basalt storage (Carbfix), on a scale of 10,000+ years
items.stakeholder_positions: S1 is split; critics call DAC a fig leaf (Jacobson is quoted calling carbon capture 'the Theranos of the energy industry'). S3 favours DAC as a license to keep operating. S10 has early buyers carrying delivery risk. S9: retail subscribers prepaid and are waiting

items.name: Durable CDR market: contracted vs delivered, and prices (2024-2026)
items.mechanism: Voluntary offtakes and prepurchases (Microsoft, Frontier, Google) across BECCS, biochar, DAC, ERW, ocean and biomass burial
items.trl_and_scale: Cumulative contracted durable CDR 50.5 Mt; delivered 1.7 Mt (CDR.fyi homepage, read Oct 2026). Delivery is 3.4% of contracted, and contracts equal 0.14% of one year of fossil CO2. Monthly volumes are lumpy: 362 kt in June 2026, 22 kt in July, 128 kt in August
items.energy: n/a
items.cost: CDR.fyi average price $337/t (trailing). WEF/Oliver Wyman/ClimeFi 2026 report (data mostly to Aug 2024): DAC $500-1,200/t, BECCS $200-600, ERW $200-500, biochar averaging $192. CDR.fyi May 2026 pricing survey: the buyer-supplier price gap narrowed from $107/t to $98/t, and durable CDR is 'unlikely to broadly reach $100 per tonne by 2030'
items.potential: WEF sold-to-delivered ratios: DAC 750:1 (<1.5 Mt sold, >2,000 t delivered); ERW 200:1; biochar 4:1. Microsoft's public CDR.fyi profile shows 2.34 Mt contracted in Mar-Aug 2026 alone (Liferaft 1 Mt, BioCirc 650 kt, North Star 626 kt)
items.bottleneck: Delivery and financing. The market is demand-concentrated in a few tech buyers, prices sit 2-10x above buyer willingness, and offtakes are prepaid against unbuilt plants
items.permanence_or_durability: Varies by method: DAC and BECCS with geological storage 1,000+ years; biochar 100-1,000+ years with uncertainty
items.stakeholder_positions: S10 and big tech buy now; S1 accepts durable removal but distrusts offsets. S3: Occidental/1PointFive was the largest DAC seller (1.29 Mt sold by Aug 2024). S7: the policy pull (45Q, EU CRCF) is the key unknown

items.name: Electrochemical pH-swing DAC with spatially isolated phenazine electrode (Harvard; Aziz, Gordon)
items.mechanism: Proton-coupled electron transfer of poly(phenazine sulfide) solid electrodes swings the electrolyte pH. Keeping the O2-sensitive reduced phenazine away from air removes the O2-oxidation loss that hurt earlier organic redox DAC
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4, lab flow cell (Nature Energy, Aug 2025)
items.energy: Measured 104 kJ/mol for DAC = 2.36 GJ/t = 656 kWh/t, all electricity. That is 5.1x the 0.465 GJ/t floor (eta_II about 20%). 73 kJ/mol on simulated flue gas (10.7x that floor). Coulombic efficiency 99%. Scaled up, 1 Gt/yr would take 656 TWh, about 2.2% of world electricity, at stack level only (excludes fans and compression)
items.cost: Not reported
items.potential: Stack energy is about 3-8x lower than the commercial thermal DAC energies reported in this item set
items.bottleneck: Not yet shown: scale-up, durability over thousands of hours, and air-contactor fan work. At 75% capture and a 100-300 Pa pressure drop, fans add roughly 0.3-1 GJ/t
items.stakeholder_positions: Electricity-only operation suits S5, which sells the power. S1 prefers it to fossil-heat DAC

items.name: Electrified reversible surface mineralization DAC on MnO2
items.mechanism: Electrochemical reduction gives Mn(III), which mineralizes CO2 as MnOOCO2H. An oxidative potential reverses it. The process stays inside the water-stability window and is insensitive to O2 and humidity
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3. Scaled to 20 cm2 without loss. More than 1,000 h with over 90% capacity retention (Nature Energy, Feb 2026)
items.energy: 4.1 GJ/t measured from air (0.04% CO2, 21% O2) with 80% single-pass capture, <150 Pa pressure drop. That is 8.8x the floor (eta_II about 11%). The authors put liquid-carbonate systems at 6-10 GJ/t
items.cost: Not reported
items.potential: An inorganic, O2-tolerant electrode chemistry built from an abundant metal
items.bottleneck: Authors' own list: material utilization, electrolyte, gas flow and pressure drop, CO2 purity
items.stakeholder_positions: Same profile as the phenazine cell: S5 and S1 favourable, S3 neutral

items.name: Thermal Ca/Mg exchange to activate Mg-silicates for passive CO2 removal (Chen and Kanan, Stanford)
items.mechanism: CaCO3 or CaSO4 plus Mg silicate (olivine, serpentine) in a kiln gives Ca2SiO4 plus MgO. These carbonate passively in wet ambient air within weeks, or within hours under 1 atm CO2. Kiln process CO2 is captured and sequestered
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3, lab chemistry (Nature, Feb 2025). The untreated silicate showed no reactivity over 6 months
items.energy: Modelled at less than 1 MWh/t (3.6 GJ/t, eta_II about 13%), roughly half of leading DAC by the authors' estimate. Not measured at scale
items.cost: Not reported
items.potential: Mg-silicate resource can remove >1e5 Gt CO2. Passive uptake avoids fan work, which matters because the verifier shows forced-air processing dominates costs at ppm concentrations
items.bottleneck: A kiln-scale demonstration of the exchange reaction is needed. Kiln process CO2 must be captured; it is a concentrated source, so its floor is about 0.11-0.16 GJ/t. Mining and spreading logistics remain
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (cement and lime): uses existing kiln skills and assets, a possible new product line. S6: keeps kiln jobs. S11: mining footprint

items.name: Enhanced rock weathering: field-measured removal far below models
items.mechanism: Crushed silicate rock or industrial slag spread on fields dissolves and converts CO2 to bicarbonate
items.trl_and_scale: Commercial start-ups have raised more than $250M (Beerling et al., Nat Rev Earth Environ 2025). Swiss vineyards: 3 sites, 1,000 days, 20 t/ha basalt (EST, Nov 2025). Scotland: 1.5 yr, 23-126 t/ha (Front Clim 2025). US Midwest: 3 yr, slag vs basalt (Front Clim, Jan 2026)
items.energy: Low: grinding and transport only
items.potential: Measured removal: Swiss 100 +/- 30 kg CO2/ha/yr, 10-30x below earlier upper estimates; most standard proxies showed no significant change. Scotland 0.33-0.53 tCO2/ha after 1.5 yr, only at 78-126 t/ha. At 0.1-0.3 t/ha/yr, 1 Gt/yr needs 3.5-10 Gha, i.e. 2-6x global cropland (frontier_calcs.py); at modelled 1-3 t/ha/yr it needs 0.3x cropland. Review potential 0.5-2 Gt/yr by 2050 is modelled. US trial: steel slag on acidic soil gave clear removal; coarse basalt gave none
items.bottleneck: MRV signal-to-noise and soil-specific outcomes. The 200:1 sold-to-delivered ratio is a credit-quality risk. Confounds: temperate climates, coarse feedstock and short duration, so tropical sites with fine rock may do much better
items.permanence_or_durability: Bicarbonate in the ocean 10,000+ years, but with lags and losses from soil to ocean
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (steel): slag becomes a revenue stream. Farmers and S11 gain liming co-benefits but face trace-metal concerns. S8: tropical deployment (2025 XPRIZE winner Mati Carbon, India, not re-verified this run). S1: generally supportive

items.name: AI sorbent discovery: OpenDAC (ODAC23 and ODAC25) and its critique
items.mechanism: DFT plus machine-learned interatomic potentials screen MOFs for CO2/H2O adsorption
items.trl_and_scale: ODAC23: 38M+ DFT calculations on 8,400+ MOFs. ODAC25: about 60M DFT single-points for CO2, H2O, N2 and O2 in 15,000 MOFs, with released ML potentials (arXiv 2508.03162). No experimental validation in either abstract
items.energy: Not addressed. Binding energy is not process energy
items.cost: Free and open (Meta fairchem); runs on GPUs
items.potential: A verifier-ready dataset a small team can use
items.bottleneck: Jin, Garcia and Smit (ACS Cent Sci, May 2025) argue the recommended ODAC23 DAC structures 'are artifacts of the methodology used'. Adsorption-energy ranking does not capture co-adsorption, kinetics, stability or regeneration energy. MOFSimBench (npj Comput Mater, Dec 2025) finds data quality matters more than model architecture
items.stakeholder_positions: S2: Smit and colleagues are skeptical of the screening methodology

items.name: Fast COF sorbents tested in outdoor air: COF-999 and COF-1000 (Yaghi lab)
items.mechanism: Covalent organic frameworks with grafted polyamines; humidity increases uptake
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3, gram scale. COF-999 (Nature, Oct 2024): 0.96 mmol/g dry and 2.05 mmol/g at 50% RH from 400 ppm; more than 100 outdoor cycles in Berkeley; regenerates at 60 C. COF-1000 (Nat Sustain, Jan 2026): 1.31 mmol/g dry, 2.19 at 75% RH, half-capacity in 6.8-8.1 min, 50 outdoor cycles in 3 days
items.energy: Not reported. The 60 C regeneration permits low-grade waste heat (Carnot factor about 0.12 at 60 C, versus 0.20 at 100 C)
items.cost: COF synthesis cost is not reported and is likely high
items.potential: 22.1 mmol/g/day outdoors works out to 2.8 kg sorbent per t/yr of capacity, about 2,800 t of sorbent for a 1 Mt/yr plant if the lab cycling holds (frontier_calcs.py)
items.bottleneck: Synthesis cost and scale, multi-year stability (100 cycles is days, not years), contactor pressure drop
items.stakeholder_positions: S2 is enthusiastic; Yaghi shared the 2025 Chemistry Nobel for MOFs (from memory, not re-verified this run)

items.name: CO2 electroreduction to ethylene from high-pressure captured CO2
items.mechanism: In/Cu catalyst in a membrane electrode assembly at 20 bar uses captured CO2 without depressurizing, and high pressure moves bicarbonate formation to suppress salt precipitation
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4, lab scale (Nat Catal, Aug 2025). 85% Faradaic efficiency to C2H4, 750 mA/cm2 partial current, more than 1,500 h at 600 mA/cm2, 99.9% purity C2H4
items.energy: Thermodynamic minimum 47.5 GJ/t C2H4. At an assumed 2.5-3.5 V (cell voltage not in the abstract) and 85% FE: 121-170 GJ/t = 34-47 MWh/t, about $1,000-1,400/t in electricity at $30/MWh. Break-even grid intensity is about 32-44 gCO2/kWh against an assumed 1.5 tCO2/t of cracker process emissions, or about 115 g/kWh if fossil-feedstock end-of-life carbon (3.14 t/t) is credited (frontier_calcs.py)
items.cost: TEA review (Nat Rev Clean Technol 2025): gaseous products need single-pass conversion above 30% for CO and above 10% for ethylene to compete
items.potential: A use for captured CO2 that keeps the chemicals industry (S4) whole, but it only cuts emissions on near-zero-carbon power
items.bottleneck: Cu catalyst instability: multi-year operation is still unsolved (Kok, Buonsanti, Burdyny, Nat Rev Mater 2025), and 1,500 h is about 2 months. Electricity is 34-47 MWh per tonne of product
items.permanence_or_durability: Utilization, not removal: the carbon is re-emitted at product end-of-life unless the product is durable
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 and S3 find it attractive (preserves product lines). S5 gains a large load. S1 is skeptical of utilization as mitigation

items.name: High-temperature CO2-to-CO electrolysis (SOEC) with encapsulated Co-Ni alloy
items.mechanism: Solid oxide electrolysis at 800 C. A Sm-doped CeO2-encapsulated Co-Ni catalyst prevents agglomeration
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 4 (Nature, May 2025). 90% energy efficiency, more than 2,000 h at 1 A/cm2, about 100% CO selectivity, 90% single-pass yield. The previous state of art was below 70% and below 200 h
items.energy: About 7.1 GJ per tonne of CO2 converted (2.0 MWh/t), or 11.2 GJ/t CO, assuming the 90% applies to the enthalpy. Efficiency basis not checked
items.cost: Not reported
items.potential: Syngas route to e-fuels and chemicals; can heat-integrate with industrial waste heat
items.bottleneck: Hours to commercial life: 2,000 h against the roughly 40,000 h needed. Needs low-carbon electricity
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 and S3 (synthetic fuels from existing infrastructure); aviation

items.name: Electrochemical ocean alkalinity enhancement field trials (Ebb Carbon/PNNL Sequim; Tasmania NaOH)
items.mechanism: Electrochemically made NaOH released through existing outfalls raises alkalinity, and the ocean then takes up atmospheric CO2
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 5. Sequim Bay, WA, Feb 2025: mixing-tank pH raised to the permit limit of 9.0; the signal was measurable only within about 2.5 m of the discharge; no measurable change in temperature, salinity, turbidity or O2. Tasmania (Sci Rep, Dec 2025): alkalinity +545 umol/kg at release, pCO2 -370 uatm at the source but only -22 to -77 uatm downstream (signal <1-5%)
items.energy: Electrolysis energy not reported in these trials
items.cost: Not reported
items.potential: Durable (10,000+ yr) and potentially Gt-scale (modelled)
items.bottleneck: MRV: removal happens through air-sea gas exchange over weeks to months and far from the outfall, so it must be modelled, not measured. Ecological and permit limits (pH 9.0 cap). ACS Energy Lett 2026 perspective lists seawater failure modes and the lack of benchmarking standards
items.stakeholder_positions: S11 and fisheries are cautious; S1 is split on marine CDR; S7 regulators keep tight permits. Using existing wastewater plants lowers barriers for S11

items.name: Porous solid electrolyte electrochemical capture with recirculation (long-duration)
items.mechanism: OER/ORR-driven Na+ transport with sodium (bi)carbonate as a cyclic mediator; regenerates CO2 at over 99% purity with no chemical input
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 3-4 (Nat Commun, Nov 2025). Over 2,000 h DAC stability at 30 mA/cm2 with more than 93% removal efficiency. About 8,820 kg air/day/m2. Flue gas 3,060 mL/h at 10 A on 100 cm2
items.energy: Not given in the abstract
items.cost: Not reported
items.potential: One device for both point-source and air capture
items.bottleneck: Energy per tonne must be reported and checked against the floor
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (modular point-source fit), S5

items.name: Enzymatic capture (carbonic anhydrase) in potassium carbonate
items.mechanism: Immobilized carbonic anhydrase speeds CO2 hydration so low-regeneration-energy K2CO3 can replace amines (MEA)
items.trl_and_scale: Commercial pilots exist (e.g. Saipem CO2 Solutions; not re-verified this run). This 2025 EST paper is a mass-transfer model
items.energy: Not quantified. The appeal is lower-temperature regeneration than MEA
items.cost: Not reported
items.potential: The model finds enzyme activity gains cap out against CO2 diffusion in the liquid film. Only carriers below 0.35 um sit inside the film and beat the MEA benchmark; fixed-packing immobilization is 'impractical'
items.bottleneck: Enzyme stability and the diffusion ceiling. Gains are bounded by mass transfer, not by catalysis
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 and S5 (retrofit-friendly, non-toxic solvent); S11 (fewer amine degradation products)

items.name: Computational verifier stack usable by a small team (OCx24, Matbench Discovery, MOFSimBench, fairchem/UMA, OptiLex physics.py)
items.mechanism: Open benchmarks that tie ML predictions to DFT and, in OCx24's case, to experiment
items.trl_and_scale: OCx24 (Meta and partners, 2024): 572 synthesized samples, 441 gas-diffusion electrodes tested in zero-gap CO2RR/HER up to 300 mA/cm2, plus about 20,000 materials screened with 685M AI-accelerated relaxations. Matbench Discovery (Nat Mach Intell 2025): an accurate regressor can still have high false-positive rates near the hull. MOFSimBench: 20 uMLIPs benchmarked
items.energy: n/a
items.cost: Free and open source; GPU-hours
items.potential: Lets an idea engine score candidate catalysts and sorbents against an executed calculation rather than LLM judgment
items.bottleneck: The gap between predictions and experiment. OCx24's data-driven volcano re-identified Pt for HER, validating the pipeline but rediscovering a known answer
items.stakeholder_positions: S2

items.name: Failures and setbacks 2025-2026 with measured data
items.mechanism: Mixed
items.trl_and_scale: MASH Makes (biochar) went bankrupt in 2026: technically successful, halted by financing delays (CDR.fyi Aug 2026 recap). Climeworks under-delivery (item 1). MethaneSAT (methane-monitoring satellite) lost contact on 20 June 2025 and was declared likely unrecoverable on 1-2 July 2025 (Wikipedia, citing EDF/MethaneSAT and RNZ)
items.energy: n/a
items.cost: n/a
items.potential: n/a
items.bottleneck: Recurring failure mode: finance and delivery risk rather than chemistry. The mechanism still applies to current CDR start-ups. The MethaneSAT loss was a hardware/power failure and is not evidence against satellite methane monitoring
items.stakeholder_positions: S10: delivery risk is now priced in

bottlenecks: Realized DAC energy and availability: Mammoth's early operation used 5,000-6,000 kWh/t (19.8 GJ/t, about 43x the 0.465 GJ/t floor) and delivered 105 t in 10 months (0.35% of pro-rated nameplate; partially commissioned). The best lab electrochemical DAC is 2.4-4.1 GJ/t at cell or 20 cm2 scale. The bottleneck is scale-up of the low-energy chemistries, not the thermodynamic floor.
Delivery gap: 1.7 Mt delivered of 50.5 Mt contracted durable CDR (3.4%). For DAC, the sold-to-delivered ratio was 750:1 as of Aug 2024. Prepaid offtakes are financing unbuilt plants.

Price vs willingness to pay: average $337/t (CDR.fyi); DAC $500-1,200/t; buyer-supplier gap about $98/t. The May 2026 CDR.fyi pricing survey says durable CDR is unlikely to broadly reach $100/t by 2030.
Air contacting: at ppm concentrations, fan work at 100-300 Pa is comparable to the separation floor. Passive uptake (Ca2SiO4/MgO, ERW, OAE) avoids it but moves the problem to MRV.

MRV for open-system CDR: ERW measured 0.1-0.3 tCO2/ha/yr in temperate trials, 10-30x below upper modelled rates, which would need 2-6x global cropland per Gt/yr. OAE signals dilute within about 2.5 m of the outfall, or to <1-5% downstream.

Catalyst lifetime for CO2 utilization: Cu-based CO2-to-ethylene runs about 1,500 h at best and SOEC CO 2,000 h, against the roughly 40,000 h (multi-year) needed. Ethylene single-pass conversion must exceed 10%.

Electricity carbon intensity for utilization: CO2-to-ethylene takes about 34-47 MWh/t, at an assumed 2.5-3.5 V cell voltage. It cuts emissions only on grids below roughly 30-115 gCO2/kWh, so it is not a near-term mitigation lever on most grids.

AI sorbent screening validity: binding-energy rankings from DFT/ML (ODAC23) have been criticized as methodology artifacts. Sorbent screening needs process-level metrics (co-adsorption, kinetics, regeneration GJ/t, stability).
open_problems: Process-level sorbent verifier: build a cheap scorer that maps ODAC25/UMA adsorption outputs (CO2, H2O, N2, O2) to parasitic energy (GJ/t), working capacity under humid air, and regeneration temperature. Validate it against the Jin/Garcia/Smit critique and measured COF-999/COF-1000 data. This is the 'conventional core plus one imported mechanism' pattern: process modelling imported into ML screening.

O2-tolerant redox carriers for electrochemical DAC: the 2025 phenazine paper isolates the O2-sensitive species, while the 2026 MnO2 paper stays within the water window. An engine could screen redox-active molecules or oxides with DFT for pKa swing per electron, O2 inertness and solubility. The scoring target is kJ/mol against the 20.5 kJ/mol floor.

Industrial waste as passive CDR feedstock: steel slag gave field-measured removal where basalt did not (US 2026). Kanan's Ca/Mg exchange reuses cement and lime kiln know-how. Pair specific slags or kiln products with soil types and quantify removal per tonne with a geochemical model. This gives S4 (steel, cement) a revenue line and S1 a durable removal.

Utilization only where the grid is clean: build a siting and timing verifier that runs CO2 electrolysis only below the computed break-even grid intensity (about 30-115 gCO2/kWh). This could use curtailed renewables, paired with high-pressure captured CO2 to skip recompression.

MRV-first design for ERW and OAE: design deployments, such as fine-grained feedstock on acidic tropical soils or OAE at sites with fast air-sea exchange, where the signal-to-noise of measured removal is high enough to verify within 1-3 years.

Delivery-risk forecaster: use CDR.fyi and WEF sold-to-delivered data plus plant ramp curves (Mammoth: 0.35% in the first 10 months) to price delivery risk. That serves S10 and buyers, and helps decide which pathway to back.

Catalyst lifetime prediction: use OCx24-style experimental datasets to learn degradation features, such as Cu reconstruction, and screen for 10,000+ h stability rather than initial Faradaic efficiency.

Coverage gaps (WebSearch budget exhausted; sources found via the OpenAlex API and direct fetches): not verified this run were the current status of US DOE DAC hubs (Project Cypress, South Texas), Stratos start-up beyond CDR.fyi's 'end-2026' statement, Climeworks' 2025 layoffs, Running Tide's 2024 shutdown details, XPRIZE Carbon Removal results, and point-source CCS capture rates (Brevik, Boundary Dam).

key_claims.claim: Realized DAC is far below nameplate and the durable CDR market has delivered only a small share of what it sold. Climeworks Mammoth captured 105 t in its first 10 months (0.35% of pro-rated 36,000 t/yr nameplate; partially commissioned) at a CEO-stated 5,000-6,000 kWh/t. Market-wide, 1.7 Mt delivered against 50.5 Mt contracted is 3.4% (CDR.fyi, Oct 2026). Any strategy that relies on DAC volumes before about 2030 carries large delivery risk.

Lab electrochemical DAC now measures 104 kJ/mol (2.36 GJ/t, about 5x the thermodynamic floor), and an O2-tolerant MnO2 cell measures 4.1 GJ/t over more than 1,000 h. That is below the 6-10 GJ/t of liquid-carbonate DAC and far below Mammoth's 19.8 GJ/t, but only at cell or 20 cm2 scale. So capture is not thermodynamically blocked; the binding constraint is scale-up and contactor engineering.

surprises: The flagship AI sorbent dataset was publicly challenged: Jin, Garcia and Smit (ACS Cent Sci, May 2025) argue that ODAC23's recommended DAC MOFs are artifacts of the screening methodology. That is a direct warning against trusting computed binding energies as a novelty or soundness signal.
Climeworks' lifetime capture (about 2,400 t) was below its own 2023 corporate footprint (1,700 t/yr), per Heimildin citing company and Puro.earth data (May 2025).

Electricity-only electrochemical DAC in the lab (2.4-4.1 GJ/t) now beats every commercial thermal DAC energy reported in this item set. That flips the usual assumption that electrochemical routes are the long shot.

Steel slag removed CO2 in a 3-year US field trial where crushed basalt did not, so an industrial waste outperformed the canonical ERW rock. Swiss vineyard basalt gave only 0.1 tCO2/ha/yr, 10-30x below earlier upper estimates.

High-pressure CO2 electrolysis to ethylene ran for 1,500 h at 85% FE, yet still needs about 34-47 MWh per tonne of ethylene (assumed cell voltage). It cuts emissions only on grids below about 30-115 gCO2/kWh.

OCx24's data-driven volcano independently re-identified Pt for HER without Pt samples in the dataset. The AI-experiment pipeline works, but its showcase result is a rediscovery, consistent with OptiLex's 'recombination over invention' evidence.

CDR.fyi's August 2026 recap reports that Occidental's Stratos is targeting 500,000 t/yr starting at the end of 2026. If true, an oil major would be the first to operate DAC at about 14x Mammoth's nameplate.

Heimildin (15 May 2025), citing Puro.Earth registry data, reports that Climeworks Mammoth was credited with 105 t of CO2 in its first ten months of operation (from about May 2024). That is 0.35% of the full 36,000 t/yr nameplate pro-rated to 10 months (30,000 t). The plant was only partly built: at its May 2024 opening, 12 of 72 planned machines were installed.
