CEO Jan Wurzbacher said each tonne would need "up to" 5,000-6,000 kWh; this is a stated figure, not a measured one. Heimildin also reports that Orca (4,000 t/yr nameplate) captured just over 2,400 t in total from 2021 to May 2025. Across the market, CDR.fyi's live dashboard (checked Oct 2026) shows 1.7 Mt delivered against 50.5 Mt contracted cumulatively, or 3.4%. Biochar dominates the delivered tonnes, and many contracts are scheduled for delivery years from now, so this ratio measures how slowly deliveries are arriving, not a default rate. Any strategy that relies on large DAC volumes before about 2030 carries large delivery risk.
verifs.caveats:
The figures from the source are accurate: 105 t, ten months, 36,000 t/yr, 12 of 72 machines and "up to 5,000-6,000 kWh". The arithmetic also checks out: 105/30,000 = 0.35%, and 1.7/50.5 = 3.37%. The corrections are about context:

(1) The 105 t comes from the Puro.Earth registry, so it most likely counts verified, stored removals that earned credits, not everything the plant pulled from the air. Measuring it against the full nameplate overstates the shortfall, because only 12 of 72 machines were installed at opening. The fair comparison is against installed capacity, at about 2%, which is still very low.

(2) The data is old. The article is dated 15 May 2025 and covers roughly May 2024 to March 2025, so it is about 17 months old as of today. Mammoth's later output was not checked and may be higher.

(3) The energy figure is something the CEO said, as reported by Heimildin. It is not a measurement, and it is phrased as "up to".

(4) The CDR.fyi page shows no "as of" date, and a blog post dated August 2026 suggests it is current. It does not state its permanence threshold for "durable". The 3.4% is cumulative deliveries so far divided by cumulative contracts, many of which are multi-year offtakes due in the 2030s. It shows the market is early and back-loaded, not that sellers have failed to deliver. Biochar makes up most delivered tonnes, so DAC's share of deliveries is far smaller than 3.4%; I could not get the per-method split, which is behind CDR.fyi's paywall.

(5) Web search was unavailable because the session's search budget ran out. The verification therefore rests on the Heimildin primary article and the live CDR.fyi homepage. Sources: https://heimildin.is/grein/24581/ and https://www.cdr.fyi/

verifs.claim: Lab electrochemical DAC now measures 104 kJ/mol (2.36 GJ/t, about 5x the thermodynamic floor), and an O2-tolerant MnO2 cell measures 4.1 GJ/t over more than 1,000 h. That is below the 6-10 GJ/t of liquid-carbonate DAC and far below Mammoth's 19.8 GJ/t, but only at cell or 20 cm2 scale. So capture is not thermodynamically blocked; the binding constraint is scale-up and contactor engineering.
verifs.corrected_claim: Jin, Ji, Aziz, Gordon et al. (Nature Energy, online 22 Aug 2025, "Direct air capture of CO2 in an electrochemical hybrid flow cell with a spatially isolated phenazine electrode") measured 104 kJ/mol CO2 for DAC, which is 2.36 GJ/t and roughly 5x the minimum of about 19-20 kJ/mol for going from 400 ppm to pure CO2. They also measured 73 kJ/mol for simulated flue gas, which was 20% CO2 and 20% O2, and a coulombic efficiency of 99%. The 104 kJ/mol is the net electrochemical cycle work only. It comes from a 4 cm2 electrode cycled at 10 mA/cm2 for 5 DAC cycles, each with a 15 h air feed at 1 L/min, and it leaves out air-moving, electrolyte pumping and vacuum energy. The MnO2 result (4.1 GJ/t over more than 1,000 h, about 20 cm2) and the Mammoth and liquid-carbonate figures do not appear in this source and are unverified here. Because those are system-level totals, often mostly heat, comparing them with a cell-only electrical number is not like-for-like. So the cell-level electrochemistry is not thermodynamically blocked, and whether system-level energy beats incumbents is still unproven at scale.
verifs.caveats:
Source checked: the nature.com article page (the abstract was readable; the main text is paywalled) and the open Supplementary Information PDF (41560_2025_1836_MOESM1_ESM.pdf). The web-search budget for the session was used up, so I could not look up any other source.

1) The two phenazine numbers are confirmed. The abstract says 73 kJ/mol for simulated flue gas and 104 kJ/mol for DAC. 104/44.01 = 2.36 GJ/t, and the ratio to a floor of about 19.4-21 kJ/mol is about 5-5.4x, so "about 5x" holds.

2) Scale is smaller than the claim implies. SI Notes 4 and 6 give an active geometric area of 4 cm2 (a 2x2 cm CPS-CNT electrode), not 20 cm2. The anolyte was 6 mL of 1 M KCl and the posolyte was ferro/ferricyanide. DAC durability covers only 5 cycles at 10 mA/cm2 (SI Figs 22-23 and 33-34) plus a rate test from 10 to 60 mA/cm2 (SI Fig 31). That is roughly a hundred-odd hours, not 1,000 h.

3) Measured, but only cell work. SI Note 6 defines molar work as net electrical cycle work (sum of U·J·A·dt, deacidification minus acidification return) divided by ΔDIC. It excludes the peristaltic pump, air blowing (a mass flow controller supplied 1 L/min of air), and the vacuum pump. In the main DAC protocol, release went into a pure-CO2 sweep at 5 mL/min, and SI Fig 33 covers a vacuum-release variant.

4) The MnO2 4.1 GJ/t / >1,000 h claim, the "20 cm2" figure, Mammoth's 19.8 GJ/t and the 6-10 GJ/t for liquid carbonate are not in this paper. Each needs its own primary source. For reference, Keith et al. 2018 (Carbon Engineering) gave 5.25-8.81 GJ/t, mostly natural-gas heat. Mammoth's figure is unconfirmed here.

5) Comparing these numbers needs care. The electrochemical figure is electricity, which is high-exergy energy, measured for the cell alone. The incumbent figures are system totals that include contactors and fans and are mostly low-grade heat. "Below" is therefore directionally plausible but not like-for-like. The conclusion that the binding constraint is scale-up and contactor engineering is reasonable, but the source does not demonstrate it. Oxygen tolerance here comes from spatial isolation (air never contacts the reduced phenazine), not from an intrinsically O2-stable chemistry.

title: Physical, material and system limits at gigatonne scale

items.name: DAC second-law gap: about 5% efficient by energy, 12-25% by exergy if driven by low-grade heat
items.mechanism: The minimum work to capture CO2 from air at 420 ppm with 75% capture is 0.47 GJ/t (OptiLex verifier). House et al. (2011) analysed operating commercial separation and trace-gas removal systems and concluded that air capture is likely to need more than 400 kJ/mol, about 9.1 GJ/t, at a system cost of roughly $1,000/t. The IEA Net Zero Roadmap (2023) implies a similar figure: 3.3 Gt/yr of DACS needs about 30 EJ/yr, or 9.1 GJ/t. Both give about 5% second-law efficiency on an energy basis. Solid-sorbent DAC is different because its heat is low-grade. Assuming 5-8 GJ/t of heat at 85-120 C plus 1-2 GJe/t electricity, my exergy calculation gives 1.8-3.9 GJ/t of exergy, i.e. 12-25% exergetic efficiency. The floor itself is fundamental. The gap between the floor and practice is an engineering problem, and much of that gap disappears if the heat is waste heat.
items.energy: Per Gt/yr: 0.47 EJ at the floor (0.08% of world primary energy); 6 EJ at 6 GJ/t (0.97%); 9.1 EJ at 9.1 GJ/t (1.47%). At 10 Gt/yr: 0.8% / 9.7% / 14.7% of world primary energy. Fan work alone is about 0.29 GJ/t at 100 Pa pressure drop and 60% fan efficiency.
items.cost: House 2011: about $1,000/t (2011 estimate from as-built trace-gas systems). IPCC AR6 WGIII SPM C.11: DACCS at $100-300/t (medium confidence, modelled). IEA 2023: about $1,000/t for today's developed DAC technologies.
items.potential: Energy rather than physics limits scale. At 9 GJ/t, 10 Gt/yr would use about 15% of today's primary energy.
items.trl_and_scale: S-DAC is at demonstration stage and L-DAC at prototype stage (IEA NZR 2023). Operating capacity is kilotonnes per year.
items.permanence_or_durability: Durability depends on the storage route (geological or mineral).
items.bottleneck: Supply of low-carbon energy and heat. On an energy basis the gap to the floor is 10-20x; on an exergy basis it is about 4-8x.
items.stakeholder_positions: S1/S8 are wary of DAC as cover for continued fossil use. S3 backs DAC (e.g. Occidental/1PointFive) as an offset route. S5 sees DAC as a new large load.

items.name: Prudent geological storage is finite: about 1,460 Gt, roughly 39 years of today's fossil CO2
items.mechanism: Gidden et al. (2025, Nature) start from a technical storage potential of 11,800 GtCO2. They then apply risk exclusions: protected and polar areas, seismic zones, 25 km population buffers, offshore water deeper than 300 m, storage depth outside 1-2.5 km, transboundary basins and disputed territories. About 87% of the potential is excluded, leaving a 'prudent planetary limit' of about 1,460 (1,290-2,710) GtCO2. Used entirely for removal, that storage reverses only about 0.7 C (0.6-1.2 C) of warming. IPCC 1.5 C pathways need 8.7 (5.9-13) Gt/yr of storage at net zero, a 175-fold increase on today, and an average of 15 Gt/yr by 2100. At those rates the prudent limit lasts 168 and 97 years respectively (my calculation). The IPCC AR6 SPM (C.4.6) gives technical capacity 'on the order of 1000 GtCO2' and flags regional availability as a possible limit.
items.potential: 1,460 Gt prudent (1,290-2,710). For comparison, fossil CO2 in 2024 was 37.4 Gt, so the prudent limit equals about 39 years of current emissions.
items.permanence_or_durability: Well-chosen sites can permanently isolate CO2 (IPCC AR6 SPM C.4.6).
items.bottleneck: Storage is a depletable shared resource. Every tonne of storage used to keep fossil fuels running is a tonne no longer available to reverse warming. The size of the limit is set by geology plus societal risk choices, not by engineering.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 sees storage as a business line, since O&G has the subsurface skills. S1/S2 would likely argue for reserving storage for removals and unavoidable process emissions. S7/S8 face storage that is unevenly distributed across countries. S11 drives the population-buffer exclusions.
items.trl_and_scale: Storage is mature for gas processing and EOR (IPCC AR6).

items.name: Injection-rate and well-count limits: about 1,430 wells per Gt/yr
items.mechanism: Ringrose & Meckel (2019, Sci Rep) combined pore-space use, subsurface pressure limits and historic offshore well-drilling rates. Their P50 injection rate is 0.7 Mt/yr per well (P90 0.33, P10 1.06) over a 25-year life. Reaching the 2 C scenario needs 6-7 Gt/yr by 2050, about 100-120 Gt cumulative, and 10,000-14,000 injection wells. My calculation: 1 Gt/yr needs 1,430 wells at P50 or 3,030 at P90; the IPCC net-zero rate of 8.7 Gt/yr needs 12,400 (P50) to 26,400 (P90). Realized performance is mixed. Gorgon (Australia, design 3.4-4 Mt/yr) started injecting in August 2019, two years late, and stored about one-third of its CO2 in 2022-23 because of reservoir pressure management. That figure comes via Wikipedia citing Energy Intelligence and is not checked against Chevron data.
items.potential: The authors say the required wells are a fraction of the historic worldwide rate of offshore petroleum well development. A Gulf of Mexico-style build-out could reach 7 Gt/yr by 2043.
items.bottleneck: Pressure build-up, i.e. injectivity per well and per basin, is a geological constraint that varies by reservoir. The number of wells is an engineering and capital constraint.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3 and S6 have the drilling and reservoir skills, giving the O&G workforce a direct transition role. S11 raises concerns about induced seismicity and groundwater.
items.trl_and_scale: In 2019, 19 large-scale facilities captured 36 Mt/yr, and 4 dedicated offshore stores injected nearly 4 Mt/yr.

items.name: CCS growth: 45 Mt in 2022; 0.37 Gt by 2030 is the feasible upper end against 1 Gt needed
items.mechanism: IEA NZR 2023 (measured): 45 Mt CO2 was captured in 2022. The NZE scenario needs 1,024 Mt by 2030, 2,421 Mt by 2035 and 6,040 Mt by 2050, of which 1,041 Mt is DAC and 1,263 Mt is bioenergy. Even if all announced projects are built, 2030 capture reaches only about 400 Mt (roughly 40% of the 2030 need). Project lead times average about 6 years. Of the more than $8.5bn of public CCUS support offered after 2008, under 30% was spent. Kazlou, Cherp & Jewell (2024, Nature Climate Change) use historical growth of policy-driven technologies. If plans double and failure rates halve, CCS could reach 0.37 Gt/yr by 2030, given today's 0.04 Gt/yr and a historical plan-failure rate of 88%. Only 10% of mitigation pathways (4% of 1.5 C, 14% of 2 C) are feasible, and almost all feasible ones store less than 600 Gt by 2100. My calculation of compound annual growth: 16%/yr historically (about 1 Mt at Sleipner in 1996 to 45 Mt in 2022); 48%/yr needed for the NZE 2030 target; 19%/yr for 2050.
items.potential: Under feasibility constraints, less than 600 Gt cumulative by 2100. Assuming no failures and growth as fast as flue-gas desulfurization roughly doubles this.
items.bottleneck: Deployment rate and project failure. The constraint is institutional and economic, not physical: 88% historic failure rate and 6-year lead times.
items.stakeholder_positions: S3/S4 are announcing large pipelines, but only about 20 capture projects had reached FID by June 2023. S10 is exposed to the risk of project failure. S7 policy is volatile, and the 2026 SoCDR notes US policy dismantling.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 for gas processing and EOR, with about 80% of captured CO2 historically going to EOR (Wikipedia citing Nat Commun 2024). Earlier-stage in power and cement.

items.name: CDR today: 2.2 Gt/yr, 99.9% conventional; novel CDR is 2 Mt/yr against a 5.2 Gt/yr gap in 2050
items.mechanism: The State of CDR 3rd edition (June 2026, measured and inventory-based) reports total removal of 2.2 GtCO2/yr, or 5% of gross CO2 emissions, almost all from forests and soils. Novel CDR (BECCS, biochar, DACCS, ERW) is 0.002 Gt/yr, growing 40%/yr, which is similar to solar, and is dominated by biochar and BECCS. Operating plus under-construction projects would reach 0.008 Gt/yr (8.4 Mt) by 2030, and only 20% of recently planned capacity was actually built. The gap against the highest-ambition Paris scenarios is 0.3 Gt/yr in 2030, 1.2 Gt/yr in 2035 and 5.2 Gt/yr in 2050. Contracts signed last year covered 0.04 Gt. Reliable lower-bound potentials are about 1 Gt/yr per method. IPCC AR6 SPM C.3.5 gives cumulative 2020-2100 BECCS of 30-780 Gt and DACCS of 0-310 Gt in 1.5 C pathways.
items.cost: Below $10/t to over $1,000/t. Most methods have upper estimates above $200/t, which is well above carbon prices.
items.potential: About 1 Gt/yr per method at reliable lower bounds.
items.bottleneck: Demand and price: voluntary-market prices are far below novel CDR cost, and Article 6 and CORSIA prices are low.
items.stakeholder_positions: S1/S2 are wary of mitigation deterrence. S3/S4 are buyers of removals (e.g. Microsoft and Occidental contracts). S7 in the EU, UK and Switzerland is exploring inclusion in compliance markets.
items.trl_and_scale: Novel CDR is 2 Mt/yr in total.

items.name: Real DAC plants: measured LCA removal efficiency of 85-93%, but achieved throughput is far below nameplate
items.mechanism: Deutz & Bardow (2021, Nature Energy) did a life-cycle assessment of Climeworks' operating TVSA plants. Carbon capture efficiencies were 85.4% at Hinwil and 93.1% at Hellisheidi, so embodied and energy emissions take back 7-15% of gross capture with low-carbon energy. They found that scaling to 1% of global CO2 would require a large expansion of amine production. Orca (Iceland, 2021) has a nameplate of 4,000 t/yr. English Wikipedia states, without a citation, that Orca averaged about 600 t/yr, roughly 15% of nameplate; Icelandic press (Heimildin, 2025) reportedly made similar claims, which I could not fetch. Mammoth (May 2024) has a nameplate of 36,000 t/yr. German Wikipedia reports harsh-weather problems needing retrofits and links a May 2025 article on mass layoffs.
items.bottleneck: Availability and capacity factor of first-of-a-kind plants in real climates, plus sorbent supply chains.
items.trl_and_scale: Kilotonne-scale plants. The largest nameplate is 36 kt/yr (Mammoth); Stratos (500 kt/yr) has been under construction since 2023.
items.stakeholder_positions: S10 has seen a credibility hit. S1 cites underperformance as evidence that DAC is a distraction.

items.name: Learning curves are modelled, not observed: DAC costs plateau around $100-600/t by 2050
items.mechanism: Young et al. (2023, One Earth, CC-BY) combine bottom-up first-of-a-kind (FOAK) cost estimates with learning rates for 4 DACS technologies. They find costs can fall to $100-600/t, mostly through capital-cost reduction from aggressive deployment, and plateau from 2050 to 2075. That remains above the US target of $100/t. Coupling DACS to intermittent renewables generally raises costs, and grants are best spent on small early projects. The only observed DAC learning data point is Climeworks' Hinwil to Orca step. CCS has no observed cost-decline record comparable to solar or wind. Kazlou 2024 used flue-gas desulfurization, an end-of-pipe technology scaled by regulation, as the optimistic growth analogue.
items.cost: $100-600/t by 2050 (modelled). Today above $1,000/t (IEA 2023).
items.bottleneck: Too few deployed units to establish a learning rate. Projections depend on assumed learning rates and doublings.
items.stakeholder_positions: S10 needs credible cost curves before committing capital. S7 sets cost targets of $100/t (US DOE).
items.trl_and_scale: Learning-rate evidence comes from n=2 Climeworks generations.

items.name: Land: BECCS needs about 68 Mha per Gt/yr, about 49x more than DAC powered by solar PV
items.mechanism: IEA NZR 2023: capturing 2 Gt/yr from bioenergy needs feedstock from about 135 Mha, slightly less than the land area of Peru. That is about 68 Mha per Gt, or roughly 4.3% of world cropland (assumed 1,570 Mha). 3.3 Gt/yr of DACS on solar PV needs about 4.5 Mha (about the size of Denmark), i.e. 1.36 Mha per Gt. Biomass land demand is set by the low efficiency of photosynthetic energy capture, which is a near-fundamental biological limit. DAC's land need is set by PV area, which is an engineering parameter. The IEA Delayed Action Case assumes the sustainable bioenergy supply stays capped at 100 EJ.
items.potential: The IEA NZE assumes 1.26 Gt/yr of bioenergy capture in 2050. The Delayed Action Case needs 2 Gt/yr of BECCS.
items.bottleneck: Land and sustainable biomass supply for BECCS. Energy supply for DAC.
items.stakeholder_positions: S8 is concerned about land grabs and food security in the Global South. S4 (pulp, ethanol) has cheap concentrated biogenic CO2. S6 includes agricultural and forestry jobs.
items.trl_and_scale: BECCS on ethanol plants is TRL 9 at about 1 Mt/yr (e.g. Illinois).

items.name: Point-source capture is closer to the thermodynamic floor, and going from 90% to 99% capture costs almost nothing at the floor
items.mechanism: From the OptiLex verifier, floors at 90% capture are 0.22 GJ/t for gas flue (4%) and 0.155 GJ/t for coal flue (12%). Going from 90% to 99% capture raises the floor by only about 5% (gas: 0.219 to 0.231 GJ/t; coal: 0.155 to 0.166 GJ/t). Assuming amine reboiler duty of 2.6-3.5 GJ/t at about 120 C, the exergy is 0.73-0.95 GJ/t, giving 16-30% second-law efficiency. That is 3-6x better than DAC on an energy basis. The isothermal compression floor from 1 to 150 bar is 0.28 GJ/t, which is larger than the separation floor itself for coal flue gas. IPCC 2005, cited via Wikipedia, gives an energy penalty of 14-40% more coal and 11-22% more gas per unit of electricity.
items.energy: Separation 0.16-0.23 GJ/t (floor) and about 0.7-1.0 GJ/t exergy in practice (assumed). Compression floor 0.28 GJ/t, about 0.3-0.4 GJe/t in practice (assumed).
items.cost: $15-25/t for concentrated streams and $40-120/t for dilute ones (IEA 2021, via Wikipedia, not checked against the primary source).
items.bottleneck: Residual emissions at 90% design capture, and actual capture rates below design. Thermodynamics is not the constraint.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (cement) has process CO2 that cannot be abated another way. S5 faces a capacity penalty. S3 sees a natural-gas-with-CCS market.
items.trl_and_scale: TRL 9 for gas processing. About 45 Mt/yr captured globally in 2023.

items.name: Mineral storage (Carbfix-type): over 95% mineralised in under 2 years, but needs 17-27 t of water per t CO2
items.mechanism: Matter et al. (2016, Science; pilot field injection at Hellisheidi) found over 95% of injected CO2 mineralised to carbonates in basalt in less than 2 years, against the common expectation of hundreds to thousands of years. Because the CO2 is dissolved in water before injection, it is not buoyant and does not need a caprock, which widens where storage is possible. My calculation with ideal Henry's law (kH 0.034 mol/L/atm, 25 C, which overestimates solubility at high pressure) gives about 37-59 g/L at 25-40 bar, i.e. 17-27 t of water per t CO2 or 17-27 km3 per Gt. That is about 0.4-0.7% of global freshwater withdrawal (assumed 4,000 km3/yr); seawater variants are being piloted. Stoichiometric rock demand is 1.6 t olivine, 2.1 t serpentine or about 3.3 t basalt per t CO2, so each Gt of CO2 mineralised in situ consumes 1.6-3.3 Gt of rock.
items.permanence_or_durability: Permanent carbonate minerals. Leakage risk is very low after mineralisation.
items.potential: Basalt and peridotite capacity is large, but these rocks are often not co-located with emitters.
items.bottleneck: Water volume, location of reactive rock, and the 2016 pilot scale (hundreds of tonnes).
items.stakeholder_positions: S11 is more accepting because there is no buoyant plume. S8 has basalt provinces in India, Africa and South America.
items.trl_and_scale: Commercial at kt/yr scale in Iceland (Orca and Mammoth storage).

items.name: Materials at Gt scale: tonnes of rock, sorbent replacement and amine supply
items.mechanism: My calculations: stoichiometric rock demand for mineralisation is 1.6-3.3 Gt per Gt CO2, equal to 18-38% of global coal tonnage (assumed 8.7 Gt/yr). For enhanced weathering, the Beerling et al. (2024, PNAS) US Corn Belt field trial reports 10.5 +/- 3.8 t CO2/ha over 4 years from about 200 t/ha of basalt. That is about 0.05 t CO2/t rock at field level, roughly 17% of the theoretical ~0.3, implying about 19 Gt of rock per Gt CO2 before downstream losses. This figure comes from a sibling worker's script and I checked only the paper's significance statement. For solid-sorbent DAC, assuming 0.5-2 mmol/g working capacity, 2-4 cycles per day and a 0.5-2 year lifetime, sorbent replacement is 4-125 Mt/yr per Gt CO2. Deutz & Bardow 2021 state that capturing 1% of global CO2 by TVSA would need a large expansion of amine production. Realmonte et al. (2019) are cited on Wikipedia as estimating that 30 Gt/yr of sorbent DAC needs 16.3-27.8 Gt of NH3; I could not check this and the figure looks implausibly large.
items.bottleneck: Sorbent lifetime is the main materials lever: a 4x longer life cuts replacement 4x. For ERW, rock grinding and haulage scale with the roughly 19x rock-to-CO2 ratio.
items.stakeholder_positions: S4 (mining, quarrying, chemicals) gains a new market. S6 jobs in mining regions. S11 objects to dust and quarrying.
items.trl_and_scale: ERW is at multi-year field-trial stage, with tens of thousands of t CO2 credited. Sorbents are at kt scale.

items.name: Air throughput: 3.3 Gt/yr of DAC processes about 0.13% of the atmosphere each year
items.mechanism: At 420 ppm and 75% capture, each tonne needs 1.76e6 m3 of air (OptiLex verifier), or 1.76e15 m3 per Gt. 3.3 Gt/yr means 0.13% of the atmosphere's moles per year, which matches the IEA NZR 2023 statement that this would mean 'filtering 0.1% of the earth's atmosphere every year'. The contactor area and fan work (about 0.29 GJ/t at 100 Pa) are fixed by the dilution and do not fall with learning. Only lower pressure drop or passive (wind-driven) contacting can reduce them.
items.energy: Fan work 0.29 GJ/t at 100 Pa, which is 62% of the whole separation floor.
items.bottleneck: Contactor surface area and pressure drop. These are fundamental consequences of 420 ppm dilution, though the engineering response can vary.
items.trl_and_scale: IEA lists passive DAC as early-stage (<$100/t potential, unproven).

bottlenecks: Prudent geological storage is finite: about 1,460 Gt (Gidden 2025), equal to about 39 years of 2024 fossil CO2 and at most about 0.7 C of warming reversal. Fundamental (geology plus risk choices); depletion takes 97-168 years at the 8.7-15 Gt/yr rates in IPCC pathways.

Deployment rate: 45 Mt captured in 2022 against 1,024 Mt needed in 2030 (IEA NZE), i.e. 48%/yr growth versus a historical 16%/yr. The feasible upper end is 0.37 Gt by 2030 (Kazlou 2024), and historic plan failure is 88%. Institutional and economic, not physical.

Injection wells and pressure: about 1,430 wells per Gt/yr at P50 0.7 Mt/yr/well (3,030 at P90). 8.7 Gt/yr needs 12,000-26,000 wells. Gorgon stored about one-third of its design rate in 2022-23. Geological (pressure) plus capital.

DAC energy: 6-9 EJ per Gt/yr (1-1.5% of world primary energy per Gt). The floor is 0.47 GJ/t, the energy-basis efficiency is about 5%, and fan work alone is about 0.29 GJ/t. The floor is fundamental; the 10-20x gap is engineering.
Novel CDR scale: 2 Mt/yr today, a 2030 pipeline of 8.4 Mt, and a 5.2 Gt/yr gap in 2050 (SoCDR 2026). Demand and price are binding: 0.04 Gt contracted last year, with costs mostly above $200/t.
BECCS land: about 68 Mha per Gt/yr (about 4.3% of world cropland per Gt; IEA 2023). Near-fundamental because of photosynthetic efficiency.
Compression to storage pressure: the 0.28 GJ/t floor exceeds the separation floor for coal flue gas. It applies to every geological route and is fundamental for supercritical injection.

Materials: rock at 1.6-3.3 t/t CO2 stoichiometric (about 19 t/t at ERW field rates), and sorbent replacement at 4-125 Mt/yr per Gt depending on sorbent lifetime. Engineering, with lifetime as the lever.
Water for dissolved-CO2 mineral storage: 17-27 km3 per Gt (about 0.4-0.7% of global withdrawal), unless seawater can be used.
open_problems: A rule for allocating storage: a socio-technical mechanism that treats the about 1,460 Gt prudent storage as a depletable commons. It would give priority to unavoidable process CO2 (cement) and removals, and give S3 and S4 tradable, priced access, for example a carbon-takeback obligation with storage licences. This is an imported mechanism from fisheries quota and spectrum allocation, applied to a conventional CCS core.

Pressure management to raise injectivity per well and per basin. Brine extraction and co-production (lithium or desalination brines) could cut the 1,430-wells-per-Gt requirement and the Gorgon-type underperformance. This would reuse S3 and S6 reservoir skills and workforce.

Matching DAC to waste heat: exergy accounting says S-DAC on 85-120 C waste heat reaches 12-25% second-law efficiency rather than 5%. Map global low-grade industrial and geothermal waste heat against the 6-9 EJ needed per Gt, and test which co-locations (refineries, steel mills, data centres) cut the net cost.

Avoiding the compression floor: capture or mineralise at low pressure, as with Carbfix dissolved injection or surface mineralisation. Quantify the trade-off between the 0.28 GJ/t compression floor and the 17-27 t of water per t CO2.

Closing residuals with 99% point-source capture instead of later DAC: going from 90% to 99% raises the floor only about 5% at the point source, while DAC removal of the same residual costs 2x the floor and 10-20x in practice. Build an engineering-cost model (column height, solvent) to find the economic optimum capture rate.
Sorbent lifetime as the main Gt-scale materials lever (4-125 Mt/yr of sorbent per Gt). Ageing-resistant sorbents, and measured degradation data from operating plants, are an open problem.

That limit allows at most about 0.7 C of warming reversal if it is used only for removals. IPCC 1.5 C pathways need 8.7 (5.9-13) Gt/yr of storage at net zero.

Kazlou, Cherp & Jewell (2024, Nature Climate Change) use historical growth and failure rates of policy-driven technologies. They find CCS could reach at most about 0.37 GtCO2/yr by 2030, from 0.04 Gt/yr today with an 88% historic plan-failure rate. Only 10% of mitigation pathways are feasible, and virtually all feasible ones store less than 600 GtCO2 by 2100.

surprises: Compression is the bigger floor. Ideal isothermal compression of CO2 to 150 bar has a floor of 0.28 GJ/t, which is more than the minimum separation work from coal flue gas (0.16 GJ/t) and about the same as from gas-turbine flue (0.22 GJ/t). For point sources, the irreducible cost lies more in getting CO2 into the ground than in separating it.

Near-total point-source capture is thermodynamically almost free. At 4% CO2 the floor rises only from 0.219 to 0.231 GJ/t between 90% and 99% capture, so residual emissions are an engineering and cost choice, not a physical one.

The '5% efficient DAC' headline depends on the accounting basis. On an exergy basis, solid-sorbent DAC driven by 85-120 C heat is 12-25% efficient (my assumed inputs), so waste-heat pairing closes much of the apparent 10-20x gap.

The IPCC AR6 SPM's 'on the order of 1000 GtCO2' technical capacity is smaller than Gidden et al.'s prudent 1,460 Gt after exclusions, which itself comes from 11,800 Gt technical. The headline numbers rest on different bases and should not be compared directly.

Novel CDR is growing at 40%/yr, matching solar's early growth, yet stands at only 2 Mt/yr. Even solar-like growth reaches only about 1.1 Gt by 2045 (SoCDR 2026 chart), far short of 1.5 C needs of several Gt/yr.

My independent calculation reproduced the IEA's statement that 3.3 Gt/yr of DAC means filtering about 0.1% of the atmosphere per year (I get 0.13%). This is a useful sanity check that the verifier and the IEA energy figures are consistent.

Historic CCS growth from Sleipner in 1996 to 45 Mt in 2022 averaged 16%/yr, close to the 19%/yr needed to reach the IEA's 2050 level. The 2030 milestone (48%/yr) is the implausible part, which suggests the binding constraint is near-term ramp speed rather than end-state size.

verifs.caveats:
Checked against the full text of the primary source: Gidden, M.J. et al., Nature 645, 124-132, published 3 Sep 2025, open access under CC-BY. Every number in the claim matches. The caveats below concern wording and how the figures should be used.

(1) The paper calls 11,800 GtCO2 the "initial global physical storage potential", not "technical potential". Risk layers cut it by about an order of magnitude, to 1,460 GtCO2. About 70% of that is onshore and 30% offshore. The figures are modelled, spatially explicit, risk-based estimates, not measured capacity.

(2) The 0.7 C is a modelled cap on "total warming that can ever be sustainably reversed", assuming all 1,460 Gt goes to durable removal. It uses the IPCC central TCRE of 0.45 C per 1,000 GtCO2 and assumes the climate responds symmetrically to negative emissions. The abstract's range is 0.35-1.2 C, covering storage and climate-response uncertainty. The main text gives 0.6-1.2 C when only exclusion-criteria uncertainty is counted. At the low end of the TCRE likely range (0.27 C per 1,000 Gt), the reversal is only about 0.4 C (0.35-0.7 C). The authors say even this overestimates real-world reversal because residual emissions persist. Any storage used for fossil CCS reduces the removal budget one for one. So "at most about 0.7 C" is the central estimate, not a hard ceiling.

(3) The 8.7 (5.9-13) GtCO2/yr refers to AR6 scenario-database pathways that limit warming to 1.5 C with no or limited overshoot (C1), at net-zero CO2, which arrives around 2050-2055. These are modelled scenario outputs. The paper notes this is a 175-fold increase over today and comparable to current global crude-oil production. It also notes that most IPCC scenarios stay within 50% of the limit at net zero, but nearly all would exceed it before 2200. "Need" slightly overstates it: these are injection rates the scenarios use, not physical requirements.

(4) The paper also finds that the countries most robust to the risk assessment are current large fossil extractors. This is relevant to the user's goal of satisfying high-carbon industries.

(5) The 18 Nov 2025 update only replaced a duplicated Supplementary Fig. 2b. It did not change these numbers.

verifs.corrected_claim: Kazlou, Cherp & Jewell, "Feasible deployment of carbon capture and storage and the requirements of climate targets", Nature Climate Change 14, 1047–1055 (published online 25 Sep 2024), project CCS growth using reference cases: historical CCS plans and failure rates, and the growth of other technologies (wind, solar, nuclear, flue-gas desulfurization). The paper puts operational CCS at about 0.04 GtCO2/yr today. CCS projects from 1972 to 2018 failed at an 88% rate, and at that rate today's plans give only about 0.07 Gt/yr by 2030. The paper estimates a 76% failure rate for the current, more diversified pipeline. Its "upper feasible bound" for 2030 is 0.37 Gt/yr. That bound is a modelled, optimistic scenario: planned capacity doubles between 2023 and 2025, and the failure rate falls to 45%, the rate for early US nuclear plans. The paper gives the realistic 2030 range as 0.07–0.37 Gt/yr. That is below the IPCC AR6 1.5°C median of 0.9 Gt/yr and around the 2°C median of 0.3 Gt/yr. Only 10% of IPCC AR6 C1–C4 pathways (14% of 2°C pathways, 4% of 1.5°C pathways) meet all the CCS growth-feasibility constraints. Virtually all of those store less than 600 GtCO2 by 2100 (95th percentile), against up to about 1,400 Gt in the unvetted pathways. Under less realistic relaxed assumptions (zero plan failures, growth like flue-gas desulfurization), the figure rises to about 1,100 Gt.
verifs.caveats:
I checked this against the full text at nature.com (DOI 10.1038/s41558-024-02104-0). The numbers 0.37, 0.04, 88%, 10% and <600 Gt are all correct. The errors are in framing:
(1) 0.37 Gt/yr is not a forecast. It is an optimistic modelled ceiling that assumes the plan pipeline doubles and failures roughly halve to US-nuclear levels. Under the historic 88% failure rate, the paper's figure for 2030 is 0.07 Gt/yr.
(2) The 88% is a historical rate for 1972–2018, when failed plans were mostly power-sector projects (over 90% failure). The paper's estimate for today's plans is 76%. The claim's wording runs "0.04 today" and "88%" together, as if 0.04 to 0.37 happens under 88%. It does not.
(3) "Only 10% of mitigation pathways are feasible" overstates the finding. The 10% are the pathways (IPCC AR6 categories C1–C4) whose CCS growth meets the paper's feasibility constraints. The paper does not judge any pathway infeasible on other grounds.
(4) The <600 Gt limit is a 95th-percentile figure. Under relaxed (FGD-like, zero-failure) assumptions it rises to about 1,100 Gt.
(5) Scope: this paper is about deployment-rate and institutional feasibility (plans, failure rates, growth analogues). It says nothing about the thermodynamic efficiency or cost of capture, so it should not be cited as evidence that capture is physically inefficient. The data run to about 2022–2023, and pipeline changes since then (for example under the US 45Q credit or in Norway and the UK) are not reflected.
